PEARL LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. ANNUAL REPORT AND STATEN! ENT OF ACCOUNTS For the year ending 31st December, 1891. Presented at the Twenty-eighth Annual General Meeting, held at the Offices of the Company, London Bridge. City, 8.0.. Friday. February. 19th. 1892. It is with great satisfaction your Directors present thi• year's Report and Statement of Accounts. Notwithstanding the grave depression in the general trade of the country and tho serious and heavy mortality resulting from the Influenza epidemic, it will be very gratifying to the Shareholders to know that the Company has made satisfactory progress, both as regards Premium Income and the increase in its Reserve Fund. . . . . . . _

The Actuaries, Messrs.Rothery and Ryan,having completed the Valuatim of the liabilities of the Company as at 31st December, 1890; the Directors are able to declare with their full concurrence, a Reversionary Bonus of £1 per cent. on the Participating Policies in the Ordinary Branch of the Com- pany. NEW POLICIES.-431,911 Policies were issued during the above period, representing a new Annual Premium Income of '£191,911 Bs. Id. INCOME—The total income for the year amounted to £320, 405115. 40. PREMIUMS—DECEMBER. IE9I —The Premium Income, on the Policies in force on the Company's books in December last amoupted to £343.914 19s. Id., which, it may be confi- dently hoped, will be well sustained during the presentyear. CLAIMS.— The Company has paid 20.085 claims and grants during the year amounting to £146,029 6s. 100. which, added to the sums previously paid in claims since the estab- lishment of the Company, makes a total of £983,819 15s. Od. ASSURANCE FUND.—The Life Assurance Fund has been Increased during the year by £20,332 14s. 40., and the Assur- ance Fund, with capital paid up, now amounts to £284,131 125.34. . .

STAFF.—A considerable addition has been made to our staff of Superintendents, Assistant-Superintendents, and Collec- tors, during the past twelve months, many srf whom have proved themselves very efficient in sustaining and extending the business of the Company. Div DENn.—The Directors recommend that a dividend of KI per cent, be paid on Monday next, 22nd inst. The Direct°, sretiring this year are Messrs. Theasby and Moullin, who, being eligible, offer themselves for re-election. It is with the most painful sorrow and regret your Directors have to record the sudden death of the venerated Chairman of the Company (the late Mr. Keene), from the effects of the present epidemic. To fill the seat vacant at the Board they recommend Mr. G. Shrnbsall, a gentleman who has done excellent service for the Company during the part 21 years. The Company's Auditors, Messrs. James and Hall, also over themselves for re-election.

The thanks of the Directors are due to the Company's Staff for the success of the past year. and they hope to be able to conglatulate the Shareholders at the end of each suraTeding year on the still greater progress made by the Company.—By Order, P. J. FOLEY, Managing Direotor.

DUD inen's tales—Wills. A fraLLEN star—A dismiseed policeman. A onssnow of time—Theerection of Tab& - clocks. Die Baltimore teller is not_ - always inclined to tell. - - A NOTE of warning—People who steal watches, are apt to wind up in jail. A LAWYER is not necessarily a sensible DIM because he always stands to reason. ; THZ cowboy poet recently discovered in, Wyoming is to be called the poet lariat. Is there any creature that has its toes behind fi Yes, a tug' its tows are always behind. IT may seem pe.radoxical, but it is nevertheless true, that floating debts will sink a corporation. A WESTERN GENTLEMAN advertises for a self- supporting wife. A CLOSE GLASS BOOKCASE once provoked from Dr. Drake the remark that he never could stand "Locke on the Human Understanding." THE man who robs a clothes line Is not necessarily a laundryman, but he generally "takes In" washing, and he is likely to be ironed if he is caught. "JOHN, what is the best thing to feed a parrot on?" asks an elderly lady of her bachelor brother, who hated parrots. "Paris green," gruffly answered John. WOMAN has maey advantages over man; one of them is that his will has no operation till he is dead, whereas hers generally takes effect in her lifetime. THE Japanese say—" A man takes a drink; then the drink takes a drink, and next the drink takes the man." Evidently the Japanese "have been there." THE man in the moon aiwaa s smiles, and he I ought to. He is the only fellow who can stay out all night without excitiug anything but favourable comment. A YOUNG MAN mice(' his sweetheart if she had ever read "Romeo ajid Juliet." She replied that she had read Romeo, but she did not think she had ever read Juliet. "AN Old Settler Gone," read Dr. Bolus in the obituary columns of the local paper, and then he added, thoughtfully: "Well, Benks may have been an old settler in one sense, but he always managed to forget to settle with me." PROFESSOR CRAM calls a primrose "a corol- linoral dicotyledonous exogen, but he wouldn't do it if the primrose was able to hit back. Some men are terribly overbearing towards the weak. " You had better ask for manners than for money," said a dandy to a beggar. "I asked for what I thought you had most of," was the keen retort. "Humra 1" said the deacon, as he looked into the contribution box after passing it round— " Humph I This is rather a catch-penny affair l" TEACHER (to pupil)—"lf you were president of a county fair and wanted a gate-tender, what would you do ?" Pupil—"l'd boil it tender." LITTLE FLAYPN HArc.--"Papa, it's raking." Papa (somewhat annoyed by work in hand)— "Well, let it rain." Little Flaxen Hair (timidly) —"I was going to." "I HEAR that young Mr. Philkins is very ill," said Mrs. Joggins. "Yes, poor fellow," replied Mrs. Snooper; "he leads such a sedimentary life that his health is shattered." Finer CONNOISSEUR—" There is a certain ingenu- ousness about the picture that I admire exceed- ingly." Second Connoisseur—" It is certainly artless, if that's what you mean." "I SAY, Jenkins, can you tell a young, tender chicken from an old, tough one ?" "Of course I can." " Well, how ?" "By the teeth." "Chickens have no teeth." "No; but I have." A YOUNG correspondent wants to know : " What is the critical period in a man's life ?" "Well, my boy, it usually begins about six weeks after he is married, and lasts some time." A FARMER said—" One thing I don't like about city folks—they be either so stuck up that yer can't reach 'em with a pole or so blamed friendly that they forget to pay their board." "I BEGAN with nothing," boasted a millionaire who had made his money in crooked ways. "And that is the condition in which you have left those who dealt with you," was the blunt response of a bystander. It is not always advisable to exhibit our best traits, even to a police officer. For instance—The boy who clandestinely entered a garden, and made away with some of the ripening fruit, was arrested for his pluck. Two students ring a hated Professor's bell at midnight. Ho puts his head out of the window and wants to know what's up. "One of your windows is wide open." " Where r exclaimed the startled Professor. "The one you are looking out of." ON a wet day a number of persons took shelter in Rowland Hill's chapel during a heavy shower, While he was preaching. Hill remarked, "Many people are greatly to be blamed for making their religion a cloak, but I do not think those are mach better who make it an umbrella." A COMPOSITOR at Sydney is supposed to have died a violent death the day before Christmas. The editor wrote, "Old Gifts in New Lights," and and it appeared in print, "Old Girls in New Tights." The compositor is supposed to have mis- taken the editorial for an article on the ballet. CHILD, at Washington—" Who are all those men lounging around outside the capitol?" Parent— " They are United States senators, my child." "Are there any more senators besides them?" "Only one." Where is he?" "He in inside making a speech." A GENTLEMAN said to one of his friends that for some years his wife persisted in saying that she was only twenty years old. "Mine is more reason- able," replied his friend. "I have succeeded in making her enter her thirties; but I have failed to make her come out of them." AT a street corner up town is a blind man who carries a board upon his breast with this singular sign: "Blind by Birth and by Accident." "See here, my good man," said a passer-by, "your sign is positively distracting. Can you tell us how you happen to be blind by birth and by accident at the same time ?" "Easy enough," said the old man. "You see, I'm blind by birth myself, and I've bought out a blind man who did business round the opposite corner. He was blind by accident." Burnham You No's 117 children were taught to sing "Father, dear father, come home," one sing- ing the solo, while the other 116 joined in the chorus, until each one bad successively given a tug at their father's domestic affections. The chorus tears Brigham's tender vitals to finders. WHEN preaching at St. John's, Wapping, on one occasion, observing that his auditory was un- usually large. and made up chiefly of seafaring persons, Rowland Hill remarked "I am come to preach to great sinners, notorious sinners, profane sinners," aud, with peculiar emphasis, exclaimed "yea, to Wapping sinners." HERE is a bit of conscious rustic wit. John Mann had been sent by his shrewish wife to market to sell the pig. Oa toe way he got drunk, the pig strayed and never turned up again. A few weeks afterwards John was asked if he had "heard anything of the pig yet." An American /recently met at Rome an old schoolfellow whom he had not seen for years, "You here ?" "Yes, y dear fellow; I have just been married, and am me to spend the hom y moon in Italy." "And your wife?' "My wife? Oh, I left her in New York 1" "You have the advantage of me," said the old merchant, blandly. " Ton will have to get some one to identify you." •• Id..ordfy me ? "hut my son did not look like a fool, wear 1 monkey-tail coat, skin-tight pants, and toothpick shoes, nor did he su,k cane-handles. Sir William Harcourt on Tuesday received a let- ter irom Mr. Gladstone in which he announced his intention of being in town at the end of the week. He heipes to be in his place in the House of Com- mons•da Monday next.

I hear that the succession to Colonel H. S. Olcott in the presidency of the Theosophical Society will devolve upon Mr. William Q. Judge, president and general secretary of the American section of the Society, who is at present in the United States. Sir William Farmer,the co-sheriff of Sir Augustus Harris, has let Cowarth Park, Sunningdale, to Mr. Andrew Carnegie for three months. Mr. Carnegie, who is now in the States, will come to England next month and take up his residence at Sunning- dale until Midsummer. The "New York World" says Sir William Gor- don-Cumming is on the point of adopting the free Republic as his home, and that he will there find lots of friends—the Schencks, the Crosbys, the Mays Randolphs, ard lowlands—in fact." all the yacht- ing crowd." All this is probably news to Sir William. ap-

Young Lord Blandford, in behalf of whom the plication was made on Tuesday to compel the Duke of Marlborough to contribute more towards his support, is at present being educated at Cam- bridge, Be will be twent3 -one on 13 Nor. of this year. He is a pale weak-looking, young man of quiet habits and some promise.

I lave an interesting addition to the stories co n cerning Cardinal Manning. This, perhaps, is the \more important in that it gives us the Cardinal's own description of his political faith. "Goodbye . give my love to your Archbishop," he remarked to a' distinguished visitor from Thurles College; " he and I are two honest Radicals."

In Tuesday night's" Gazette" notices the titles of the new Peers are disclosed. Sir Frederick Roberts is now "Baron Roberts of Kandahar, in Afghanistan, and the city of Waterford ; " Sir Arthur William Acland Hood is " Baron Hood, of Avalon, in the county of Somerset ; " and Sir William Thomson is " Baron Kelvin,of Largs, in the county of Ayr."

Mr. De Cobain is remarkable in appearance; he is medium-sized, stout even to corpulence, brown, sandy hair, scrupously divided at the middle of his head, brown eyes, slight whiskers, and sallow com- plexion. He always wore in the llouse a double- breasted frock coat, which was invariably closely buttoned, and he never either winter or summer was without a white carnation in his breast, which was quite as conspicuous as Mr. Chamberlain's now forsaken orchid.

Dr. Boyd, principal,of Hertford College and Vice- Chancellor of the University of Oxford, who has been just chosen to represent Oxford at the ter-1 centenary of Trinity College, Dublin, is one of the most popular among dons both with his fellows and with under-graduates. Well stricken in years, but still hale and hearty, Dr. Boyd presents a fine type of old English gentleman, and it is long since there has been a vice-chancellor whose robes of office have sat more becomingly upon him.

A young gentleman strayed on Tuesday night into the smoking-room of the House of Commons speci- ally reserved for members, and entered into close converse for a moment or two with a Tory county member. The "stranger " seemed quite at ease, al- though the fact that he wore an overcoat, carried an umbrella, and, had gloves, proved that he was not" at home" in the House. It sulosequertly tran- spired that he was a person who could never be, at any time, a member of the House of Commons, as he is a peer of the realm who bears the immortal name of Byron.

Theatrical advertisements are often very amusing reading, but here is one of a tragi-comical nature. It has been inserted in a contemporary by a clever young actor, and reads thus :—" Mr. concluded ten weeks highly successful engagement at the T, R. London Hospital, as leading man in the exciting drama, entitled, ' Typhoid; or, tne Theatre Drains, preceded by the laughable farce' 'Seven weeks on Milk ; or, Sneci Outdone.'" This light-hearted mode of celebrating one's recovery from a serious illness is quite remarkable, and yet there is a grim irony underlying the jest. —.......

Rather a good story of Canon---, a popular London clergyman, is going the rounds, says a gossip. He was having a friendly game of billiards at the Squire's. The Canon lost a "life," and took from his pocket a threepenny piece to pay for it. " 01)," said Barrister Wigsby,another of the guests. "I see, Canon, you have had your finger in theplate." The Canon drew himself up to his full height (a good six feet), and looking the man of law, full in the face, said, "I'm surprised that you,Mr. Wigsby in the presence of this respectable company, have the audacity to recognise your own paltry con- tribution."

M. Maurice Rouvier, Minister of Finance in the late French Cabinet, who has been entrusted by M. Carnot with the formation of anew ministry,is not a novice at the work, having been Premier from May to December, 1887. Since his marriage six months ago, he has occupied the Ministerial apart- ments at the Louvre. Amongst the eleven out- going Ministers the only one who will not have to remove to his private dwelling should he not again be entrusted with a portfolio is M.de Freycinet, the recent Premier,who lives with his `wife and daugh- ter at Passy, and only uses the Ministry in the Rue Saint-Dominique for official dinners and as an office.

Costebella—a name which is likely to become familiar to the English public within the course of the next month—is the place that has been chosen by the Queen for her residence. in the South of France. It is a beautiful hill, which rises from the plain midway between ilyeres and the Mediter- ranean, healthy owing to the proximity of the sea and the fragrance of pine forests, and famed for the ruins of medieval chateaux and the abundant traces of long-vanished Roman towns. The hotel in which are the royal apartments is situated on the south side of the hill, at some distance below the Ermitage, a church with a tall steeple sur- mounted with a statue of the virgin, which is visible for miles around and forms a centre for the pil- grimages of the superstitious natives, who have covered the walls of the interior with their votive offerings.

Truth says :—The following is the truth about the " Speaker "controversy :—When Lord Beacons- field resigned in April, 1880, he advt'sed the Queen to send for Lord Hartington, on the ground that he had been for some years the de jure leader of the Liberal party. Lord Beaconsfield was really anim- ated by a malicious wish to place obstacles in the way of Mr. Gladstone by creating jealousies and difficulties. Lord Hartington declined to make any attempt to form a Government, and he very pro- perly advised the Queen to send at once for Mr. Gladstone. Lord Beaconsfield resented this action of Lord Hartington's, and, during the remainder of his life, he frequently jeered and sneered at him, describing him as being "hare-hearted " and " cowardly" for having, as he absurdly expressed it," deserted his Sovereign when she had demanded his strviees."

Mrs. Gertude Master, who receives .f.. 5,000 under the will of the late Hon. Algernon Grey Tollemache, is the wife of Mr. J. 11. Master, J.P., of Montrose House, Petersham, and the intimate friend and "right hand "of the Duchess of Teck. Mr. and Mrs. Master are extremely wealthy, and a kind-hearted, charitable couple. They built a pretty mission-room in Petersham, and a few cases of genuine necessity appeal to them in vain. Mrs. Master has been con- nected with the management of the Princess Mary Adelaide Training Home for Servants since its foundation and it was through her influence that the Hon. Algernon Tollemache bought and presented the present premises occupied as the Home on Richmond green. Mr. J. H. Master is one of the Richmond magistrates. The daughters are extremely musical, and give entertainments to the villagers at the Petersham mission-room.

In last year's division on the Welsh Disestablish- ment question there was an attendance of 438 m mbers, and the majority against the motion was 32. In Tuesday night's division 487 members took part, and the resolution was rejected by a majority of 47. Several Dissentient Liberals were absent, and those in attendance did not act together. Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. T. W. Russell, and Mr. Powell Williams were amongst those who voted in the minority for the resolution, whilst Sir Henry James Mr. Parker Smith, Mr. Finlay, Mr. Fraser Mackin- tosh, and Mr. Coghill voted with the Government in the majority. Eighty members paired on the

Welsh Disestam", Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Chit, Samuel Smith (who, on unable to remain in the House after moving his resolution), and the Hon. C. B. Spencer, being, amongst those piked against the Government.

. One of the most remarkable episodes which has co( a connection with the great opium ques- tion is the recent" declaration of opinion " by over five thousand medical men of England, Scotlaad,and Ireland denouncing, first, the habit of opium smoking or of opium eating as morally and physi- cally debasing ; second,its unrestrained sale in India as a grave danger and evil; third, recommending its sale in India as in England by chemists only; and fourth, recommending that the Government of India should prohibit the growth of the poppy and sale of opium, except as required for medical pur- peses. This memorial ought to give the death-blow to the controversy as to the advantages or disad- vantages from a medical point of view of opium- eating or smoking, as a considerable number of the signatories have have had experience of India or China, and some of them have had long and ample opportunity of watching the effects of the opium habit. England, Scotland, and Ireland are alike represented, and the declaration is most emphatic and unhesitating, ,ti.s.;r:ell as strikingly spontaneous.

AO had come down to the vil- lage tc; see the . „ unireithe care of Mrs. Ai the housekeeper—was taken in, before the banqu.... -6-6—ninienbed, to view the whore as it looked_.ere attack upon it laid it in ruins, and it vanished. before the hearty appetites of the assembled Os* like snow before the summer sunshine. - And Lady Callerley won Bessie Carr's heart by praising everything indiscriminately, and insisting upon tasting a thin piece of the bride cake, and having a sip of the exceedingly strong punch corn: pounded by the groomsman, Jim Craster, whose proper function this was. Silvia was exceedingly amused by the whole scene. She drank the health. of the bride and bridegroom right merrily, and wished there was a wedding in the village once a week. Everyone laughij at this. "Who will be the next, I Wonder ?" she said, "Bell, my girl, why don't you follow your brother's example, and keep the wedding in this
net:l'

fashion ?" Bell, who was look frg very handsome in her muslin gown, with its pattern of moss rosebuds, blushed at this sudden attack. • Silvia, who had no idea that her random shaft would strike home with euch certain aim, merrily laughed at the confusion it had caused: • - "We'll be able to tell. ye who'll be the next " couple when the posset's-saten and the stockin's thrown !" remarked Bessie Carr, alluding to certain wedding customs whioli *ere: 'kept Up amongst the fisher folks. : She did not wish to draw'attention to Bell's love affair. Dick Daglish had hot yet put in an appear- ance, and Bessie hciped that nothing unpleasant had happened; no scrimmage with the coastguard, or anything of that sort, •to account for his pro- longed absence. Lady Callerley was exceedingly wishful to wait and'see some-of the dancing—more especially as it was rumoured„ that two of the oldest inhabitants of the village were to be egged on to perform various stepdances, for which they had been famous half , a century ago-but Jack Breamish, who had come .to ioin in the festivity as one of the most popular men in the neighbOurhood, very shrewdly guessed that Sir Lancelot would not approve of this delay. . Besides, when the drink had circulated freely, a lady's presence would not be desirable. It would be much better for Silvia to leave before the rougher sort of foaling began • So, all unwillinglY, Silvia *as induced to go without seeing the commencement of the ball. A whisper to Mrs. Moor was sufficient: for that sensible woman. The housekeeper had herself been to many a rustic weddinglottrty;laiid- Inew, only too well what lay iii the future; what licence' of speech and action when the ' blood got heated and the tongues loosened. Lady Callerley had scarcely deigned to notice the fact of Jack's presence, so he could not advise bar on the point himself; besides, it was a delicate matter to do so, though easy enough to manage through a third party, and one of Mrs. Moor's age and gravity. "Well, well, since it must be so, I shall have to submit I" said Silvia, -pettishly; then turning to Bell, she whispered, "but when you are married, Bell, I shall certainly stay to have one dance," remember that !" •

CHAPTER XVII. A HANDSOME COUPLE. When Lady Callerley and her attendant left the Inn, the former felt strongly reluctant and unwill- ing to rettuln home immediately. It was a calm, sweet summer evening, and the chakm of the hour fell upon her spirit. She lin- gered, therefore, and looked pensively over the bank at the little harbour, lying so still and peace- ful under the sunset light. Within shelter of the two rough stone piers the fleet of fishing boats lay moored. The water, lapping gently against the sea wall just below, had a pleasant and dream-like sound. It ought certainly' to have awakened nothing but gentle and dream-like echoes in Silvia's breast. Instead of this, however, a sudden resolution sprang td life there which was anything but gentle , and dream-like. i .

Yes, her opportunity had come at last, and she muat.seize and make the best of it. What would Lancelot say? If Lancelot chose to treat her in an unkind and suspicious manner, and to shut her out from his confidence, why, he must not blame her for finding out things for herself. Besides, there was no need • that he Should kpow anything about it. As Lady Callerley --debated within herself the rights and the wrongs of the plan she had made, the twilight stole over the scene before her. A cool air breathed ,in from the sea, and the ,ripples changed their lines of gold and "opal to darker and more sober tints, though overhead the sky still retained its brightness. Far away on the horizon glimmered two or three tiny specks of fire. These marked the spots where those of the salmon fishers who had been able to re- sist the temptation to frolic presented by the wedding, had gone instead to keep their night watches upon the deep. The road leading up the village street was steep and uneven, and as Silvia picked her way amongst the heaps of refuse thrown in the Futter, afier the manner of the people who lived there, she stumbled over some rough stones, and would Inevitably have fallen had not Jack Breamish sup- ported her. He had followed her out, and now walked by her side. Ratner to his surprise, she scarcely thanked him, put aside his prof erred arm, and behaved altogether in such a cool and lofty manner as perfectly to be- wilder the poor young man, and to set him wonder- ing what could he possibly have done to offend her. Lady Callerley was a creature of impulse, or she would certainly never have chosen this stupid way of resenting Madam's insinuations. It had shocked and revolted her to find that Mrs. Breamish should have dared even to hint at any such impropriety. Had she known how far beyond all this Madam's malice ventured, and would venture, things would have been different in the future. But she ought at least to have been just, and to have considered the pain which her cold manner gave to one who , had certainly never done anything to deserve such , treatment at her hands.

It was not until long afterwards, however, that she recalled the sad, wistful, puzzled expression which crept into poor Jack's eyes at her frigid words and looks. When the Widdrington's cottage was reached, Lady Callerley stopped. "lam going in to visit old Nanny, Mr. Breamish, and must wish you a good evening," she said, with a stately bow, and Jack took his dismissal with grave dignity, too proud to ask for an explanation. There was, therefore, nothing better for him to do than to return to the festive scene, and amid the sounds of mirth and revelry endeavour to forget the soreness produced by an undeserved snubbing. The ballroom was brilliantly illuminated by candles stuck in tin sconces around the walls, and at one end Blind Davy, a strolling fiddler, much in request for his powers of endurance, was perched upon a high seat, improvised for the occasion from a barrel with a plank placed across it. He was ready to begin with the reels and jigs and country , dances as soon as ever the company were all ' I assembled. There were few seats, because the majority came to dance, not to look on; but a form was placed behind the door, where some of the elder members of the community were accommodated. There the expressionless wooden countenance of old Carr, expressionless, save for a pair of light grey eyes that twinkled out from a mass of wrinkles like the phosphorescence from a midnight sea, might be seen, aide by side with Willy Graeey and Betty Beldon, the ancients of the village, who had been drawn thither and induced to promise the attempt at their step dances by the prospect of un- limited toddy. The dour face of Cuddy VViddling- ton, too, was now and then visible, as he hovered about the entrance, restless and miserable. Time I Was when he had not himself disdained to take part in such pleasant frivolities as country dances, and when the mischievous speeches of some rural •oquette or other had brought a softer look into his ziowing eyes, but since his religious tendencies had leveloped properly such gatherings were shunned as sinful, and leading straight to perdition. Why everything that was happy and gay must needs also be wicked he would have found it diffi- ,mlt to say, like many others of his creed ; but the Calvinistic theory of Salvation was the only one that held ground at that time, and all else was dust and ashes. But when Bill made a point of his elder brother's presence, the latter who in his heart of hearts loved the merry, free-spoken, dare-devil youngster better than augbt else in the world, could not refuse.

div.head: – BRAG'S SHOOTING PARTY.
div.p: - BRAG'S SHOOTING PARTY.

BY JOHN' ALMOND. It was a fine day—one of the few wonders which aappened in '9l—and I decided to have a stroll in the country, and look up my old friend Dicky Ed- minson. Dicky is, and always has been a character, and is well known at " Th' Cottom's " as is the water spout in the hedge which supplies the village with the wherewithal to dilute its whisky—l mean to make its herb beer, its coffee, and its tea with. It was a fine day, ten days or so before Christraas, and I footed it merrily towards" Childer Nook," where, for anything I knew to the contrary, my old friend yet resided, for I had neither met him, nor heard from him, owing to a very serious illness which nearly did for me--for many months. It was a fine day, as I have said before and when I arrived at the cottage I found his highness of the snuffy-name *sitting in the porch quietly puffing away at a long churchwarden, seemingly in the best of health and enjoying himself, and looking not a day older than when I had last seen him. It was a fine say, but having known Dicky so long and so intimately, and having so shamefully neg- lected him for some time past I was not quite sure whether my reception would be in accordance with the brightness of the atmosphere, or whether there would be some clouds knocking about which would wane clearing away before the comparison could be fairly established. However there was I, and and there was Dicky, so I advanced and said" Good morning, Dicky," as nearly in the old way in which I had been used to address him as I.ossible. He took his pipe from his mouth and resting one hand on one knee, raised his

other as if to shade his eyes. " Well "—he said—' aw spooase as id's manners to say good mornin' to them as says sooa to yo', even iv yo' doarned know em, 3ooa good mornin' to yo' whoever yo' are, and aw hooap as yo're weel." I could see by the lurking twinkle in his eyes that the old fellow knew me quite well, and was only, as he would have put it, " hevin' me on" a bit, so I said "And so you don't know me? Perhaps your eye- sight is beginning to fail you, or your memory is getting dull. You used to know me, Dicky." I knew that would fetch him, for he was proud of both eyesight and memory, both of which were certainly wonderful for a man of his age, especially the memory, which I have known to be even of 3a

stretchable nature. " Aw once knew a chap as wer varra like thee, as used to come smokin' mi bacca, and drinkin' mi whis—hem ! mi herb beer, and geddin mi to tell' tales sooa as he could put em it papper—dash his cheek." And then with almost the alacrity of a " young-en" he sprang from his chair and grasping both my hands with such force that he smashed his pipe into "smithereens "and all but pulverised my fingers, saying : " An sooa tha's condescended to look th' owd chap up once moor, hes ta Aw knew tha'd bin on the travels, bud tha's bin sich a long while away as aw welly begun a thinkin' as tha'd o'ther popt eaught o' together,er thad takken thi hook into forrin perts. Come an sit tha deawn an hey a smook, same as tha used to do, an a drop o'—herb beer. Dolly put on't table 'pipes an bacca for two, an tha I:nows wad, snuff for four." Dolly was Dicky's bigger and of course better half and did not always do as Dicky told her, nor let him have his own way quite as often as he would have liked. But this time she was extra gracious and she made my reception extra pleasant. When we were left to ourselves in the cosy capacious kitchen, and had squared certain enquiries on both sides, I asked v hat sort of a Christmas it was likely for being in his neighborhood. " Well "—he said—" awm nod sure as ther's gooin to be much to doo o' onny sooart this year, tnings seem rather quite somo heaw; nod becose t' cotton lords er preichin thad way, fer ther allus cryin' boggart, bud no'bdy seems as breet as they should doo; whey even owd Billy-up-at-th'-Reaundabeaut says as fooak dornd hafe ged drunk as they used to do; happen as they cornd o' stan id same, and as long as he hes. Aw dornd think as we's hey a cooarsin perty deawn this year, same as we hed last year abeaut this time." "A what ?"—I said, "I was not aware there was ever any coursing in this neighborhood." "Well "—Dicky almost invariably began a fresh sentence with "Well." "Aw downa know as tha'd co' id cooarsin'; happen tha'd be inclined to co' id a shootin' perty. Bud aw'm nod sure as this doo as aw'm meonin' owt o'ther to be co'd a shootin' perty er a cooarsin' match. Happen aw'd better tell tha o' abeawt id. Well, tha knows Brag, doesn't ta— tha's nod forgetten him, aw know. Well, his fay- ther hes a bit o' land deawn it valley, as Brag wants to think is his shootin' greawnd, an', to be big like, he thowt he'd like to ged up a grand shootin' perty. Ther is some trees on't land, an't country reawnd abeawt o' varra nice, as yo know, bud ther's nod much game,an this wer't both erin' point. Ov cooarse ther could be a shootin' perty beaut game, bud thad ud herdly be good enough fer chap wi sich big notions as Brag. He wer in a Sooart ov a fix. He , couldn't consult his friends, becose thad ud a let th' ' cat eawt o'th' bag. sooa be hed a bit o' talk wi his gamekeeper (1) a chap as dud odd jobs at factory, an's went deawn to "to my shooting place" abeawt hale a day every week to mend th' hedges an' pick up bits o' tree branches for firewood, an' gether eggs, an' happen kill a pigeon er two, fer' ther wer a dacent lot o' cock an' ben an pigeon game, iv ther wer nowt else. Well, Giles couldn'd see onny way eaut, bud he sed a mate ov his as lived o'er th' hill ud know o' abeawt heaw th' job should be managed. Brag went "o'er th' hill," an Barney torn'd eawt to be th' just chap as wer wanted; he could get as monny pheasants as wer needed, at a price. Oh! price wer nowt ; money no object to him, thad wer his feyther's look eawt. Sooa it wer arranged as Barney should ged a hundred or two o' pheasants ready for 't shootin' day. Brag wanted to send for a theasund on em, bud Barney tied as t' lot o' shooters as ud be theer woddend kill moor ner abeaut a dozen among em, iv they wer o' put together in a heap; he thowt a hun- dred or two wer anuff to be freetn'd away. Bar- ney suggested, as t' birds ud hey to come o' th'way fro' tf•cotland, id ud be best to hey em a week er two before t'doo come off, but Bragg sed that worn'd his way o' dooin' business. He wanted em to ged on th' greaund t' same mornin' as party sooa as they Gould be thrown up just as they wer wanted, an their nooan on em ud be lost. Brag hed once bin to a rapput coorsin' doo wheer they pood th' poor little things eawt ov a hamper as they'd bin croo'd up in fer heawrs, an put em on t' greaund to be killed o'ther bi t' sods er stooans' as wer sent at em to mek em run, or else bi th' dogs as wer sure to catch em. An' he'd bin at a pigeon shootin' doo er two it public heause back-yard at side o'th factory, wheer tbey put th' birds one ut once in a cot, and then let 'em eaut, when t' shooters bed gotten o' ready for kill in' 'em, an' he thowt id ud be a good idea to doo t' pheasants same way; sooa before t' day coom he arranged wi' some odd chaps, fer two pints, some cheese an bread an' sixpence a piece, to run afoor t' shooters and let t' birds eart just sooa as to give em a fair chance o' bein' killed an' earnin' t' price as hed bin agreed to be paid for 'em. One o'th chaps axt heaw it ud be if one o' them were popt off astid o'th birds, an' recited summat about th' only way o' bein safe wer gooin befoor a kickin hoss an' behind a shooter, bud another chap, as sed he knew whoa ud be t' party, towd him ther wer no fear iv t' shooters only aimed streight at o'ther t' birds or them, or any damage being done. An' sooa everythin' seemed nicely settled, an' th' invitations were sent eaut,

Then Barney, sed he'd getten a little bill for t' birds as he'd like settlin', a hundred an'-ilfty at eleven bob, eighty- two pound ten. Brag stickin' his hands in his hands in his britches pockets an' rattlin' his brass an' his keys, sed as he allus paid his accounts at factory, an' id ad hey to be co'd for theer. Barney sed he'd rayther hey t' brass afoor t' birds wer shot, but Brag sed as men like him wornd i'th' habit o' pa 3 in' for things afoor they geet 'em. Beside, he hed'no time to bother neaw, as t' shootin' ud be abea wt beginnin'. " Well," sed Barney, "an' t' chap as aw deeal we isn'd i'th' habit o' sendin' birds to puffed= up no'bdy's as he doesn'd know beaut hevvin' t brass fost. " Ah ! ah I "—laughed Brag—" then he'll have to make an exception for once. Why where do you think the birds are by this time ?" • Why," —sed Barney—" as they hevn'd bin sent eawt o' Scotland yet, nor wern'd be tell yo' pay up, aw spooase as they're enjoyin' thersels on t' moors yet ! " Brag's shoetin' perty wornd a success thad time yo may be sure, an' aw doarnd think as he's heerd t' last ont yet. Nay, yore never gooin' are yo ? Oh I catchin' train are yo? Well, just another swig, an' mind yore nod so long afoor yo come ageon. Ta, to:' "A RIFLE BILL AND A CHRISTMAS- BOX."

" At the battle of Gettysburg a rife ball broke my right arm just below the shoulder, and I never knew till then what a difference there is between an a 7 ns to lift with and an arm to be lifted." So said an American officer the other day when a few of us were talking about the mystery of life in the human body. Yet lots of people understand the prin- ciple. What do they mean when they say " I could scarcely crawl," I had to fairly lug myself along," &c. ? Why, simply that the body had lost its surplus power : it had become a burden, instead of an instrument to carry burdens. A woman writes in this wag: " I had constantly to lie down on the couch and rest. I had barely strength to crawl about. This was in the summer of 1882. The first trouble came upon me in 1876, when I was forty- two years old. Before that I had always been strong and healthy. Then, however, I began: to feel tired, weary, and languid, and gradually I had to consider myself a weak, sickly woman. At first I had a bad taste in the mouth, and a sinking sensation at the pit of the stomach. My appetite was poor, and what little I ate gave me pain in the chest and sides. My fcod seemed to create wind, which rolled all over me. I got so bad that night after night I was unable to sleep. I was at times in great agony, and if I had not been obliged to work I should have taken to my bed. As it was, I struggled on as best I could ; I saw a doctor and took various medicines, but none of them appeared to do me any good. "I continued in this wretched state for seven years- -1876 to 1883. Then came the help I had waited for so long and so hopelessly. In December of that year a little book was left at my house telling of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Syrup, and my husband road of a case I like mine having been cured by it; and I felt a strong desire to try the medicine, but we could not spare the ; money.

"However, when my husband returned from Bungray on Christmas Eve he pulled out of his parcel a bottle of Seigel's Syrup and said, 'See, I have brought you a Christmas-box,' and it proved to be the most valuable one I ever had in my life. I began taking the medicine at once, and found great relief. It seemed to lift a weight from my whole body. My appetite returned and I gradually gained strength, and by the time I had taken six bottles I was a new woman. I could go about my laundry work with ease and pleasure. I still take an occa- sional dose, and keep in good health, for which I have to thank Mother Seigel's Syrup. I know of many in this district who have received great benefit from the Syrup, one or two of the neighbours stating that but for it they would not now be alive. I desire others to know of what did me so much good, and to this end you have my consent to publish this getter, should you think it best to do so.

div.p: "Yours truly,' "(Signed) Mrs. GOODERHAN, " Earsham, Norfolk.

"July 11th, 1891." We gladly extend our congratulations to Mrs. Gooder- han upon her recovery, and beg to say for the general behoof that the ailment which oppressed her for so long long a time is unfortunately no stranger. Indigestion and dyspepsia lies at the very root of most diseases, for the reason that it arises in the stomach, upon the normal action of which good health necessarily de- pends. If we cannot digest our food everything, of course, goes wrong. For therein is the source of all power, strength, and vitality. From indigestion and dyspepsia proceed those poisons which, entering the blood, disorder every organ and process of the system. Rheumatism, gout, bronchitis, neuralgia, nervous pros. tration,most forms of diseases peculiar to women,chronic headache, pain and weakness in the muscles, mental dulness, and loss of ambition all these and other affec- tions are nothing more or less than results and signs of impaired or paralysed digestion. In short, they are mere words, the true and real disease being indigestion and dyspepsia. _ .

_ In its ability to cure this lies the secret of the success of Seigel's Syrup over what seems to be—but is not—a multitude of different maladies. It simply dislodges the keystone, and the arch falls to the ground.

div.head: DISAPPEARANCE OF A SOMERSET BANK MANAGER.
div.p: THE DISAPPEARANCE OF A SOMERSET BANK MANAGER.
A ROMANTIC STORY.

The mysterious disappearance of Mr. William Robert- son Lidderdale, the Ilminster bank manager, on the eve of his marriage with a young lady to whom he has for some time been engaged, has entered upon a new and startling phase. Mr. Lidderdale's departure was followed by the receipt of a communication announcing his death from an accident on board a yacht calleil th;Foresight. The accident, it was stated, took place on the Bth January, and Mr. Lidderdale, it was alleged, suc- cumbed to his injuries on the 30th of that month. A firm of city solicitors—Messrs. Pritchard and Marshall, Gracechurch-street—now offers a reward of £25 for an authentic copy of the certi- ficate of death. There was nothing in Mr. Lidderdale's social or business affairs to suggest a reason for his leav- ink home. His accounts at the bank were found correct, and he had recently furnished the house to which he was to take his bride. Inquiries made by a Press re- presentative in an authoritative quarter have elicited that there is now little doubt Mr. Lidderdale was kid- napped by a lady admirer, who had oo several occasions in letters, which he showed to certain intimate friends, expressed her determination never to permit him to be- come the husband of another. One, at least, of these letters contained a threat to murder him. The lady is an American, a spinster,about thirty years of age,and until recently occupied a flat in the neighbourhood of West- minster. She is said to be a woman of large means, and keeps a yacht. That the missing bank manager is on ' the yacht owned by this lady, and that a successful stratagem on her part placed him where he now is in- voluntarily confined, is firmly believed by those who have been entrusted with the secret. Energetic efforts L are being made by the Government to trace the yacht.

WHERE IS HE? The Central News learns that the whereabouts of Mr. Lidderdale, the missing bank manager, has been ascer- tained, and no further anxiety on his behalf need be felt, as he is in good health, and in extremely comfort- able circumstances. Information has also been obtained which throws light upon Mr. Lidderdale's movements since quite voluntarily he left Ilminster, and upon the means taken to conceal them, and to mislead those who desired to trace him.

OF THE CALI
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, 1 43, Author of " Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where tar • North Wind Blows," 'e., dc. ten
he

Caarruu XVL HB X 1' 171310171 WEDDING. Among the fisher folk, weddinge used to be ode- kated with a considerable amount of ceremony and quaint observance. Even to this day some of the original custams are held to; and it is considered an extremely shabby and mean thing to cheat the village popula- tion by any approach to a private marriage. The reverse must be a trying ordeal for shy or sensitive people; but rather than become unpopular, and have their misdemeanour cast up to them for life— as would most assuredly be their fate dld they dare to break through conventional usage—they brave it out and try to appear as though quite need to, and in fact rather liking the fuss than otherwise. But it is no wonder if a nervous, shame-stricken bridegroom should be so bewildered, shaken, and otherwise bereft of his self-possession as to mistake matters completely, and to endeavour to wed the wrong person from failure of finding the proper finger to fit the ring; a state of things not =fre- quent in those parts. What with cheers, partly encouraging and partly ironical, what with banging of drums extemporised for the occasion from old pans and kettles covered with sheep skin—popping of pistols and volleys of musketry, since every rusty old blunderbuss must needs be fired there and then regardless of cost—and likewise to risk of human life and limb—the shrill laughter of women and the ba.nterings of masculine raillery, to say nothing of the barking of village curs; a man would require to be made of cast iron to know what he was doing and to keep cool under it. Fortunately, and to the credit of the sex be it set down, the bride generally manages to rise above circumstances, and, sustained by a calm sense of importance and subdued triumph, to restore order from chaos. She rescues her unlucky mate from his condition of helpless despair, and does not allow him to bind himself to the wrong person. She knows that in this—the most important mo- ment of her life—the eyes of her world are upon her, and accordingly she overcomes every natural tremor, retaining only such becoming bashfulness as sufficeth to enlist the sympathies of her audience. Never does she lose the self-possession befittting the principal actor in an important drama. But what are the poor and spiritless proceedings of these degenerate times, when compared with the magnificent ones formerly considered impera- tive? Those weddings of bygone days were the ones for "high links," most assuredly ! Just imagine a country wedding of plain homely people, having for guests nearly six hundred persons, and no less than twenty-five musicians, fiddlers and pipers in attendance to amuse them, and set their feet a-jigging it the big barn belonging to a neigh,- bouring farmer which was the only place capable of holding such a goodly company! This is what we find recorded of a Northumbrian wedding of the last century :—A hundred and twenty quarters of lamb, forty-four of veal, twenty of mutton, twelve hams, and a similar quantity of beef, and poultry. Such a gigantic food supply would test the powers of the cooks engaged truly, but would probably be none too much provision for so great a multitude; while the punch and claret, and home-brewed beer required to wash it down and keep up the spirit of the scene was doubtless in like ratio.

_ Of course these were well-to-do folks; but even amongst the poorer classes the hospitality shown was profuse and extravagant in the extreme. "Eh, Ailsie woman, ye mun hey a menseful wethlin', if aw've to dip reet to th bottom o' th' stockin' foot for it !" exclaimed Adam Carr, when he had become used to the idea of losing his little lass. That is scarcely the right way of putting it,.though : for since he was a widower and Ailsie his only child, it had been settled to the satisfaction of all parties concerned that the young couple should share his

cottage. "Oh, ay, feyther, but there's nee fear o' that," retorted saucy Ailsie, with a toss of her pretty head; and the fisherman laughed, not ill-pleased at the imputation of inexhaustible wealth. He was a shrewd, careful man, and all his deal- ings had proved fortunate. The principal portion of his savings were invested in the Bonny Bess, the sloop of which Dick Daglish was skipper. Dick was a lucky captain, and many was the sharp run the little vessel had given the preventive men, and very skilfully had he piloted her through all sorts of , weather, since first he commanded her when he was a mere lad of eighteen or so. Old Carr was the principal factor in pinning Dick to the life of a free trader. He was loth to lose the latter's service. Of course there was always Bill Widdrington to fall back upon, and Bill was as thoroughly well acquainted with every inch of coast between Berwick and Hull as Dick

himself. But the old smuggler believed in the maxim of letting well alone. Daglish had invariably been successful, and his cargoes had turned out well. He knew how to buy at the best and cheapest market, and was as keen a hand at a bargain as his employer. Now, Bill, though a thoroughly capable sailor, was a trifle feather-headed where money matters were concerned. It was lightly come, lightly go, with him. Any body could overreach him, when it came to squabbling about the price of brandy or

silk. Besides, Bill was young, and had not Dick's experience to guide him. It was better to wait and allow him to learn the trade thoroughly, before resting any responsibility upon his shoulders. So it came to pass that every time Dick Daglish made a resolution and a promise to Bell of giving up the life, some strong persuasion on the part of the old man—added, of course, to the natural inclinations of tke skipper, which were all in favour of free trading—overcame his will, and caused him to incur his sweetheart's contempt and displeasure. She bore no goodwill either to the one who tempted him beyond his streneth. and had it mil ben for her strong love of Bill and a little con- tempttious fondness likewise for his pretty bride isleot., she would almost have declined to form one of the wedding guests. But this would have given mortal offence to the bride an the bride's father, and for the sake of her dee.? twin this was to be avoided. And then, also, Dick was coming, and she had so few opportunities of being with her lover. He had been away from 13reamish for a month past now and the temptation of being near him, having his arras around her in the dance which was to take place in the evening, looking into his dark eyes, and hearing the music of his deep voice —all these would have been sufficient inducement for Bell's presence, without any other and more commonplace ones. Anxiously was the weather watched by the bride elect on the eventful morning. No luck attends the bride upon whom a frowning sky looks down, so this anxiety is not to be wondered at.' But, "If woolly fleeces spread the heavenly way, No rain, for sure, disturbs the summer day." And since soft white fleeces lay across the sky, Ailsie's heart was at rest; though she would rather that old Nanny had not had that nasty dream about eating green apples, told the day before to the young coeple with spiteful emphasis, an em- phasis that was not without its due effect on the fisher lass. Very pretty looked the little bride,, in a gown of sprigged French muslin, trimmed with some real Brussels lace, a gift of her father, upon which it is not certain duty had been Pahl, and a silk hat with huge bows of white ribbon, will/ a face like a July rose blushing beneath it; and the groom, in his high-collared blue coat and fancy silk waistcoat, did not shame the show, though his natural sense of fun and humour made him feel as though the whole affair was a big joke. Tic had some difficulty In composing hislace to due solemnity. The white favours were distributed to those who were to form the precession, and off they started to church, Ailsie on the arm of Jim Craster, the groomsman, and Bell and Bill following in due course. Then pop went the guns, and loud rang the cheers, redoubled as the wedding party re- teemed, scattering money among.st the crowd. Rice wiTz thrown back in handfuls, and at the door of their future home a portion of bride's cake was also flung skilfully over Aisle's bent head, accord- ing to the custom and wont of the place. After this came the wedding feast. It was to be held at the Fisherman's Re;,* and Bessie Carr, the bride's aunt, and hostess of the inn, had the res- ponsible post of providing for the company. Well 44,:iihe fulfilled her task, for the long tables groaned under every rural delicacy, and the lavish display of solids was flanked by an equally lavish one of wines, mid beer, and spirits. ...gasotankaoiool dish was a. It was proposed ifirarrfielY WeeVerwork-should be-limited to-74—hours in- cluding meal times, and that( the Act should apply to to public-houses and refreehtent bars as well as to drapers'liticips. After the motion had been seconded Mr. GEnciamoved an amendment,standing in Mr. M'L ren's Iname that the House declined to interfere further with the working hours of adult women until women had the constitutional means of expressing their opinions by the Parliamentary franchise. Ultimately the amendment was withdrawn. In the debate which I followed Sir Jokn Lubbock and Mr. Matthews took park. , The HOME SECRETARY said therOught tck be chary "la in- terfering with woman's work. '` He was confident that the proposal, if carried,' wmild displace a large number of adult women from the labour they were now follow- ing, and though be had no objection to an inquiry he should Vote against the second reading. Mr. M'Lmazx moved an amendment that the bill be read a second time that day six months. The amendment was se- conded by Sir Joint COLOMB. Mr. RORY did not think the result of restricting the employment of women to n hours a week would have the effect of throwing a large number of women out of employment. He sug- gested that they should go to the second reading,and take a Committee afterwards. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR said the Government were prepared to give an inquiry, but were unwilling to give their adhesion to a proposal they did not believe to be workable. He suggested that Mr. Provand would withdraw the bill ; but the hon. member pressed it to a division, when the motion for the second reading was carried by 175 votes to 152. The bill was read a second time and referred to a Select Committee. Mr. SEXTON complained of the extraordinary delay in the publication of the Irish Local Government Bill, and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach said itwould be circulated that day. The House adjourned at a quarter to six o'clock.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. MISCELLANEOUS.—Sir William Thomson took the oath and his seat as Baron Kelvin. A bill to amend the law of trusts was read a first time. The East India Officers Bill passed through committee after some discussion, and the Betting and Loans (Infants) Bill also passed througlicomtnittee, Loicl SALISBURY, in reply to Lard Midleton, said ,he would do his best to persuade the House to join in an inquiry regarding London fop if the House of Commons accepted a motion for •a, joint committee. The House adjourned at 5-25. HOUSE OF COMMONS, THURSDAY. THE GRESHAM Uravessrrx —Mr. Chamberlain pre- sented a petition from the Medical Schools of Manchester Liverpool, Leeds, Sheffield, Birmingham, and Bristol against the eranting of a charter to the proposed Gres- ham University. Mr. A. J. Balfour promised to endea- vour to arrange for a debate on the proposed charter by stopping Government business some night about eleven o'clock. Art AFRICAN Enzway.—The Caratcxmou of the Ex- CHEQUER, in reply to a question, said the latest informa- tion showed that on the 22nd January the survey for the Mombasa and Nyanza railway had reached a point on the Mombasa river 150 miles from the coast. Arrange- ments had been made that the Company should go on , with the survey, and the Government had given a pledge that they would ask the House t the to vote a certain portion . a the money ae ea m rliest opportunity to reimburse the Company. NEW POSFAt AERANGEMENTS.—SIF James FERGUSSON informed the hone member that it-was in contemplation by the Post-office to abolish the redirection charges on letters generally. THE CASE or ALLEGED CRUELTY.—Replying to ques- tions put by Mr. .P. O'Brien, Mr. Jackson said the course taken by the police in the case of Mrs. Montagu was exactly similar to that which would have been taken in any other case. &arca Locer. TAYATION.—The LORD ADVOCATE, in introducing a Bill to make provision for the application of sums paid to Local Taxation (Scotland) Account under the Local Taxation Act of 1890, said that of the sum of £265,000 which , was estimated as Scotland's share per annum it was proposed to allocate £175,000 to the relief of local taxation, and of the balance of £90,000 a large proportion would be devoted to the im- provement and development of secondary education and £30,000 to the Universities. Ultimately Mr. BALFOUR said he was informed that there were the gravest doubts whether the bill ought not to have originated in Com- mittee, and ia these circumstances he moved the ad- journment of the debate. The motion was agreed to, and the House afterwards went into Committee of Supply. The House adjourned at 12 10.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA

best way of promoting dattblØt wait to Ili at, peace with our neighbours.lild not to be Medellin* tie their affairs but attending to our ovni affairs:— (Applause.) With the etibiects of social had economical reform women were quite as well able, at least a great many women, to deal as were mem' and in many of those subjects they could probably teach men a great deal that it would be very well for men co know, and the conclu- sion to be drawn from all that is, that organisations such as their own were intended and calculated to do a great deal of the work which had hitherto been done exclusively by men. (Hear hear.) He need not say to that meeting that it was quite possible ter women as well as raen, notwithstaading that a con- siderable amount of their time must be devoted to do- mestic duties, yet to find leisure for the discharge of duties for the benefit of the public. They knew that Men were obliged to attend to their business and at the same time find leisure to attend to the affairs of the public. It only required a certain sacrifice, perhaps of ease, or a certain sacrifice of enjoyment and a great deal of economy of time to enable that to be done. As it was with men workers in the field of poli.des and in the field of social reform so it was with women. They would very soon learn, if they had not learned already, so to dis- pose of their time and of their leisure that, without leaving undone any of those things that ought to be done, they would at all events have a share of their lives to devote to public purposes. (Applause.) In conclusion, he congratulated the people of Warrington upon the estab- lishment of that Association. It was still very young, but, judging from the meeting that they had that afternoon, and from the meetings which had been pre- viously held in connection with that Association he thought he might predict for it a career of great pros- perity and of great utility. (Loud applause.) Mrs. Fay, who was received with applause, ex- pressed the very, great pleasure it gave her to be at that meeting, and Ueda any little that lay in her power to support her great friends Dr. and Mrs. Pious- ton. She felt sure that that meeting afforded a very happy augury of coming events. (Applause.) They were all beginning to feel a little of the excitement of the election which was drawing near, and they were all beginning to think what they could do to press forward that great Liberal cause which every man and woman who took a deep interest in their country's welfare should have at heart. She had been asked to say a few words as to the origin and object of Women's Liberal Associations. She understood it was only six months since they com- menced their Association in Warrington, but their as- sembly there that day showed what excellent and active work had been going forward. She would ask them to carry their thoughts back to 1880, when there was a very hard-fought election raging in the country, as a re- sult of which the Liberal party were returned to power. At that time the first Women's Liberal Associa- tions were formed in the towns of York and Darlington, and about the same period one was formed in Bristol. The reason they were commenced was that women had shown how deeply they interested interested in politics, although she was afraid it was not always what they might term an intelligent interest. (Hear, hear.) It was not always from a thorou,eh understanding of the questious at stake that women took an interest in politics. Recognising that fact, Associations were formed with a desire that women might be induced to take a thoroughly intel- ligent interest in the welfare of their country, and to be enabled to really master as far as they could the leading principles of their party and to await to carry desired reforms ko a successful issue. (Applause.) That, then, was really the origin of the Women's Liberal Association. She was afraid sometimes that their gen- tlemen friends thought they wanted to do some very terrible thing, that they wanted to take women out of their proper sphere and out of their homes, and do man's , work. But they could never do man's work. Men had one work to do and women had another. What they wanted was only, that women tnightseek to understand the great questions of the day,which affected their well-being and the happinese of their homes. (Hear, hear.) Hav- ing referred to the questioe of a free breakfast table which she pointed out, closely affected women, Mrs. Fry alluded to the Irish question. They might say the Irish question was a difficult one, but she would encourage them to read, simple papers so that they might be thoroughlyconvinced about it. As to the simple ptin- ciple Of Home Rule she thought that came very near to a woman's kingdom. (Hear' hear.) It was only the desire of the Irish to manage their own affairs in their own way in their own capital. It was not that they were asked to make any great sacrifice, for it was only to allow the Irish to manage their own national affairs in the same way that their colonies did. (Hear, heart) They had to be in Ireland to realise how strong the national sentiment was; how very strongly they loved their home, and how very strongly they felt the sorrow of a forced emigration from that home. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the difference be- tween the Women's Liberal Association and the Prim- rose League, she chanced to come amiss the Organ of the Primrose League, which contained a bit which was just suited for that day. It spoke of a certain, habitation which had been particularly successful, ,be- cause the ruling dame who had it in charge had, in ad- dition , te what she was expected to do, been good- enough to give the people a good deal of political in- formation. They would see they had turned it upside down. .The first object of the Wornen's Liberal Associa- tiott wag to give information. (Hear,hear.) They were told that they,were ap electioneering machine, and stie was not ashamed pf it. It was the outcome of what they were formed for. When they had obtained that political knowledge and information which they had farmed themselves together to attain, was it not a logical consequence thit they should want to see good men and true returned to the British House of Commons ? They wanted to ' see men returned who would put forward their best interests, and therefore they exerted them- selves that they might be returned. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mrs. CROSFIELD said Mts. Efotaston wished to, be excused froth making h. speech. She was net accustomed ecapeechtnaking, but the next time she came over &din ,Irelandsbe would prepare a speech, and hoped td ad- dress them on that occasion. (Hear, hear and laughter.) Mrs. WINS= moved a vote of thanks to Dr. Housten and Mrs. Fry, and this, having 13.3 en seconded, by Miss Dutton, was heartily accorded. Mrs. FRY moved and Dr. Houston seconded a vote of thanks to Mrs. Croslield for presiding, and this haying been accorded, the meeting terminated. 4

law 41.14141rawhe Wits received with applause, kid fliti Nfitrasidtlisnce would no doubt remember thatil *de " In the fullness of the heart the mouth speaket6.° Now,for the last two or three days, his heart had been very full with one subject, and that was the wonderful performance which took place the Thursday night previous, in London, and the theatre was the British House of Commons. The principal actor was Kr. Balfour. Some gentleman in the House of Commons, speaking to Ifr.Disraeli about Mr.Dalfour,referred to his groat intellect, his talents,and the probability of his being a great success in the House. Some of them might know that Mr. Balfour had a curious habit of reclining on the bench in such a way that they hardly knew whether he was sitting or lying. Mr. Disraeli shook his head and said," Well, I never knew a man who was successful ha the House of Com- mons who sat on his shoulders." (Laughter.) It would never have strack him that a man who sat on his shoulders would not be a successful man. He began to suspect, however, that there was something in it, for 1 Mr. Balfour had been anything but a success lately. He I (Mr. Balfour) sincerely believed the Irish Local Govern- I ment Bill was so perfect in its way that it would Niacin- ate the Irish without very much offending the Tories. I How could he have got that idea into his head he could I not say, but he would tell them what ha heard that morning. A Tory acquaiatance of his, when he picked up his paper on Friday morning, and read the report in question said he could fancy he could hear a bell toll. He supposed it was for the departure, or forth coming departure, of the present Government. (Laugh- ter and applause.) With regard to Home Rule, there were in England a great number of men, moderate men, thoughtful men, who, perhaps, became frightened by I the use of the word "disintegration " of the empire, but they had gradually found out that this Consti- tutional Government, who prided themselves upon being constitutional, were the most unconstitutional which had been in office during his time. (Applause.) He thought plenty would bear him out in that remark, and he believed his Conservative friend was prophetic about the bell. There might be a goad deal in it. (Laughter and applause.) Clearly one result might come about, and that was that the coming election would be upon them sooner in consequence. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

Mrs. Houston and Mist Daly sang with great suocess "Across the dark lagoon," and on being encored they gave "My boat is waiting here." Miss Fleming followed with a fine performance on the piano. Dr. Housrox, who was enthusiastically received, said he aheuld content himself with adverting to a few events which had occurred in the political world since he last had an opportunity of addressing them. He thought the matter to which he should have the pleasure of adverting were matters upon which they and himself had every reason to congratulate themselves. The first of these was what he would call the virtual defeat which the government sustained upon Mr. Sexton's amendment to the address—(hear, hear)—because he thought the petty majority of 21 by which that amendment was negatived was tantamount -to a Government defeat. All the moral and material advan- tages of the debate and the division Were with Mr. Sexton. (Hear, hear.) That division taken by itself was full of significance. In the first place it was the smallest majority which the present Govern.. merit had had since they came into office, but, in the next place when it was taken in connection with other divisions that had been taken upon the Irish question it was only the last of a series of continual diminishing majorities. (Hear, hear.) The figures were instructiv and it would not take him a moment to enumerate them He would just go through the divisions that had taken place on the Irish question since the year 1888, and they might judge what the significence of those figures was; In the year 1887itheilate lamented Mr. Parnell moved ittl amendment to the address,' and on that occa- sion the amendment , was negatived by a majority of 108. In 1888 Mr. Morley moved an , amendment condemning the administratjon of the Crimes Act in Ireland, and that was negatived by a majority of 92. In the next year, 1889, Mr. Morley again moved an amendment condemning the adminis- tration bf justicein Ireland, and that was negatived by the majority of 79, showing a considerable falling off. In 1890 Mr. Morley moved another 'amendment which was negatived by a majority of 87, showing still a continuous decline in the government majority, and' now they had in the year. 1892, a miserable majority of 21. (Hear, hear, and applause.) As surely as steadily, and as rapidly as a falling barometer pre- dicted the coming storm and the ensuing shipwreck (laughter)—so did that series of figures the coming storth that would beat upon the Tory Government and their disaster at the next general election. (Applause. That was the first subject upon which he thought they wete entitled to congratulate themselves, and the next was the precious Irish Log& Government Bill. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He would ask was there ever such II measure seriously introduced into the legislature, and was ever any measure introduced by such' a speech. That speech reminded him first of Paul Pry and next of Mr. Toots. (Laughter.) Mr. Paul Pry was always in the habit of apologising for his intrusion, and Mr. Balfour occupied a very considerable portion Of his speech in apologising for intruding that measure; at all. (Laughter.) He deprecated the hostility of his Tory friends and his Unionist friends. as much as said he really would not have introduced the measure at all if he could by any possibility have avoided it. , At the close of his speech he reminded him very much of Mr. Touts. Mr. Toots when he asked a question and did not get an answer that exactly pleased him always said "Oh, it was of no consequence," and consequently Mr. Balfour, at the close of his speech was very careful to impress upon the House of Commons that really that hip Local Government Bill was of no consequence whatever. He assured them that so long as the Irish people were in the free and unlimited enjoyment of the blessings of coer- cion, tempered with an occasional light railway Act,with the prospect that at some time or other possibly the Land Purchase Act might be got into working order; that they could ask for nothing more and they deserved a great deal lass. (Laughter.) The Tory government had missed a splendid opportunity as their chairman had observed. The Liberal party and the Irish Parliamen- tary party would have,receiveci any reasonable measure of Irish local goverdniint for Ireland with indulgence not to say favour but instead of that a measure that has been introduced under the name of local government was an absurdity and was an insult. (Loud applause.) It was (rained upon the assumptionc the impudent as- sumption, that the Irish people were a dishonest, cor- rupt and rapacious people whose only object in life was to oppress and plunder their neighbours, and in point of fact was based upon the assumption that the Irish people were not fit for local government at all, and ac- cordingly a measure was introduced which took away with one hand what it professed to give with another. (Hear, hear, and applause.) There was also a provision as to the representatieni, of minorities, a provision that was introduced for what purpose ? For the purpose of protecting the Protestant minority in the South from the Catholic majority there, and protecting the Catholic minority in the North from the oppression of the Pro- testant majority there. Why that was an indictment of a whole nation! (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) He hoped the Liberal Unionist Nonconformists of the North of Ireland liked the compliment which Mr. Balfour was paying them by making that a part of the measure he has introduced. (Hear, hear.) But that was not all. Mr. Balfour next proceeded to put the County Council
