div.p: LIBERAL RECEPTION AND CONCERT.

--- On Monday evening another reception was held by Dr. and Mrs. Houston at the Co-operative Hall. Winwick-street, Warrington, ar d agsin there Was a very large attendarce. Between seven and eight o'clock probably over 700 persons entered the, hall ar d wc-e intiaduced to Dr. and Mrs. Houston) At the concert which °ollowed, there was an attend- ance 07. about 800. Mr. John Rylands, J.P., presided, and there were also present, in addition to Dr:, hnd Mrs. Houston, Mrs. Fry, of DarlinVon ; Miss Daly, of Manchester; Dr. Gornall, Coancillors J. H. Flem- ing, J. Bonnell, J. Shaw-Green, S. J. Beaman; Messrs. W. Pierpoint, T. Morris, J., Winser; T. Birchen, Tinnion, S. Kenyon T. Birtles, J. Guest, C. J. Holmes, Jeffrey, Winskill, F. R. Roberts, H. Bond, J. Hall, J. Gandy, &c.

that he had established under the thumb of the grand jury. (Laughter.) The County Councils were practic- ally to have no initiative at all except under_ the control of a new nody which was erected for the purpose. What was that and how was it to be constituted ? Mere w to be seven representatives of the County Council a 'there were to be seven representatives of the grand( ufiys j . That as it stood would have been a very unsatis- ,factory arrangement, but, at all events, there would I have been an off-chance that the County Council would ' have had a little of their own way, but, in order that there might be no independence exerted by the County Council who was thrown in as the casting voice, so that there might be a permanent majority against the County , Council, but the High Sheriff? (Laughter.) Why, the High Sheriff of a county was more of a grand juror than the grand jurors themselves, and the consequence would be, if tke provision were introduced, that prac- tically the County Council would be strangled in its birth. (Hear, hear.) There was another portion of the measure which was even more odious still, and that was the proposition that the County Council were liable, at the instance of 20 ratepayers,—people who, according to Mr. Balfour's own statistics might be only contribut- ing 4d. a head per annum—yet 20 of these fourpenny— (laughter)—ratepayers were to have the right to drag the County Council before two judges without a jury, for what ? For persistent disobedience to the law, and for malversation of the funds, and for oppression, and H they were found guilty, what was to be done? Not ' that a new County Council was to be appointed. That i would be too Liberal a measure entirely. The Lord Lieutenant was to appoint a County Council in their place. ("Oh," and laughter.) He was bound to say that, in his wildest moments, he never imagined that any statesman could have ever suggested the placing in Ireland of a body like the County Council before two judges of the High Court for the purpose of dissolving, and filling their place by the nominees of the Lord Lieu- tenant. (Hoar, hear.) He was perfectly aware of the great capacity of the Irish judges. They were wien of great learning and of great ability, but he thought they were deficient in one quality, and it was not their fault that they were deficient in it but the result of circumstances over which they have had no control, and that was that in political mat- ters such as were now proposed to be submitted to them, they did not possess with a very few exceptions, the confidence of the people. (Hear, hear.) He would say this : that if they wanted to prevent men of position, self-respecting men, from offering themselves as candi- dates for the County Council, then this provision was exactly the one that would be calculated to prevent men who had a consciousness of what was becoming, and what was due to themselves as candidates. (Elear,hear.) Those three provisions, if there had been nothing else in the proposed bill, were, he thought, calculated and were destined to wreck it. (Hear, hear and , applause.) He thought the probabilities were that the effect of the introduction of that measure would be in one way or another, to hasten the general election. (Applause.) He was happy to think that, when the general election came, whether it came sooner or later they would be pretty well prepared for it in Warrington. (Hear, hear and applause.) He believed that a spirit had been aroused in Warrington that was an unusual spirit, and a spirit that had not been witnessed for some time. There had been an awakening amongst the Work- ing classes and amongst the Liberals of that constitu- ency, and he believed that the effect of that would be that whether the general election be soon or whether it be late he ' should be the member by a large majority. (Loud and continued applause.) , Miss Daley tiled rendered a song in beautiful style, for which she was touchy encored. ' Miss dutton then recited a passage from Shakespeare in a singularly effective style, and for this she was very loudly applauded. 114r4. Houston, Miss Daly, and Mr. W 4 Howard then gave the trio "Oh, Memory," which waS also loudly applauded. , , , I Mrs. FRY, in the course of an able address, in which, ,as she said, she spoke on behalf of the ladies, remarked that, although women might ' not have vetes, yet they had influence, as she expected some of the gentlemen present knew. ' (Hear,hear,und laughter.) They did not want to propose anything very dreadful, but whakhey wanted was that the women of England should try to so well to understand that great Irish question that they could lend their influence and speak a word in season. (Hear, hear.) One of the greatest of English writers had often brought together the words " sweetness and light," and they wanted not only the sweetness of the ladies in their homes but their light also. She did not , think there were many men in England now who wanted , to have ignorant wives, hnd they wantei to encourage , the ladies to take an intelligent interest in the great ques- tions of the day. • (Hear, hear and applause.) • Mr. J. A. Cavastmite next gave a capital rendering of: " The little hero," and Mr. C. Furness recited " Abo' th' , Yates' speech" with so much success, that hewas loudly. recalled, and, in resPodse to the demtinds of the audience gave" Nomination Day." Mrs: Houston was warmly , applauded on ristng to sing" By the fountain" at the close of which she was heartily encored, when she gave an amusing election song, which was greatly enjoyed by the audience. It should be added that the accompani- ments were again admirably played by Mr. W. H. Payton. , , COURCin6Y BEZiItAN moved a vote of 'thanks to Mrs. Houston, Mrs. Fry, and the others who had taken an active part in .the proceedings of , the meeting. This was seconded by Councillor J. Saari Gruninr, and heartily accorded. ,Mrs. FRY responded, and moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman-, terAh, having.been seconded by Mr. C. J. HoLsras, was heartily agreed to. The gathering then terminated. , .

On Saturday, the annual meeting of ths Northwich Conservative Association, was held under the presidency of Colonel France Hayhurst. The selection by a special committee of Mr. George Whiteley, :cotton spinnbr, Blackburn as a candidate to oppose Mr. Brunner at the ensuing election was confirmed and Mr. ViThiteley's name was now submitted for approval. Mr, Whiteley addressed the meeting. He said he could not plead that he was in any respect a chicken in public affairs. The past six years had been to him a period of hard work and electioneering. He confessed that in political matters he was of a very aggressive, combative, contentious nature, and could promise that if they adopted him as their candidate Mr. Brunner would have as good a run for his money as ever was seen in this part of the country. (Laughter and Cheers.) He styled himself a progressive Conservative, recognising that they had a great country—a united kingdom—(cheers) —and a broad, a vast empire, with large possessions to preserve. He looked upon ffome Rule as the most marvellous, magnificent, and majestic specimen of a "pig in a poke" that ever an evanescent and enthusias- tic statesman had tried to palm off on an innocent and unsuspecting British public. In acknowledging a vote formally adopting him as their candidate, Mr. Whiteley said that after next Tues- day his services would be entirely at the disposal of the constituency, but he should like to have a day off to witness the Grand National at Aintree, and three days for Punchestown races, which he never missed. (Laugh- ter and cheers.)

THE QUALITY OF TEL. It having been mentioned that tenders were about to be invited for provisions, &c., Mr. Hood Wright sug- gested that some step should be taken to ascertain the quality of the tea supplied. Alderman Hannisow thought the best plan would be that the House Commit- tee should have some brewed for themselves. (Laugh- ter.)—Mr. HEATON was of opinion that excellent tea could be had for is. 6d. a pound, and the Clerk re- marked that Mr. Goschen had made a statement very much to the same effect as to what the maximum price of tea ought to be.—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON said he could get tea that suited him for is. Id. a pound.— The subject then dropped.

TITS BOARD AND THE ISOLATION OF INFECTIOUS DISEASE. The Clerk read a letter which he had received from Dr. Watkins, of Newton, with reference to the ease of a pauper suffering from diptheria. The doctor wrote that he had requested Mr. Bowes, the relieving officer, to remove the case, but he said that he had no power to do so. The Haydock Local Board had also declined any responsibility with regard to the case. He (Dr. Wat- kins) wished for an authoritative statement as to what he shoulsido.—Mr. Bowes,the relieving officer,said he had asked to remove the case of isolation but that he under- stood he couldmot do. He had, however, given an order for maintenance.—The CLERK said the isolation of cases ' of disease was for the protection of the inhabitants of a district, and he had always advised that that was a matter for the Sanitary Authority and not for the Board of Guardians.—This view of the matter seemed to meet with the general approval of the Board. This was all the business of public interest.

div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. J. Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meeting at Dutton Workhouse on Toiesday. Present Rev. .T, W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Lightburn, Taylor. Lea, Lewis, P. Hall, .T. Bate, Mounfield, J. Hall, W. Edwards, Brandreth, Stokes, J. Weir, J. Baguley, J. W. Baguley, Baxter, Heywood, Picker- ing, J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: TRE ' ESTIMATES-REDUCTION IN RATE.
div.p: TRE ' ESTIMATES-REDUCTION IN RATE.

Mr. Brandreth said the amount of accounts recom- mended to be paid by the Finance Committee was £3,440. He was glad to say that this amount included £3,291 ss. id., for the County Council whleh was overdue, and also £9O for outdoor relief in Runcorn, £3O in Frodsham and £2O in Budworth district. There was now in tie Bank £4,365, so that when they had paid these account's there would be a balance in hand- ef £925 7s. view of the estimates for the ensuing half-year, Mr. Ashton had written to Mr. Potts, Clerk to Um Cheshire County Council, asking what contribution the Council would require from the union for next year. In reply Mr. Potts said •' It is impossible to sayluntil the estimates for th 3 ensuing year are prepared as to what county rate will be necessary, but I will let you know as soon as ever I can give you an approximate idea." The Clerk there- fore had to make the estimates on last year's amount. The Clerk had taken a great deal of trouble, but

he had put the rate rather—lees than he (Mi. Brandreth) thought. judicious, as they did not know what the -county Council might want. They might want more money next year than ever before if Mr. Baxter got in. (Laughter.)—Mr. Lewis: It is more likely to be less.—Mr. Brandreth : Let's hope It-will be less if we get Mr. Baxter in. Perhaps if we get some new blood in, it will be less. We want some new blood in.—The report and estimate of the probable expenditure for the half year ending Michaelmas, 1892, was then read. The total capital for the current half- year ending Lady Day, 1862, amounted to £9,584 and the net probable expenditure is 'estimated at £7,255, which showed a balance at Lady Day of £2,329. The probable expenditure during the ensuing half-year ending Michaelmas, 1892, is as follows : Common charges, £2,159 ; county rate, £3,293; balance and contingency fund, £2,781; total, £8,213. After deducting from this total the probable balance at Lady Day. of £2,329, the amount required by contribution orders from the overseers is £5,884. The rateable value of the Union as per valua-

tion lists in force is £220,666 being an increase of £l,OlO, as compared with the corresponding period of last year. A rate of 60. in the £ will produce the sum Of £5,982, and it is recommended that a call for the sum of £5,884 be made upon the overseers in accord- ance with the detailed estimate after adding or deduct- ing the estimated balances in favour of or against each township at Lady Day, 1892, being a decrease of nd. in the £, as compared with the corresponding period of last year. The foregoing calculations are subject to altera- tions which may be made in valuation lists previous to the contribution orders being signed, the following im- portant matters pending, viz.: assessment of the Man- chester ,Ship Canal ' • assessment of the new yards at Runcorn belonging to the M.S.C. Co.; sundry supple• merited valuation lists.—Mr. Brandreth moved the adoption of the estimates, and remarked that the Clerk thought they could get the rate down to 6d. next year. —Mr. Edwards seconded the motion, which was car- ried unanimously. THE LEGAL EXPENSES. Mr. Edwards said he, some time ago, moved ftw a re- turn of the legal expenses of the Guardians anti Rural Sanitary Authority for some time past, and he wished to knew when they might expect•to have it.—The Clerk said it had been a great deal of trouble to, get up. Re should be able to bring it forward next meeting. SCIIOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICIO. , Mt Rev. J. W. N, Tanner said the ScboOl Attendance Committee had been:engaged two hours in selecting candidates for the positions of attendance officers in the three districts of the Union. There were 16 candidates, one teeing a 'cabman; and the Committee recommended the appointment qf the following, whom they considered suitable men : Frodsham Mr. • Geo Jones, £35 a year : Great Budworth, Mr. Jenkins, jun, (Warrington)," £3O; andtWeston, BAr: Tomlinson (Halton). £lO a year, re- duction of £5 a year.—The recommendations were adopted.—The Board also agreed to a rate of one-fifth of a penny for School Attendance purposes.

THE Liberals of this part of Lanca- wetnan's shire are showing themselves par- influence. ticularly active in view of a possibly ;,..413' dissolution. There were two meetings on 41-onday evening: one at St. Helens in support of 314. KENNEDY, Q.C., and another at Widnes in sup- Port of Mr. H. WADE DEACON. The Liberals of .„arrington were busy, too, on Monday; in the o.'"'ernoon there was a gathering, at the Liberal tklub, of the Women's Liberal Association ; and in 121 evening Dr. and Mrs. HOUSTON held a second ig 419 successsful reception of the principal workers (4 the party. It is gratifying to note that UIE/re Was a good attendance at the Women's iteetirig ; and it is to be hoped it will not be the ast that will be held during the campaign. Women :let° for a longtime treated by politicians—Liberal ;8 well as Tory—as of little or no account in poli- Le 4 ; and it.was not until they bestirred them- yes in demanding recognition of their rights that they were given tho privilege of voting at unicipal, Board of Guardians, and School Board ections. The power they have acquired has ,be, en wisely used, and, what is more, it has had '4lB effect of stimulating the Imperial legisla- ,tliro to take steps to remove some of the disa- Yities under which women have hitherto laboured. ur• HOUSTON was essentially in place in ad- tlressing the meeting at the Warrington Liberal eleb, for he was in a position to say that, taany years ago, he lectured, as professor of politi- ca.' economy at the Dublin University, on the in- dustrial disabilities under which women then 'B•boured. Much has been done since then ; but there is still much to do. Lord ROSEDERY, as 6t-chairman of the London County Council, re- L tau 1, rs, ed some time ago that very much of the work the County Council was of a kind which was ;36ani 0 v nt.ially suitable for women; but, such is the 'dleci of the law as manufactured by the present erlarneet, that, although well-qualified women llve been elected to the County Council, they are permitted to take part in the business. As °th Dr.llonsrox and Mrs. FRY remarked,women 14. e especially interested in all questions which afiect home life; and there can be no doubt that queAtions will form a prominent part of the Nislatien of the future. Who more than woman ,18 interested in a sober happy home P If it were left to the votes of the wives and mothers of thel tingdom to determine the licensing question, we 144 Y be quite sure that there would be a speedy ecluction in the number of public houses— :" that some plan for controlling profits :13n1d be adopted like the Gothenburg latern advocated by Dr. HOUSTON. And so with t...egarcl to war, and preparations for war. If "Mares influence were felt in the State as it c'nght to be—not only in this but in every other rall4trY—who can doubt that there would be a ...rge reduction in the vast standing armies of the and in the expenditure generally on the 4kmaitions of war, which is a heavy burden to so 1111:1141 communities P More than one statesman hal remarked of the majority of the wars hat 4ato been waged, that they might have been terted if there had been an exercise in the first :11)4 tance of good sense and kindly feeling. It is if e inilitary spirit of man which causes war, and, °PPortunity were given, it is the kindly spirit Woman which would prevent war. Dr. bus- -8 Cognises this, and it is because he is anxious ttt itistice should be done to all classes that the eirlon as well as the men of Warrington should tt, IF/ hire all the help they can, thus determining, 444 after the next election, the borough shall be tot'Nented by a politician who can be of service izt them individually while helping on the pro- of humanity.

"TOUCH AND GO." Alas for the Japanese! "A complete set of our Parliamentary debates, contained in 641 huge volumes, has been purchased for £6OO for the use of the Japanese House oZ Lords. The set is now on its way to Tokio." It is all over with the happy Jap ; his high spirits will never survive the "541 huge volumes" of Parliamentary debates. This comes of wanting to be civilised ; and he will learn too late that "where ignorance is bliss 'tis folly to be wise."

Mr. John Dillon still shows himself anxious to put an end to the split in the Irish ranks, notwith- standing the fact that his recent efforts as a peace- maker proved anything but pleasant. The Parne'- lites ought to be able to see by this that, whether they will or not, they are playing the Tory game. " Parnellism and Crime" vanished with the defeat of the "Times," but, with Parnell dead, Parnellism will become a crime if persisted in against the wishes of the mass of the people of Ireland.

The " Speaker" seems to have put its foot in it, in saying that Lord Hartington tried to form a Government in 1890, and only gave way to Mr. Gladstone when he found he could not succeed. Prod is asked for, but it is not forthcoming, and the evidence is, so far, all the other way. Lord Hartington was sent for by the Queen, and ha certainly could have formed a Government if so minded. But he knew the country wished to see Mr. Gladstone at the helm and he showed good sense in giving way to the old pilot. --- Addressing the Grappenhall members of the Primrose League, on Saturday evening, Mr. John White sounded a note of warning. He said—" if they remained in a dangerous slumber they might some day have a painful awakening." This is so rousing that Mr. White may be said to be like Macbeth in that he "does murder sleep ;" and the text should now run : _ _
Methought 1 heard a voice say. "Sleep no more ! John White cloth murder sleep." But how bye-the-bye do the Grappenhall Leaguers like being told that they are a sleepy lot?

The Small Holdings Bill of the Government is marred by the radical defeat which characterises all Tory legislation of this class—it is not compul- sory. This means that the landlords are to "boss the show." They can have their own way as to prices, or refuse land. In other words, it is a Bill to augment the price of land, and spoil the chance of the small holder. Mr Chamberlain and Mr. Jesse Collip.gs, who are pledged to compulsion, are thrown over. They don't count, it seems ; and Jesse has brought in a rival Bill full of compulsion. Oh, the union of the Unionists is a touching and a beautiful sight!

The people of Southport are mightily in ear- nest about their centenary, which is to be cele- brated this year. The chief feature is to be a fine art exhibition; and already there is promise of the loan of some of the finest paintings in the country. On Monday the Centenary Committee were in conference with the representatives of the leading railway companies,and arrangements were made for the issue of tickets at reduced fares, in- cluding admission to the exhibition. The new marine lake on the north shore will be com- pleted in time for the centenary ; and altogether the Sand-grounders are in for a big show.

It is stated that there is groat distress in Austria in consequence of the enormous number of the unemployed. The problem confronts one everywhere. How is it to be solved ? It is monstrous that an able-bodied man,willing to work, should have to starve or commit suicide because work is not to be had. If he were in the heart of Africa, he could help himself to food of some kind; but what can he do in the heart of a big city ? John Ruskin was laughed at when he suggested permanent Government workshops which would be available in such cases ; but is it not about time to cease laughing and re-consider his proposal ?

Lord Derby once said" The greatest of British interests is peace ;" and it is pleasant to find that aristocrat and plebeian are in agreement on this point. At the meeting, on Tuesday evening, of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council, a petition was adopted in favour of meeting the views of the United States Government, by concluding a treaty of arbitration with this country. It is'nt the masses who are in favour of fighting: it is the classes who see in war pickings and promotion. The fighting interest is altogether too strong in the House of Commons at the present moment, and ought to be whittled down at the nest elec- tion.

The Liberals of Warrington are fortunate in having a candidate who touches everything in the way of politics, and adorns everything that he touches. Unlike the Tory candidate, he has something beyond criticism to offer ; he has a programme to expound, and he is expounding it in a style which shows that he is master of every item. Not that he is lacking in criticism, when criticism is required, as witness his description "and analysis of the new Local Government Bill for Ireland. As we shall hear a great deal of this measure, we commend Dr. Houston's comments upon it to the attention of the electors, who will be called upon to decide between this wretched sham and the reality of Home Rule.

At the inquest held on Monday, it transpired that the little girl who was killed at Weston Point, on Friday, lost her life through trying to save a basket. She had been picking cinders, and, seeing an en gine coming, she tried to run across the line to get her basket. But she was too late; she was knocked down and killed. There seems to have been a doubt as to whether the driver kept a sharp look-out; but as the girl was out of danger when he first saw her, he could not antici- pate that she would try to run in front of the en- gine. As children seem to be trespassing when they visit the cinder heaps, the question to con- sider is whether steps should not be taken to pre- vent access to this dangerous piece of land.

Three Conservative M.P.'s have brought in a bill for the regulation of the hours of shop assis- tants, and others—not forgetting the barmaids. It is said to be so stringent that public-houses would cease to employ barmaids rather than sub- ject themselves to the provisions of the bill. But worse things than that might happen. Anyhow, barmaids are quite as much entitled to protection as any other class. Unfortunately, there is small , prospect of the bill becoming law, for the Govern- 1 ment will swallow up most of the time of the House, if, as they promise to do, they manage 1 things as badly as they did last year. Meantime, shop assistants would do well to keep themselves to the front. Why not interview candidates in every constituency? The assistants may not as electors command a large number ot votes but they have a good cause, and the sympathy of voters of all classes.

THE BOILERMAKERS' AND IRON SHIPBUILDER S SOCIETY. The annual supper of the Warrington branch of this society was held at the Blue Bell Inn, on Mon- day evening. After Mrs. Korshaw had served an excellent repast, a presentation, consisting of a marble timepiece and pair of bronzes, was made, on behalf of the Warrington branch, to Bro. Wm. Hill, late secretary of the society, by Bro. It. Rhodes,pre- sident. Another presentation to the same recipient was then made by Bro. M. Smith, district delegate, on behalf of the Executive Conncil of the society, the article consisting of an emblem. The delegate said that this was one of the .most flourishing branches of the society in Lancashire. BURTON WOOD SCHOOL BOARD. The usual monthly meeting of the above Board was held in the class-room of the Board School, Burtonwood, on Tuesday, when there were present: —Messrs. James Warburton (chairman), John War- burton, Thomas Perks, WM. Fairclough, H. Gaw- thorpe (schoolmaster), John Forster (attendance officer), Wm. Webster (clerk). The minutes of the previous meeting were read and confirmed. Two applications for the hire of the schoolroom were read, and granted. A sub-committee was appointed to confer with the architects and invite tenders for the new wall, and the Clerk was instructed to warn the parents of a number of irregular scholars pre- paratory to taking out summonses.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
WESTON BIBLE AND MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.

At the usual weekly meeting of the above class held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, on Monday night last, an essay was given on" The Deluge "by Mr. Thomas Ford. There was a good attendance of the members.

div.head: PROMOTION OF SLTPERINTENDENT LARGE.
div.p: THE PROMOTION OF SLTPERINTENDENT LARGE.

On the magistrates taking their seats on the Bench on Monday, Mr. C. Reynolds congratulated Superintendent Large upon his promotion. He hoped it would prove a good thing for him, but the magistrates were sorry to lose him.—Major Hazlehurst concurred in these remarks, and Superintendent Large thanked the magistrates for their kindness, and introduced to them Superintendent Atherton, his successor, who was present.

div.head: RUNAWAY HORSE AT WIDNES.
div.p: A RUNAWAY HORSE AT WIDNES.

On Saturday morning a horse belonging to Mr. Mc Cririe, greengrocer, Victoria-road, took fright, and dashed along the thoroughfare at a furious gallop, and the attempts of the pedestrians to stop the animal in its mad career, were fruitless. On reaching the Central Hotel the horse turned the corner, and galloped to the central station, where the way is blocked, and then sud- denly became calm, arid allowed the driver to take charge of it.

div.head: WRECK OF I RUNCORN BOUND VESSEL.
div.p: WRECK OF I RUNCORN BOUND VESSEL.

The steamship Electra, of Liverpool, landed at Llanelly on Monday, the crew of the schooner Courier, of Mon- trose, and owned at Padstow, whom they rescued off the Pembrokeshire coast on Saturday. The Courier loft with a cargo of clay for Runcorn on Thursday, and during the heavy gale of that day she was dismasted, and became a total wreck by Friday, threatening to disappear beneath the mountainous waves. The crew, who belong to Cornwall, were taken to the Sailors' home. The Courier went down soon after being abandoned.

UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN. The fourth of the series of lectures on "The History of Florence " was delivered in Bethesda School on Monday evening by the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw, M.A. There was a good audience. The subject for the evening was " Savonarola," and the persdnal characteristics and the life's work of the ancient ecclesiastic were described in a highly graphic, interesting, and original manner. The lecture was prDfusely illustrated by views shown by a limelight lantern in charge of Mr. H. W. Handley.

SALVATLON ARMY AT RUNCORN. In the Barracks, High-st., on Saturday night, "Major Governor" Wright, formerly of Runcorn, delivered a lecture on the Farm Colony in Australia. Mr. S. Pope presided. On Sunday "Sergeant Major" Lea took his farewell for the training home, the service being con- ducted by Major Governor Wright. On Monday con- tingents of soldiers and officers front Runcorn and Widnes journeyed to Manchester to meet " General " Booth at the banquet held for the purpose of raising funds for a hospital for invalided officers. AN HOUR'S EXTENSION TO • RUNCORN PUBLICAN.

Mr. Charles Dutton,landlord of Wilson's Hotel, applied to Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Hazlehurst, for permission to keep his house open until midnight on Wednesday, on the cca einn of the dinner of the Rifle Volunteer Shooting Club. In reply to Mr. Reynolds, the Superintendent said he had no objection.—Mr. Reynolds referred to Major Hazlehurst for his opinion on the application, when the latter gentleman laughingly said he must not ask him, as he was a volunteer.—Mr. Reynolds granted the application,
WIDNES AND THE COUNTY COUNCIL.-SELECTION OF LIBERAL CANDIDATES.

A meeting of the Council of the Widnes Liberal Asso- ciation was held on Tuesday evening,in Lacey-st. School, for the purpose of selecting two candidates for the approaching election of councillors to Lancashire County Council. There was a large attendance. Mr. E. Carey presided. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., and Mr. Snape delivered addresses, after which Mr. Wilkinson moved a vote of confidence in them, selecting them as candi- dates. Mr. S. Owen seconded, and Messrs. Beach, J. H. Lee, and Dr. O'Keeffe supported, and it was carried unanimously. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. :DUTTON, Sankey-st.. Warrington.— Advt. CHARITABLE CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.

In aid of the widow and eight children of the late Thomas Cox, the Besses o'th' Barn Prize Band gave two sacred concerts in Runcorn Public Hall, on Sunday. The late Mr. Cox, who was a mgmber of the Upper Mersey Waternien and Porters' Association, and the Star of Frodsham Lodge ot the G.U.O.Oddfellows, met with an accident about six years ago which resulted in a linger. ing and painful illness,ending in his death in November A committee from the two societies named therefore determined to succour the widow and orphans and ar- ranged tde concerts, which were highly successful, the building being crowded, at both the afternoon and evening concerts. The programme included music from Handel, Mendelssohn, Cowen, Sullivan, &c., and the performers of the band were of the highest degree of merit, and were much enjoyed.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON. Sankey•st., Warrlngton.—Adrt.

RuNcoax.

After treating 554 old people to a bountiful repast and an enjoyable entertainment, the Committee of the aged persons' treat have left in hand a balance of £32 18s. fid. and some discussion has taken place as to how this sum shall be disposed of. Two counter propositions have , been made. Mr. S. Taylor suggested that the poor children of the town should be given a treat in the sum- mer, and Mr. Coventry broached the idea that a few old people should be taken to the seaside for a day or two to have the benefit a a change of air. The latter project was deemed tot) expensive, if not altogether impracti- cable, and the Committee almost unanimously adopted Mr. Taylor's suggestion. A Committee to formulate a scheme, and decide upon the plan to be visited has been formed, consisting of the headmasters of the schools of the town, the attendance officers, the Clerk to the School Board, and Messrs. Grice, Taylor, Coventry, Smith, T. Wood, W. Mundin (Ship Canal missionary) and W. T. Crosley. UMBRELLAS RECIOVERED.--1. and W. Durrox, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Ada. SAIM OF WORE AT WESTON POINT, On Monday afternoon a sale of useful and fancy articles was held in the Church schoolroom, Weston Point, in aid of a fund for the erection of a fence around the playground of that building. For three months frequent meetings of a sewing class have been held, and the members succeeded in manufacturing a large assort- ment of fancy and useful articles. They were greatly assisted in their labours by the members of the local branch of the Girls' Friendly Society. rn addition to these many gifts were received from friends in Weston and district. These were tastefully arranged on several , stalls around the room. The ladies who superintended the sales were the members of the sewing class :—Mrs. William McLean, the Misses McLean, Mrs. R. Clark, ' Mrs. W. Clark, Mrs. Gordon, Mrs. Frith, Mrs. A. Mc- Lean, Mrs. Harvey, the Misses Mills, Miss Hammersley, , Miss Grounds, Miss Myers, Miss Gordon, Miss Jane Stott, and Miss Alice Dunbavin. Besides the ladies mentioned, valuable services were rendered by the Rev. J. H. Wil- cockson and Mr. L. Rosenberg. There was a fair atten- dance during the afternoon. In the evening there was an enjoyable entertainment.

ST. HELENS COLLIERS AND THE THREATENED STOPPAGE. On Saturday a mcetirg of miners employed at the Sutton Heath and Lea Green Collieries, was held at the Railway Hotel, Thatto Heath, St. Helens. Re- solutions were passed in favour of petitioning Par- liament for an eight hours' day from bank to bank, and to stand loyal to the decision of the conference by ceasing to work on the 12th of March. A resolu- tion was also passed in favour of a five days' na- tional working week. The whole of the colliery proprietors in the St. Helens district have received notices from the men that they intend to cease work in accordance with the recent decision of the National Federation of Mirers. The notices were served by Mr. Thomas Glover, miners' agent, and between 2,000 and 3,000 colliers are affected. It is stated that they are unanimously in favour of the temporary stoppage.

div.head: TEI E EXAMINER, SAT UR_DA Y, FEBR
div.p: TEI E EXAMINER, SAT UR_DA Y, FEBR
A. SI7CCESBFUL BREEDER OF SHIRE HORSES.

Mr. Beckett Chadwick, J.P., of Crofton Lodge, Runcorn, who is well-known as a lover of horses, and who for some time put has been raising a stud of shires at his farm at Sutton Weaver, sent three mares this week to the London Shire Horse show. It will be gratifying to his many friends to learn that his two year old mare, Hawthorndale, has suc- ceeded in obtaining the first place for mares of that class, thus practically proving herself to be the best two year old in the kingdom. He has also taken second place with Lively in mares under 16 hands, of five years old and upwards. It may interest our readers generally to know that Franklyn,the sire of Hawthorndale, has just been engaged to travel in this district for the Warrington Shire Horse Society, Mr. Chadwick has, we understand, always pleasure in showing his stud to anyone interested in the improvement of the breed of horses. PETROLEUM OIL.-4. 8. Garland, Ironmonger, B lge-et. Warrington.—Advt.

CHARTERED INSTITUTE OF JOURNALISTS. The annual meeting of the Liverpool District of this Institute was held on Saturday afternoon, in the grand jury room, St. George's Hall, Mr. Charles Wall taking the chair. There was a large atten- dance, there being present from Warrington-- Messrs. S. Harriron, C. Lyon, F. Wood, J. Lawton, W. Gill, H. Isherwood, and J. G. Speed. Mr. J. Mason (senior secretary), read the report which stated that the institute as a whole had been very busy considering a variety of matters, the chief of which had been the arrangement of details and the raising of subscriptions forthe orphan fund. Mr. W. Wetherell ("Daily Post ") was elected chair- man of the district. Mr. J. A.. Willox, M.P., of the " Liverpool Courier," who entered the room subse- quently, was cordially received,and afterwards con- gratulated by resolution on his return to the House of Comm .rp=, which compliment he acknowledged in a speech of some length.—Mr. G. F. Gratwicke (Exeter), attended as a deputation from the insti- tute orphan committee, and explained the progress made in founding a fund. It was decided Mat the district should contribute a donation of five guineas towards the fund, and an annual subscription oT three guineas. The question of the proposed intro- duction of a system of examinations as qualifica- tions for admission to the Institute was left over to be discussed at the next quarterly meeting. Subse- quently the members were entertained to tea at the Bear's Paw, by Messrs. Egerton, Smith, and Co.,pro- prietors of the "Liverpool Mercury," the editor of that paper presiding.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED. —J, and W. Durrox, Sankey-A., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS. MR. OCKLESTON'S CANDIDATURE.
div.p: COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS. MR. OCKLESTON'S CANDIDATURE.

Mr. W. Ockleston, the Liberal candidate for Run- 'corn North, opened the election campaign on Tues- day evening,when a public meeting was held in St. Luke's Schoolroom, Mason-st. There was a fair at- tendance of electors from the neighbourhood. Mr. A. R. Norman presided,and he was supported by the I candidate, and Messrs. Temperley, Withington, Jep- son, Posnett, and John Clark (secretary). I The Chairman said he should be sorry if that contest were conducted on other than friendly lines, and with- out personalities. They had to deal, not with Major Hazlehurst as a private gentleman—as far as he was concerned he had not a word to say against him—but it was with Major Hazlehurst, County Councillor,they had to deal. Of course, he came before them as an indepen- dent candidate, but a man was either a Liberal and took Liberal views, or he was a Conservative and took Con- servative views on things, and no matter what was said to the contrary, there were questions that must come ' forward on the County Council which most be viewed on party lines. Very shortly, according to Mr. Henry Fowler, member for Wolverhampton, who would have a seat in the next Gladstonian Cabinet, the powers of the Council would be greatly increased, and it behoved them to send as their representative one who would represent the people thoroughly. (Hear, hear.) Then there was another thing about Major Hazlehurst. He had not been at all attentive to his duties, and there could only be two reasons for this ' • either he had not had time to do it, or he had been so disinterested in the thing that he did not care to go. Whichever was the reason, he was equally at fault. Mr. Norman condetnned the practice of making gentlemen who had not been elec- ted to the Council Aldermen, and thought improvement might be made in the constitution of the. Council in this respect. (Applause.) In conclusion he advocated the claims of Mr. Ockleston, whom he said, would attend to his duties and would strive to make himself acquainted with all questions with reference to our ccunty affairs and county Government, and who would become a very popular'member if they should be able to return him. (Applause.) Mr. Ockleston, who was cordially received, then de- livered an address. He said he was very pleased indeed to meet the electors there that night and to be attic to put before them a few of the things he would support if returned by them to the Council. In the first place he was a Liberal to the backbone. (Applause) He was a Home Ruler. (Applause.) He was a Home Ruler, , not of Ireland on that occasion, but of Cheshire. (Ap- plause.) He believed in the elective council managing the affairs of the county ; and by and bye when the new Parliament was formed, a Bill giving power to form dis- trict councils would be passed and then each district could manage its own small affairs. (Hear, hear.) The question of allotments would be on for these councils to deal with, and they hoped to be able to make it com- pulsory that a man could have an allotment at a fair average price. (Applause.) With regard to finance, money was easily spent, but it was not so easily earned. (Laughter.) Somehow everybody begrudged paying rates, whether great or small,but when the rates became doubled then they began to cry out decidedly, Since the Council had been in existence they had doub'ed the rate, compared with the amount levied by the magistrates, and why no one seemed to know, but they had to pay it. What he wanted was that they should have a ratepayer to represent them. (Applause.) If they had a ratepayer to represent them, they might be sure that he would look after the rates not only for his own sake, but for theirs, but if they had not a ratepayer, he would not care whether the rate was raised to a shilling or was dropped to 3d. It made no difference to such a man, but to a ratepayer like himself the rates meant a big item, and if hh were returned as their representative he should do his best to reduce those rates. (Applause.) With regard to the police the ratepayers found the money for their existence and equipment, and the force ought to be under the rule and government of the Council as the representative authority of the rate- payers. (Hear, hen.) At the present time police were just managed by the Chief Constable, but recently a court of appeal has been formed to which constables could fortunately appeal for justice when they had any grievances, but still in his opinion they ought to be entirely under the control of the Council. As to technical education, it was much wanted amongst the poorer classes, and the clerks especially wanted a knowledge of foreign lan- guages so that they could compete with the better educated foreigner, who now catne to England and usurped their places. He specially advocated the teach- ing of German, but said that of course complete and thorough teaching in many other things was necessary for the future welfare of the nation. (Applause.) As to the lines on which that contest was being fought, he was a Liberal ; Major Hazlehurst was an Independent, but they knew what his politics were. (Hear, hear.) Some Conservatives said politics should be entirely left out of the Council and done on what they call independ- ent lines. What did independent mean P It meant that the Independent member could do just as he liked and not be called in question for it afterwards. (Applause.) But no man could be independent so far as politics were concerned. He must be either a Tory or a Liberal, and he (Mr. Ockleston) came forward as a can- didate simply and solelyas a Liberal. (Applause.) If they allowed their influence to be frittered away as an indepen- dent liked, it was their own look-out. He should not like to go to the Council without some definite principles to work upon. (Applause.) He should go to the Council bound by Liberal ties, and if he happened to break those ties they would be able to call him to order, and unless he could give some plain answer, they could say " You betrayed us. There were certain things in connection with the town he would mention. There was the pro- posed vehicular bridge. He would support the carrying I out of that project thoroughly, independent of politics or anything else—(Applause)—because it would bring good to the town and to the country. Then main roads must be looked after, and he should support having good roads and good footpaths. In conclusion he said he maintained everything stated in his address and he hoped he had spoken clearly and in a Liberal spirit; and if he were returned to the Council he would endeavour to show that they had not misplaced their trust. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Jepson moved a resolution declaring Mr. Ockleston a fit and proper person to represent the division in the County Council and pledging the meeting to use every legitimate means to ensure his return. If they wanted a good sound Liberal send Mr. Ockleston. He did not wish to go as an independent to do anything or to do nothing, but as a man anxious to represent their wishes. He W 29 a large employer of labour, and he (Mr. Jepson)was glad to say he had not joined a syndicate. (Applause.) That should be something in his favour. (Laughter and a voice "We have syndicate enough in Runcorn.") He did not see that syndicates had done much good for the workmen. (" No, no" and applause.) A fair day's wage for a fair day's werk was the plan—(applause)— and they would desire nothing more. A man was known by the company he kept. If they looked at the company' Major Hazlehurst kept they would find they had received very little benefit from the party that he was connected with. What benefits they had received as workmen he was bold to say had come from the Liberal party. He

said the Tories were trying to carry on the same game on Cheshire County Council as the Tories did in Liverpool Corporation, by their system of electing Aldermen, and if they were anxious that this should be avoided send Mr. Ockleston there, Mr. Ockleston's address was not a skeleton; it had some body in it and was well worth reading and studying, If he was not very fluent of speech he had something in his " noddle "—(laughter and applause)—and if they returned him they would have no cause to regret in three years hence. Mr. iemperley seconded the motion. They had be- fore them a tried wan and an untried man,and the former asked for votes without telling them anything about his stewardship during the past three years. (Hear, hear.) He did not see how he could have the audacity to come before the ratepayers and ask for their support after the very meagre attendances he had niade at the Council. In Mr. Ockleston they had an untried man, but he came straightforwardly and told them what he intended to do if they sent him, and he (the speaker) be- lieved they would send him. (Applause.) lie found that the working-men were in sympathy with Mr. Ockleston, who had pronounced in faveur of a fair day's ' wage for a fair day's work, and that his opponent dare not put in his address. There were many who would remember Major Hazlehurst making fair promises at the top side of the market when he was elected. He told the electors "you have done me the greatest honour possible for you to do except sending me to the Imperial Parliament," and he would not forget the ratepayers for it. (A Voice: "He didn't." Laughter.) They knew what happened in a very few days afterwards; he need not tell them, because it was present in their minds, and he thought that was one reason why Major Hazlehurst did not put that phrase in his address, because he would have been tackled upon it pretty sharp. (Applause.) Mr. Withing,ton supported the motion in an able speech. Mr. Posnett also supported the resolution. He said there were two great evils that the working-men had to fight against, and the first of these was overcrowded dwellings. Both parties had shown themselves in favour of allotments, but the difference between the two parties was quite clear. The Liberal party said the allotments must be made compulsory so that if a man wanted a piece of land—whether it belonged to the Marquis of Cholmondeley did not matter—he must have that land at a reasonable price and have a decent dwelling. The Tory party brought in an Allotment Bill last night, but this compulsory clause was not inserted, and this fact killed the Bill altc,gether. If a landlord chose to keep his land to himself he ought to pay the full rateable value for that land. (Applause.) The great scandal of the present age was that landed property was not rated to its full value. (Applause.) The other great evil was an overcrowded labour market. This over- crowding might be caused by had trade, by paupers coming into the country; it might be caused by— (" Prins" loud laughter)—anything they liked; but whatever the cause, they wanted to get rid of it. An I eight hours bill had been suggested, but while he be- lieved in it for miners, he did not think it was practic- able for working-men all round. He believed that if they had a minimum wage for adult men in England they would have solved the question as near as it could be solved. A minimum wage would prevent sweating, for it was sweating that caused a man to be unable to obtain a fair day's wage for a fair day's work. (Ap- plause.) He believed that the Liberal party was the I party that would be for the benefit of the working-men 1 in the long run, and he believed that they would be do- ing the best they could by sending a Liberal to the County Council. (Applause.) , The motion was carried unanimously,and Mr. Ockles- ton in reply said if elected he would do his duty. He moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman. Mr. John Clark seconded. He trusted this was only Mr. Norman's introduction to public life. They had read a good deal in the newspapers of the proceedings of the Board of Commissioners, and he thought if the ratepayers would take a genuine interest in local affairs and choose sound men to attend to them, they would gain very much in the long run. (Hear, hear.) They could not do better than keep their eyes upon Mr. Norman for one of the vacant positions. . _
The motion was carried unanimously, and the meeting terminated.

MEETING IN DUKE'S FIELD. A public meeting was held on Thursday night in the Mission Hall, Duke's Field, in furtherance of the candidature of Mr. Ockleston. There was a good attendance, and Mr. A. R. Norman presided. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman condemned the cry that was being raised about independency, and described it as nothing less than a Wind, but he hoped the electors of the North Division would be wide awake to their interests. (Hear, hear.) In Runcorn they appeared to have some very weak-kneed Liberals, and this cry of going on independent lines was to enable these gentlemen not to declare themselves one way or the other. It seemed to him that if they were alive to their interests, they would make it hot for these gentlemen who would take a neutral or would not take a straight- forward action either one side or another. (Applause.) In any matter not connected with politics, no one would give a more fair and unbiassed consideration than Mr. Ockleston, but supposing any political matter was brought before the Council, which was not unlikely, then they knew what Mr. Ockleston r.s a thoroughgo- ing, Liberal would do. (Applause.) Mr. Hazlehurs t claimed to be independent but they knew that he was a Conservative and in any political matter he would vote according to his political principles—(hear. hear)—and it therefore behoved them to send a representative who held the political views they themselves did. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. Ockleston, who was applauded on rising, went over the ground of the speech delivered on Tues- day evening. Referring to finance lie said he would try to keep down the rates. Their late member was not a ratepayer, so that it did not much matter whether the rate was a shilling or threepence. It did not affect his pocket, but it certainly affected theirs and his (Mr. Ockl.,!ston's). (Applause.) He met a gentleman the other day who said he (Mr. Ockleston) did not spend any money in the town. He replied that perhaps personally he did not spend much, but, he pointed out that he paid wages to the extent of at least £5,200 a year, and thus caused a large amount of money to be spent in the town. The gentle- man replied that he had never thought of that. His opponent did not live in the town, had no works in the town, and he wondered what money he spent in the town if he (Mr. Ockleston) did not. (Hear, hear.) After a reference to various matters mentioned in his address, Mr.Ockleston spoke of the cry of independence, and said it was raised by the Tories because they knew that they had not the slightest chance if they fought the contest on a straight issue. (Applause.) Mr. T.Cooke,who had taken the chair in consequence of Mr. Norman having to leave the meeting,said three years ' ago when Major Hazlehurst was returned, it was claimed that he Was a large employer and a large ratepayer, and now he was neither. Major Hazlehurst ought to be ashamed to coins before them again when during three years he had had the audacity to appear in the Council on only three occasions. (Hear, hear.) Mr. T. Dean moved a resolution pledging the meeting to use all legitimate means to secure Mr. Ockleston's triumphant return.—Mr. Withington seconded in a vigor- ous speech.—Mr. William Handley supported the resolu- tion, and pointed out that Runcorn North was the largest division in Cheshire and therefore an important point of attack, and had it been a Tory stronghold he did not think they would have heard anything about conducting the contest on independent lines at all. (Hear, hear.) He pointed out that Major Hazlehurst voted against the County Council having the control of the police, and also that various questions of a political character of which the Liberal party were in favour, would be brought before the County Council, and they might judge for themselves which way Major Hazlehurst would vote. (Applause.)—Mr. D. Bisbrown and Mr. Jepson also supported the resolution, which was unani- mously carried. A vote of thanks to the Chairman con- cluded the proceedings. MAJOR HAZLEHURST'S CANDIDATURE, A public meeting in support of Major Hazlehursts candidature for Runcorn North, was held in the Mersey Mission Room, Bottom Locks, on Wednes- day night. Mr. S. Taylor was voted to the chair, and on the platform were the candidate and Mr. T. H. Annett, his agent. Amongst those present were Messrs. E. Inison, T. Jones, W. Sharrocks, J. K. Digges, Hewitt, Toone, J. Tickle, H. ffoward, W. Mellor, J. MeadoWeroft, &c. There was a good attendance.

The Chairman said he had no idea of taking the chair when he appeared there that night. He was present because Mr. Hazlehurst was coming out on independent iines a course of action which he himself had advocated during this election. He had come out for the South Division on independent lines, and those lines only, was unpersonal feeling to anyone, out he had a strong feel- ing that no one should be sent to represent Runcorn only on independent lines. (Applause.) As to Mr. Ockleston there was not a gentleman in Rencorn for whom he had more respect ; he had known him from a boy, and he was extremely sorry that politics had been introduced in this matter, for there was not one iota of reason why they should be. Major Hazlehurst, who was received with applause, said it had been reported that it was impossible for him to be an independent candidate, that he must be biassed one way or the other—he must either be a Conservative or a Liberal. Three years ago he assuren them that he would have nothing to do with politics so far as County Council work was concerned, and that promise he had faithfully kept. He had nothing at all to do with poli- tics, and ha stood in precisely the same position now as he did then. He had never voted politically. When- ever a debate had taken place he had listened with the greatest attention possible, and when it came time to vote, the whole thing had resolved itself into the ques- tion "What is the proper thing to do for the ratepayers ?" (Applause.) As to his attendance, it had many times bern absolutely impossible for him to attend,and he was not present because he was was shirking his work. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the complaints made of the high County Council rates, the speaker said he had obtained some authentic figures from the county auditor, which he would lay before them. it would appear by merely taking the several amounts at which the rate had been levied during the past ehree

k years that there was some excuse for the opinion which 1 the ratlepayers might have that the management of the ' Council was a more expensive matter under the County Council then it was under the old regime, but if circum- stances were closely looked into, such was not the fact, but that the work was managed quite as economically ' when it was performed by the magistrates, and notwith- standing that the work of the County Council had been increased more than four-fold, and is very much more completed, and in many respects more important. Dur- ing many years past previous to the County Council,the county rate was not lower than 3d. in the £, and very often 4d. in the £, and in the year 1872 was 51d. in the £, notwithstanding that in that year there were no main roads charged in the county rate, and also that the River Weaver then paid a large grant to the county. And the rates levied by the County Council had only been to meet actual expenditure incurred. The magistrates, it appeared, levied only as it were upon an estimate three months in advance, or practically speakhag,for immedi- ate requirements without taking into account actual liability incurred. And when the County Couacil came into existenco on the let April, 1889 there were liabilities outstanding of about £26,000 and the usual county rate of the preceding January unlevied. So that the County Council to commence with, had to provide a budget for its own estimated liabilities for the 12 months and also for the £26,000 liabilities and also no rate levied for the previous Janu- ary so as to provide for • working balance. The year also was the first year in which the county had to provide for the total cost of main roads (not a quarter as prev- iously) as well as for new items of expenditure, such as the cost of County Council elections, and other matters not previously heard of. And the result of all this was that speaking only of the County rate, the County Council had at once to provide for a rate of eid. in the £, or double what it had been in the previous year under the magistrates. Hnd also this first year the County Council had to take into account a newiprinciple i.e. to estimate fcr actual expenditure incurred so that each year might provide for its own expenditure and the ratepayersaccordingly saddled only therewith. But in the following year the Council felt the benefit of having fully met its liabilities and the county rate then fell to 30. in the £, notwithstanding the large expenditure on main roads and the usual monies, £lO,OOO or £15,000 from the river Weaver not being received. The present year's estimate brings the county rate up to sd. in the £, and that was in order to meet its actual liabilities for with a growth of expenditure upon main roads and no receipts from the river Weaver and other matters. But it might be anticipated that as the main roads expendi- ture continues to increase by reason of other roads being declared main roads and their maintenance thrown upon the connty rate, the county rate must increase accord- ingly. But as the relief was in to Highway Authori- ties, whether rural or urban, n the maintenance of their main roads by charging the whole on the county rate and thereby spreading the c)st thereof over the whole county area, there should be a very considerable de- crease in the local highway rates of the county which were levied by the Local Boards, Highway Boards, and boroughs. It might be mentioned that one of the grants paid by the county was the grant for " costs of Union offieers," and this was an entirely new payment to the Unions anii the County Unions together benefitted to over £15,000 per annum by this. So that it was really not the County Council which was more expensive but that its work was different and it had greater liabilities to meet. The Highway and Local Boards shonld, however, show a considerable reduction in /their ex- penditure equal at least to 2d. in the £, and the Unions should also show a reduction in their expenditure to the above £15,000 for costs of Union .officers.— In conclusion he said he could afford more time to this work than he had during the past three years, and any , work entrusted to him by the ratepayers should be car- ried through in the best possible lorm for them. (Ap- plause.) He stood by his andress and he was in favour of the three things mentiosecl by the Chairman as essential to the prosperity of Runcorn, and it would afford him the greatest pleasure to give every possible effort to bring these things into an accomplished fact. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. Sanders, seconded by Mr. IP Coward a resolution was passed unanimously declaring Major Hazlehurst a fit and proper person to represent the North Division and pledging the meeting to use every legitimate means to secure his return.—ln reply- ' ing Major Hazlehurst expressed his satisfaction at Ir. Taylor's support and moved a vote of thanks to him for presiding.—Mr. W. Shaw seconded and Mr. W. Mellor supporthd and it was carried.—The meeting then de- parted.

div.head: MAJOR HAZLEHURST AND THE LIQUOR
div.p: MAJOR HAZLEHURST AND THE LIQUOR
TRADE.

A deputation of the Licensed Victuallers of Run- corn waited upon Major Razlehurst on Thursday, at the offices of Linaker and Linaker to ascertain his views on the licensing question. The deputation was headed by Mr. Thomas Jones, president of the Licensed Victuallers' Association.—Major Ilazle- hurst in reply said he was opposed to the direct veto or local option, and that he was in favour of Sunday Clos- ing in the publicans' interest; but he had grave doubts as to the benefit it would confer upon the cause of tem- perance. As a business man he was opposed to taking away from any legalised trade that which had been paid for, and consequently he would give fair and reasonable compensation for licenses that were compulsorily taken away in the absence of bad conduct. RETIREMENT OF MR. TAYLOR.

Since last week a great change has taken place in Runcorn South. Mr. Philip Speakman the pres- ent member) and Mr. Samuel Taylor were in the field and a contest of an exciting character seemed not only probable but certain. Both candidates had organised a band of workers, and canvassing was being briskly carried on in their respective interests. When it became known that Mr. Taylor had retired in favour of Mr. Speakman, the following correspondence, which has passed between the two gentlemen, will explain the position : " Rydal Mount, February, 20th, 1892. My dear Speakman,—l am pleased to learn that you have have now decided to stand on independent lines, and have given pledges all round to act in this spirit in mat- ters affecting the welfare of the division. In view of this declaration, I do not deem it advisable to provoke a contest, on personal lines, with its attendant unpleasant- ness to our mutual friends,and have,therefore,decided to withdraw my candidature in your favour.—Yours faith- fully, SAMUEL TAYLOR."—" The Mount, Higher Runcorn February 20th, 1892. My dear Taylor,—l keenly appreciate your kindness in retiring in my favour, and can assure both yourself and your supporters that I will do all in my power to convince them that my sole aim shall be the welfare of the division.—Yours faithfully, P. SPEAXISM" As both gentlemen are connected with the Liberal party, and are, moreover, closely associated in public work, this termination to the contest is gener- ally approved. In public estimation the two gentlemen deservedly hold a high position, and a contest between them must have had more or less a personal character, which is now happily avoided. It is highly probable that Mr. Speakman will be re-elected without opposition to the honourable and responsible position he has filled for the past three years.

div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS..

TRIIRSDLY.—B—EiO-I:o—Mr. J. Birchall and Mr. J. Stone. MiscaraANEons.--Joseph Harrison, no fixed abode,was bound over to keep the peace for fighting. A fine of Is and costs was imposed upon Walter Allen, Pleasant-st., for allowing the chimney of his dwelling to be on fire. THE ALKALI UNION AND THEIR WED:MTS.—The United Alkali Company were summoned for having in use for trade at the Widnes works of Messrs. Liddell and Co., weights which were unjust. Inspector Kilpatrick found 12 weights used for weighing caustic soda drugs, which were 330 z. 15dr. light in the aggregate. A fine of 40s. and costs was imposed.

div.head: FRODSHAM PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Dr. . Steele.
div.p: FRODSHAM PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Dr. . Steele.

A FEROCIOUS Doo.—Wm. Humphreys, a gentleman, of Dunham o'th' Hill, was charged with allowing a ferocious dog to be at large and not under proper control on the 20th January. Evidence was given showing that the animal had bitten a number of people. The defen- dant expressed himself willing to destroy the dog, but his wife objected.—Mrs. Humphreys said the place was lonely and many beggars frequented the locality. They were obliged to keep the dog for pretection.—The Bench made an order for the dog to be kept under proper con- t:ol, the defendant to pay costs £1 Bs. 6d. A WARRANT.--Joseph Allman failed to appear to a summons charging him with assaulting John Mercer, in Bridge-lane, on the 20th February, and a warrant was granted for his apprehension. AN IMPORTANT ANNOUNCEMENT.-A number of sum- monses were withdrawn and Mr. Reynolds said the magis- trates had determined that in future all cases should be adjudicated upon and not to allow summonses to be with- drawn at the individual's desire. He believed many summonses were taken out as a means of extorting money.

div.p: PENKETH.

St7CCESSOF A. PENICETH STUDRNT. I The certificate lists from the different training colleges have just been published, and from these it appears that Miss M. S. Routledße, who has just completed her two years' training, comes out as a second girl, first class, in her college. Miss ' Routledge served as pupil teacher at the Penketh Wesleyan School under its present master, Mr. James Watson. A DANCE. Another dance, inaugurated by Mr. Pownall, in aid of the funds of the Sankey Brass Band, was held on Saturday evening, in the Conservative Club. There were a large number of couples present. The Sankey Brass Band supplied the music, and Mr. Kent and Mr. Sutton officiated as masters of the ceremonies. Refreshments, provided by Mr. Pow- nail, were partaken of during the evening.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

I see that Commissioner Kerr has been severely rebuking a policeman, at the Old Bailey for saying of a prisonAr on trial that he was "well known t the police as a bad character." Some of the police at Warrington are rather too much addicted on occasions to making these additions to their evi- dence, and I think such statements, which are often thrown in to bolster up, in an indirect way,cases not particularly strong in themselves, and unsupported by any testimony of previous conviction are im- portations into evidence which ought to be sternly discountenanced by our magistrates.

There is another thing that is deplorably common in the police courts of this country, including those of this district,and that is the habit constables have of suppressing in their evidence facts which. might tell in favour of defendants, while, however, not necessarily saying anything that is not the literal truth. Of course they are precluded some— times, by being narrowed rigidly down by solicitors to the simple replies of " Yes " or " No." But policemen are, even in cases in which there are no solicitors concerned to check the free use of their tongues, too much accustomed to conceal circum— stances which might militate against conviction. If these happen to be dragged out of them in a pressing cross-examination, and it is inquired why they did not mention them before, they calmly content themselves with replying that they were never asked.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, an instance in point occurred. Two men were charged with poaching. One of them was promptly extri- cated from his unpleasant position by Mr. Bro vne, solicitor, without any evidence being heard ag.4nst him, as the man was dismissed on account of the summons being illegal. The proseci ;;ing con- stable in the case, in his evidence, stated that the two men accounted for one of them having posses- sion of two dead rabbits, by saying that they had got them from the farm of Mr. John Lightfoot, at Stretton ; but on going to Stretton he could find no Mr. Lightfoot there. Now it happened that there was a Mr. Samuel Lightfoot, a farmer,living at An- trobus, and just on the borders of Stretton. Mr. Browne asked the constable whether there was not a farmer named Lightfoot living at Antro- ' but he replied "Not at Stretton." But he showed by this and other answers to Mr. Browne that he well knew there was a farmer of that name at Antrobus. The statement of the men was therefore practically correct and was probably sincere, since they could have no motive for,and there would have been no use in, saying Stretton instead of Antrobus when Lightfoot could not fail to be discovered.. As to their giving the farmer's Christian name as John instead of Samuel the constable might easily have been mistaken. But why did the constable merely say he could find no Mr. Lightfoot at Settle, when he knew perfectly well that there was a man of that name in the immediate vicinity? And why did he not call on Mr. Lightfoot to ascertain whether the men's statement was true, or if he did call, why did he not state in court the result of his call ?

An equestrian magistrate was seen while coming from Daresbury Sessions the other day to be riding on the footpath. An examination of the pathway gave unmistakable indications of a horse, probably the worthy magistrate's, having been ridden on it that morning in a contrary direction. It is true that in both cases this breach of the law had been committed to avoid stones laid down in the road for a short distance, and that the rider was not long on the footpath, and nobody was inconvenienced for a mement. But, then, whenever a bicyclist or somebody else is brought up for a like offence at Daresbury,or anywhere else, these same excuses are almost always urged and are always unavailing. O'Connell said he could drive a coach and six through any Act of Parliament ever framed. I have seen horses ridden at a leap through a gigantic ring-encircled sheet of tissue paper placed on high at a circus. But there was a risk to the rider in this exploit,and so there might be to the rider, even if a magistrate, who attempted too often the feat of riding through an Act of Parliament. He, at least, ought not to set the fashion of trying a modest realisation of O'Connell's boast.

The good people at Bartonwood, who have until just recently been considered a quiet easy-going sample of the farmer class, cannot somehow or other get along comfortably with their new vicar. For years they have been accustomed to the very low Church worship, but since the new vicar was installed by the Rector of Warrington, on the death of the Rev. W. Wilson, the congregation have been treated to some very high church notions, such as the eastward form and early sacraments. Collections every Sunday at the close of each service are also objectionable to the people when they have been in the habit of having, say, only three collections dur- ing the year.

The wardrns hare actually rebelled, and a week or two ago, when the vicar announced that a collec- tion would be made at the end of the service, the wardens absolutely declined to make it. The vicar, seeing the position of affairs, said that as his wishes had not been carried out he hoped the people would make use of the offertory box at the door, which turned out a forlorn hope.
Of course I cannot say where the business is going to end, but I fancy that at Easter there will be a general clearing out, and no doubt one or two lively episodes.

Mr. Aylward, the headmaster of the Warrington School of Art is one of those fortunate individuals who are honoured in their own country. At least I gather ss much from the flattering reception which he received the other evening, when he lectured on" Venice" to a crowded audience at the Brassey Institute, Hastings. The " Hastings Observer," speaking of Mr. Aylward, says—" Our School should be and is proud of him, as he is proud of his early connection with the school. Amongst the several capable art teachers that Mr. Sullivan has given to the country Mr. Aylward stands, if not premier, at least high in the front rank. If our old yet, in point of age, young, townsman has a warm corner in his heart for Hastings, and especially for the Institution in which he acquired the rudiments of his calling and was fitted to go forth and attain a position of distinction in the certificated Art teaching world. Hastings—or at all events, that cultivated section of Hasting, which now for many years has nestled snugly away in the commodious Brassey Buildings, Claremont—holds him warmly, not to say affectionately, in its memory." MERLIN.

div.head: PEARL LIFE ASSURANCE CO., LIR TED.
div.p: PEARL LIFE ASSURANCE CO., LIR TED.

The 28th annual report and balance sheet of this company has been issued, and is of a highly satis- factory character. The directors declare a rever- sionary bonus of £1 per cent. on the participation policies in the ordinary branch of the Company. During the year 431,911 policies were issued, representing a new annual premium income of £191,911 Bs. Id. The total income for Ithe year amounted to £320,405 'is. 4d. ' The premium income on the policies in force on the Company's books in December last amounted to £343,914 198. id. The Company has paid 90,085 claims and grants during the year, the amount of these being £146,029 Gs. 101(1. This, added to the sums previously paid in claims since the forma- tion of the company, makes the splendid total of £983,819 158. The life assurance fund has been in- creased during the year by £20,332 14s. 4d., and the assurance fund, with capital paid up now - reaches the sum of £284,131 12s. 3d. The directors, recommended the payment of a dividend of 10 per cent. on Monday last. It will be gathered from% these facts and figures that the Pearl Life Assur- ance Company is in a flourishing and prosperous. condition. The energetic superintendent for this. district is Mr. J. A. Cavanagh, of 8, ArPleY-st..

div.head: CHARGES OF GROSS CRUELTY AGAINS- A MOTHER.
div.p: CHARGES OF GROSS CRUELTY AGAINS- A MOTHER.

At Coleraine on Thursday, Mrs. Margaret Montagu- was committed for trial at the Londonderry Assizes, charged with the manslaughter of her daughtrr Helen, aged three years. It is alleged that she caused the girl's death by ciuelty—that she tied the child by the arms to a ring in a dark closet. Evidence was given by a governess to the effect that the little one was sent into the wardrobe-room for misbehaviour, and the next time she saw the child it was lying dead. After Mrs. Montagu had been committed, bail being ' allowed, the magistrates decided to hear the evidene against her on the additional charge of systematic cruelty. The allegation in this case was that she had greviously ill-treated three boys—Walter, Gilbert, and Austin Montague—tying one to a tree, suspending another by cords in a dark closet, and dragging the third by the legs, his head trailing on the floor. Mrs. Montagu was also committed for trial on the second charge,
