div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
ABRAIILT ON A MAIL CART DRIVER.

At the Warrington borough police court, yesterday, Felix Magian, 13, White-st., a mail cart contractor, was summoned on a charge of assaulting Robert Lowe, in his employ as a driver. The assault was admitted, and arose through the complainant, as alleged, putting a wet rug on a clipped horse and his refusal to do big duty, and being insolent. The complainant denied this. rhe defendant, who said he struck the complainant to com- pel him to do his work, was ordered to pay the costs, the Chairman informing him that this was not a record of conviction, and the complainant that there was much fault on his side; though the defendant's remedy was dismissal.

div.head: THEFT or A Er strnazrtemEr.
div.p: THEFT or A Er strnazrtemEr.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday, Wm. Scott. fireman, 13, Jackson's-court, and John Whalley, engine cleaner, Napier-st., were charged with stealing, or receiving, knowing it to have been stolen, A silk handkerchief, the property of Edgar V. Morton, pawnbroker, St. James's-st., Latchford. Scott went to the shop with Whalley' s watch and chain, and said he wanted to pawn them, and was observed to put the handkerchief in his pocket. He ran out, but was pur- sued and given into custody. He told the police he'had given the handkerchief to Whalley. Whalley was sent for to the Police Station, and on being questioned, pro- duced the handkerchief. Scott was lined 20s.and costs, and Wkalley 10s. and costs; in default the usual alter- native.

div.head: BRUTAL Wiz ASSAULT.
div.p: A BRUTAL Wiz ASSAULT.

At the Warrington borough police court, yesterday, Thomas Massey, fareman fustian cutter, of 2, Lord Nelson-st., was charged with violently assaulting his wife Mary Massey. Mr. Browne appeared for the pro- secution. From his statemeat and Mr 3. Massey's evid- ence it appeared that he had come home under the in- fluence of drink and asked her for another shilling, and because she refused it dragged her by the hair of the head, pulled a quantity of her hair out, struck her, nearly pinched her noseoff, and threw her into the fire- place. This cruelty had been going on for years,and she considered her life was in peril. Mr. Browne asked for a separation order and an allowance of 15s. a week, but she did not desire him to go to prison. The magistrates made the order requested and fined the defendant 51.

div.head: Two JUVENILIA NIGIT ARAM.
div.p: Two JUVENILIA NIGIT ARAM.

At the borough magistrates' court, on Wednesday, Charles Rowe, aged le, lividg at a lodging-house on Town Hill, and John Tate, aged 13, late of Liverpool, were charged that they being persons of suspicious character were found frequenting Leigh-street, at a quarter past three that morning with intent to commit a felony.—P.C. Jones produced an article of very rough construction, which he,described as a ladder, and said it , had been brought to him as having been found at the back of No. 58, Legh-street, where an attempt had been made to break into the house. He went there three times, the last time being at W minutes past one, and examined the place, but could not hear or see anyone about. At a quarter past three he heard some noise, and found the prisoners in the entry close by, in a stooping position against the wall.—Rowe said Picker- ing, of London, had had a van in Warrington and he had been travelling with it, and when it left the town had been thrown out of employment.—Tate said he had been in a day industrial sch)ol at Liverpool.—lt was stated that Rowe had been brought up for stealing a watch from a woman living at 66 Buttermarket-street, who had maintained him.—The prisoners denied their guilt, and any knowledge of the ladder.—Tate was remanded till Thursday that his parents might be communicated ' with, and Rowe was dismissed, with a threat of the ' Refot matory if brought up again. Tait was brought up on Thursday morning, and was sent back to the Indus- trial school at Liverpool at which he had formerly been, his fare being paid out of the poor box.

div.head: . MINOR CASES. WARRIN6TON BOEOUGII POLICE COURT, Sertrarar.—Before Mr.. Voisez fin the chair) and kr.
div.p: . MINOR CASES. WARRIN6TON BOEOUGII POLICE COURT, Sertrarar.—Before Mr.. Voisez fin the chair) and kr.
John Ge-ddes.

DESERTERS.—Thomas Callaghan and John Elliot were charged with being deserters from her Majesty's East Yorkshire Regiment, stationed at Manchester.—Re- manded to Strangeways Gaol to await an escort. THREATS.—Peter Farrell was charged with using threats towards his wife on the 29th January.—lt was stated that the wife was a very industrious woman. She had a daughter about 16 years of age, who worked in the factory. They could do very well without the prisoner, who lived upon their earnings.—He was bound over in two sureties of £5 to keep the peace, or in default one month's imprisonment. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) (chair- man), Aldermen Harrison and Chandley, and Maj Pickmere. D RUNK .—John Towey, drunk at the Police Station, on Saturday morning, who had walked into the Station with his head bleeding, and been there and then locked up. was fined 2s. the lock-up-fee. ta DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Wm. Stringer, labourer, a married man, 6, Pocket-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the street and assaulting Mary Ann Shaw, a widow, with whom he lives. He was in the house,quarrelling about the children being in the house, and he gave her a black eye with his hand, and threatened her with the poker. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Cl. Parr (chairman', W. Long_, J. Marson and C. Marson. CRUELTY TO A bIORSIL—Thos. Pimblett, postman, of Northwich, was charged by Inspector Dowty,R.S.P.C.A. with ill-treating and abusing a pony on the 13th inst. at Seven Oaks.—Joseph Wilkinson, farmer, deposed to the pony being confined in a field without shelter or food ' and dying on the 13th inst. There was plenty of grass OR the field so long as the weather was open, but the field was covered with snow for nine days before it died. He gave it an armful of hay the day before it died.— Servants of Mr. Wilkinson corroborated, an 4 they said at Mr:Wilkinson's request they gave the pony some hay daily, as it bad nothing else to eat.—Mr. Drmkwater of the Cock Inn, Budworth, confirmed this evidence.—Mr. Dowty also deposed to examining the horse's stomach, and expressed, the opinion that the puny had died of starvation and exposure : there was nothing in the stomach but a little dried hay.—A police sergeant cor- roborated Mr. Dowty's evidence, and said the pony was nothing but skin and bone.—The defendant did ndt- appear, but was represented by his wife. The case was, dismissed with costs.
DRI7NE AND DISORDBRLT.—IIichard Flamblett, junr. and James Dobson, both of Appleton, drunk and dis- orderly at that place on the 13th inst., were each fined ss. and costs.

Doc AT LAllol3.—John Whitelegge, of Appleton, for allowing his dog to be at large there unmuzzled on the 26th ult., was fined ss. including costs. ASLEEP ON THEIS LIIRRIES.—James Seed, of Winwick- st., Warrington, for being asleep on his harry at Apple- ton, on the 11th inst., was fined 54. and costs.—Charles James, of Latchford, asle2p in charge of his lurry at Appleton, was fised ss. CHARGES op POACNING.—James Green, tanner, of Latchford, was charged with being found at Grappen- holt on the 9th inst., coming it was suspected, from land where he had been in search of game, and that on being searched two rabbits were found upon him. Thomas Boardman, tanner, of Latchford, was charged with being found coming with him from the same direction he having a ferret in his, possession. Mr. Browne, et Warrington appeared for the defendants, and pleaded not guilty. In the case of Thomas Boardman, he took exception to the summons. It was taken out, he said under section 2 of the Poaching Pre- verttion Act. 1862, and Boardman was not found to be in possession of a gun, part of a gun, net or any "engine or instrument" that might be used for poaching men- tioned in the section, but only of a ferret which was not mentioned and was not an engine or instrument. There- fore the summons was bad; and it had been held there over and over again that a ferret did not come within the meaning of the section.—The bench accepted this plea, and Boardman was thereupon dism issed.—P.C. Millington then gave evidence as to Green's case. He said he found two warm rabbits, in the defendant's pocket, and he and Boardman said they had been to Mr. John Lightfoot, the farmer's, at Stretton, and he had allowed them to take the rabbits from his land. Witness went to Stretton but could find no Mr. Lightfoot.—Mr. Browns: Do you know there is a Mr. Lightfoot at Antrobus ?—Witness : Not at Stretton.—Mr. Browne : They are close together ? Witness admitted that they were. —Mr. Browne maintained that there was nothing beyond mere suspicion or conjecture as to the defendants having been poaching and that the Act reqnired more than this, and said the cases quoted in Stone applied only where there was some hiding of the game from the constables, lout there was nothing of this kind. They were out in the open at half-past two in the afternoon, not early in the morning.—Boardman was called as a witness and said he kept the ferret to supply rats to different people. On the 9th inst., he and Green obtained the rabbits from Mr. Samuel Lightfoot, at Antrobus. They mentioned to the constable the name Samuel not John Lighfoot. It was just on the borders of Stretton where he lived. They burrowed for-the ritbits in the hedge back.—After some consideration by theßench, the case was dismissed. TEN DSPARTIIIIN OF SUPBRINTENDEINT LARGE—Mr. Browne said as that was the last occasion on which they -would have Superintendent Large there,he would hardly like it to pass without expressing in behalf of the mem- bers of the bar practising in that Court the gratification they all felt at hearing of his promotion to the superin- tendency of Middlewich. Superintendent Large had done his duty in that court with integrity, and had not been harsh either with prisoners or advocates, and had skilfully cross-examined ; and he hoped he would have as successful a career in his new position, as he had had in his present one.—The Chairman said he was very pleased to corroborate what had fallen from Mr. Brown, and to hear of his appointment.—Superintendent Large said he was pleased to hear the very kind expressions concerning himself. He had always tried to be as fair as he possibly could.—Mr. Greenall, the magistrates' clerk said he had always had the greatest assistance from Superintendent Large.

Sr. HELENS ITNLETIC T. Lows HOUSS match was down for decision on the Lowe House ground on Saturday. Two matches had been played, and both resulted in drawn garnes. Time was called with the score : Athletic, 3 goals ; Lowe House, 2 goals. YORE-ST. Sr. MARY'S Sr. HELENS) T. PNISLET CROSS TlCS.'—The return match between these clubs was played at Littler's field last Saturday, and when time was called the result was : St. Mary's one goal ; Vice. three goals. WARRINGTON Sr. ELPHIS'S v. LITERPOOL Vie/FORZA Arnusrrc.—Played at Lister Drive, Liverpool, on Satur- ton. St. Blphin's were short of Chantler, Cook, and Timing. In the first half the visitors held their own, the bomesters scoring once; but on change of ends there was "only one team in it," and that wasn't St. Hlphin's. The defence of the substitutes completely broke down, and the Athletic scored six times, thus winning by seven goals to nil. St. Elphin's forwards played a good game, and would have made the score more favourable if they had been backed by their usual defence. ,

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION T. ST. HiILBNS JUNCTION.— This return fixture was played on the ground of the former, before a good number of spectators, several of the Rugby Ist team turning out to witness the Associa- tionists, their match being cancelled in account of the I weather. Warrington kicked off at 3.20, and immediately resumed the aggressive. Ball and Norman severely taxed the home defence, who proved equal to the occa- sion, the backs taking play to the horns quarter, Jones being called upon to defend his charge. Mather relieved with a huge kick, and the home forwards getting pos- session were soon pressing into the visitors' goal, the custodian saving miraculously. Both sides strove hard to score, but half time arrived with a clean sheet. Re- starting, the first portion was played in mid-field, but at I length the visitors, after several futile attempts, scored from a lucky shot, Jones misjudging. The home team livened up considerably after this, and Powell missed three easy chances in succession. No further score ac- crued, the St. Helens Junction winning a tame game by a goal to none.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL -RUGBY.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL -RUGBY.

lAlthough it is nearly eight months since the late Mr. Thos.Jolley died,there are not wanting a few enthusiasts in the town who valued the popular cricketer and foot- baller's merits as a player. A movement has been on foot for some time to bring about a football match in aid of the memorial which is to be erected in the ceme- tery over the grave of the deceased. A match had been arranged to take place at Christmastide, between War- rington H. Ashton's team) and Runcorn (W. Faulkner's team), but the important engagements of the champion Cheshire club necessitated a postponement. However, the match will be played on Monday evening, March 14th, when those tickets which were sold for the first arranged match will be available. Given fine weather, the fund should receive a substantial lift.

The arrangements for the great match Rest of England v. Yorkshire, at Leeds on Saturday, were admirabe, and every one of the 20,000 spectators had a perfect view of the game. Yorkshire demonstrated their superiority and won by two tries to nothing. The key of their success may be explained in a single word—combination. The advantage of having played together—pulled together in the same boat, as it were—was manifest throughout, and it was this advantage that gave them the victory. Indi- vidually they were no better than the Rest of England, but the representatives of the latter suffered from want of a better understanding, and if the teams were to meet again the result might not be exactly the same. Is the champion county, Yorkshire are to be complimented on their capital football, and it would have been a sore trial for them if, like Lancashire twelve months ago, they had failed against the "B. 0. B." It was a fitting finish to their splendid performances of the season, and they are entitled to every praise.

How much the authorities of the Rugby Union appre- ciate the play of the Yorksbiremen is seen in the 'very large flavouring in the team selected to do battle for England against Scotland. Eight out of fifteen positions is a pretty fair proportion, but perhaps no more than they deserve. The bulk of these players have fairly won their spurs, and many of them are players of admitted ability. Lancashire have been given as many places in the English team as could reasonably be expected. Tom Coop is to be congratulated on his selection. Be may not be faultless, but probably there is no more reliable full back at the present time. He put in a vast amount of work against Yorkshire on Saturday. his safety being one of the features of the afternoon. Kent and But- lough are known as two of the most genuine forwards in the country, and they may be trusted to do their share in upholding the flag of England.

Taking the cue from the matches with Ireland, we do not see why the Englishmen should not repeat their vic- tory of two seasons ago. The Irishmen were beaten by two tries at Manchester, but on Saturday they were van- quished by a try only at Edinburgh. This certainly does not point to any superiority of the Thistle over the Rose. Had it not been for the magnificent defence of Stevenson, the Scotch full back, Ireland must have won. Their forwards were just as pugnacious as they were at Whalley Range, and the backs were little if any less smart than their opponents. The Irishmen have acquit- ted themselves well in their big engagements, and al- though beaten they have the satisfaction of knowing that they gave their conquerors something to do.
There was a heavy crop of postponed club fixtures on Saturday, including Warrington, v. Oldham, Runcorn v. Burton, and Widnes v. Crompton.
ASSOCIATION.

Assocation football was in full swing as usual, all the big fixtures being brought off. Eight of the leading clubs in Lancashire were occupied with Senior Cup ties,and they furnished one genuine surprise. And yet to the initiated the result may be said to be not attoge-,her unlooked for. Bury invariably play such sound football at home that their followers believed them to be fully capable of knocking out Accrington, and this is just what happened. The visitors had searcely a look in, and they were de- feated by as many as four goals too none. Following on their victory in the previous round at Newton Heath, this was a feather in the Bury cap. Accrington were de- prived of the services of Whitehead during the greater part of the match owing to an injured leg, but apart from this mishap they were completely overplayed and fairly beaten.

Darwen are notorious for ma king great efforts in cup ties. They made one on Saturday, and for the secotid season in succession proved too clever for Burn- ley in the county competition. They won by a goal to nil only,.but the real merit of the win will be seen when it is pointed out that M‘Owen had to be removed from the field owing to an accident, and was away nearly all the second half. That Everton would easily account for Bootle was a foregone conclusion, and they ran out winners by three goals to nothing. }Liner, one of the Bootle half backs, was ordered off the ground for mis- conduct, but was allowed to return.

The Bolton Wanderers have so often conquered the Blackburn Rovers in matches of every description that many persons believed them capable of adding another to their list. But they were not equal to it this time. The Rovers were smarter all round, particularly in the forward department, and they defeated the cup-holders by three goals to two. The deciding point was scored by Southworth from a penalty kick given against Somer- ville for tripping an opponent. Somerville must have lost his head, fnr as a rule he is one of the fairest players to be found in any company.

Sunderland gave further proof of their invincibility at home by winning their replayed F.A. tie v. Stoke with comparative ease. The northerners will have a very different task against Aston Villa in one of the semi-finals on Saturday next. The victors in this tie are generally supposed to be equal to carrying off the cup, but Notts Forest must not be lost sight of. They are pretty sure to beat West Bromwich Albion and thus qualify for the last stage of all,

The only League match that was on the list enabled Notts County to vanquish Derby County, and thus mount further up the table. They are now in a very respectable position, and are well away from the last four.
MISCHLLANBOUS.

One of the most interesting gymnastic displays wit- nessed in Belfast for some time was the contest on Sat- urday evening, in the Exhibition Hall, between the Balfour Institute Gymnasium, Liverpool, and the Young Men's Christian Association Gymnasium, Belfast, who met in the second round ef the competition for the 200- guinea international shield, presented by the National Physical Recreation Society, and which is at present held by the Liverpool Gymnasium. The Belfast team won by 20 marks, the totals being 320 and 300. The result evoked great enthusiasm.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. J. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Messrs. Lewis, Edwards, Brandreth, Mounfleld, .7: Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), and J. Farrington (nuisance inspector).

div.head: TEM MEDIC-AL OFFICER..
div.p: TEM MEDIC-AL OFFICER..
Mr. ?Awards gave notice that next Board day he would move the re-appointment of Dr. Adams as medi- cal officer at the usual salary.
TITS_ SUTTON *ATMS SUPPLY..

The Clerk submitted anaccountOf £6.i. from Mr. C. De Prez, of Moore, for work done in connection with the Sutton water supply. The account was accompanied by the following letter: " I am extremely sorry to have come to such an abrupt termination of the well at Sut- ton when the water is in easy grasp. Yet / suppose the case is not compulsory. Mr. Farrington called on me with orders to stop the work, so I could see nothing more than cover the well,and send in the bill of what had been done. Hoping you will see to its being naid as soon as possible."—The Chairman suggested the matter should be referred to the Sutton Sub-Committee if it were still in existence.—The Inspector said he supposed it was still In existence but no one attended the last meeting called. ' They were rather annoyei at the Board having stopped the work.—Tite Chairman : Is that the feeling in the township ?—The Inspector: I believe there is a bit of feeling about spending all this money and no water ob- tained.—The account was referred to the Committee.

div.head: STOCKTON /IRATE SEWERAGE.
div.p: STOCKTON /IRATE SEWERAGE.

The Inspector-reported that the Stockton Heath Sewer- age Committee had examined and considered the pro- posed scheme for the eXtension and improvement of the present sewerage and found it impracticable because of the insufficiency of the fall. The Committee could not see how the new road could be sewered without passing under the Ship Canal and creating another fall in the river Mersey.—Mr. Percy Silcock, surveyor and architect, attended to submit another scheme but the Authority referred him to the Committee axing the matter in hand.

div.head: ONE ENTENTE OP k PENNY.,
div.p: ONE ENTENTE OP k PENNY.,

Mr. 13randreth read the estimate for general expenses for Michaelmas half-year, 1892. The balance in hand at Michaelmas, 1891, was £345 Os. Od. •, calls this Lady Day half-year, £6B Os. Od; total capital for half year, £413 Os. Od. The probable expenditure this Lady Day half-year, £159; probable balance at Lady Day, i 892, £263. The probable expenditure Michaelmas half-year, 1892, was : salaries, £220; sundries, £25; £245 ; balance and contingency fund, £250; total, £495. Credit pro- bable balance at Lady Day, 1892, £263; credit, amount to be repaid by County Council, £135 ; total, £398; leav- ing the amount required £97'. The rateable value as per valuation list in force was £163,712. A rate of one seventh of a penny in the £ would produce the sum of £97 Bs. 11d.—Ir. Brandreth moved that the rate named be laid for the expenses of the Rural Sanitary Authority. —Mr. Edwards seconded.—Carried.

div.head: GOOD HEALTH.
div.p: GOOD HEALTH.
The Medical Officer repor-ted---;"case of diptheria at Frodsham. The health of the union had been very good since the commeacoment of the union. _ THE FIETSBY rump.

The Inspector reported that the -township pump at Flelsby was completely done, and the tender of Mr. Sprncer to construct a lead pump with case, at a cost of £6 103., was accepted on the motion of Mr. Brandreth, seconded by Mr. Lewis. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: SOUTH DERBYSHIRE ELECTION.
div.p: THE SOUTH DERBYSHIRE ELECTION.

The writ for the election of a member for South Derby- shire to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Henry Wardle has been received, and the nominations have been axed for to-day (Saturday) and the polling to take place On the following Friday. Mr. Evans Broad, the Liberal candidate, is holding meetings daily, and is receiving considerable outside support. Mr. Beresford Melville, Conservative is also displaying great activity, and al- though the fight will be short, it promises to be unusually severe.
GENERAL BOOTH IN MINOHESTER

• There was a great demonstration on Monday of mem hers of the Salvation Army la Manchester, who wel- comed General Booth on his return from Australia. In an address at night to a crowded meeting in the Free Trade Hall, the General referred to his " Darkest Eng- land " scheme, There had,he said, in the first year been a great deal more done than he expected could have been done. Witn the means at their disposal the results achieved had been wonderful. The method described in "Darkest. England" was • likely not merely to answer, but to exceed the expectations which he had formed of it.

div.head: SULTAN AND KHEDIVE.
div.p: THE SULTAN AND KHEDIVE.
A DEADLOCK.

A Vienna correspondent says :—The Egyptian question Is tinw at a standstill. The Sutan has given up the idea of making the Khedive proceed to Constantinople to fetch his firman of investiture, and now asks that he should visit him. Afterwards a speoial envoy would take the firman to Cairo. Lord Salisbury, it is said, will not allow the Khedive to appear before the Sultan unless he has received the sanction of investiture, and the Egyptian Cabinet supports the British Premier. In this at present neither party concerned seems inclined to give way.

brought into Parliament. He (Mr. Muspratt) did not wish to say anything very strong about it, but he would like to call attention to the way in which Mr. Balfour in- troduced it. He began by making numerous apologies : but one of these apologies would have been sufficient to satisfy those present that Mr. Balfour, on the whole was about the

CLEVEREST MAN OF THE STUPID PARTY. One of the apologies was this, " There is great advan- tage in doing stupid things, which have been done before, rather than doing worse things which have not been tried before." This was a most splendid and ,lucid definition of the Tory policy. (Applause.) Did they wish to carry on the policy, or did they wish to alter it ? If it was their desire to change it, then they must return Mr. Deacon as a supporter of the Liberal party, and of Mr. Gladstose, (Applause.) Mr. DEACON on rising to address the assembly, was greeted with loud and long continued cheering. He thanked those present for the cordial reception which they had given him, and said he thought that the reason they received him so cordially was not because of any personal merits, but because he was isn advocate of true Liberalism. He knew there were some opponents pre- sent, and he was pleased to see them. When he was first asked to contest the division, he said lie would fight as hard as he could fight, and would leave nothing un- done which could be done to gain a victory ; but he would
FIGHT ,AITH &MATHS'!. AND GQOD THMPHR.

They would not all agree with everithing he would say, but he had no fear that anything said or done would injuriously affect the feeling which he was pleased to think existed between him and the people of widnes. (Applause.) Be proposed to pointout in which direction

THE GOVERNMENT HAD GONE WRONG. They had promised to rule Ireland without coercion. and with ordinary laws, but as Mr. Muspratt had said they had done the very things which they premised not to do. I Trial by jury had been almost entirely abolished, arid 1 cases of the mast delicate character had been in many 1 cases tried by resident magistrates. Deeds have been I committed by Irishmen which could not be defended, but before judging an Irishman they should remember! the born sense of injustice which is imbred in the Irish , nation, and they should never forget the harsh manner I in which they had been treated. If England was ruled by a nation quite different in temperament and religion, and was treated like Ireland, would her people not be in + a frame of mind to revolt against.it ? Wnuld not the I wilder spirits be tempted to do things which in their calmer moments they would acknowledge to be wrong? Therefore they must remember the intense brovocaton the Irish people had received, and temper justice with mercy. ,He would say deliberately that although the English people were a patienr race they would not have been more patient than the Irish people if placed in the same circumstances, and had suffered the same injustice and wrong. A change had come over the Tory dealing's of late, they had dropped coercion now. Why Y . • THE ELECTION IS AT HAND. The Tories said they had sudceeded in governing Ireland I but he (Mr. Deacon) said that English rule throughout the whole country hadlisiled,'and it was now time to follow the path of reconciliation and justice which. had 1 been pointed out by Mr. Gladstone. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Moss had said at Garston that he hoped a great deal from the Local Government Bill ; it would bring back peace and prosperity to Ireland again, but he spoke before the Bill was brought before the House of Com- mons. Though the Bill was brought in now, it was promised years and years ago ; it was only at the last moment that the Government had done something to redeem Itself. And like the prodigal son, they had wasted their youth in riotous living, and now in the sere and yellow leaf of old age they had begun to repent and turn their thoughts to the dissolution and general elec- tion, from which they will never return. (Applause.) Therefore, like other sinners, they were going in for

A DEATH-11ED IIIiPHNTANCE and brought forward this Bill, which was received with gladness by the Conservatives, and with much merri- ment by the Liberals. It certainly had a difficult en- trance Into the world; and its parents would scarcely get over it. But would the little one live ? It seemed like one of these'unfbrtunate 'children which were born into the world through no fault of their own, but very often were removed by a- merciful Providence. (Laughter.) This would'doubtless be the fate of this little infant, as the parents and nurses were already half inclined to strangle it (Applause.) Lord Salisbury had said that if the Liberals brought forward

A ROME RULE BILL, the Rouse of Lord! would throw it out, and force a dis- solution. They had no right to force a dissolution. In 1832, when the great Reform Bill was passed by the Rouse of Commins, the Rouse of Lords threw it out, but there was no dissolution. The rumber of peers w. Increased, in order to • • swath. TRH ROUSE OP LORDS,

and the Bill was passed. ilie-LiiCe;;Tedici not want to do that, but itavas an absurdity for the House of Lords to interfere with the authority of the people, an he hoped such a step would not be forced upon them ; if it was, they would fight it to the bitter end, which would mean the end of the House of Lords as it at present exists. (Applause.) • With regard to the expenditure on army and navy, he said they .had to have their homes and commerce protected, therefore they must spend money on their army, but they must have the responsi- bility of their army and navy fixed upon the right men. They ought to havefl someone who was responsible for each department, and not have one man over half-a- dozen different departments and fulfilling none of his duties properly; but this could not, be done until the people were taken into the confidence of the Govern- ment. Then' there was Mr. Goschen's

SYSTRM Or TAXES.. The people did not mind paying a fan. proportion of the rates and taxes, if the landlords did the same. Who had to pay for the improvements which were being car- ried on in all large towns? The occupiers of the houses. They paid probate duty, succession duty, and other rates, whilst the landlords paid none except succession duty. Thousands and thousands of pounds were spent annually in improving the property of the landlords without the owners spending a single shilling. The landlords said they had not received justice. Perhaps not, but they would have after the general election. In concluding,he hoped they would help him in the contest, and he would do his utmost, if returned, in passing these

reforms, and he would work in the interests of Widnes and those of the country. (Loud applause.) Ma. T. SIMON Trams, J.P., then moved a resolution pledginwthe meeting 0 support Mr. Deacon, and in the course of his speeali said he had known Mr. Deacon for 26 years and many people did not realise

They had to fight railway companies and deputations. In the House of Commons, and Mr. Nikon had been a practical member of this association. He had been a member of the School Board for 15 years. He was also connected with the Council of Education. He was chairmen of the Library Committee. He had also been a magistrate for a number of years, and at one 'time a member of. a Arne who employed a large number of men in the to*n. Mr. Timmis appealed to all present tb think whether Mr. Deacon was not the right member ft* Widnes. (Applause%2 Mr: F. flairrtawroseconded the resolution in a capital speeth, and it Was supported by Mr. Lawrence Gane, M.P., who had arrived at the meeting late. div.head: ST. PETER'S ANNUAL TEA PARTY.
div.p: ST. PETER'S ANNUAL TEA PARTY.

The annual tea • party in connection with St. Peters's Church, took place in St. Peter's Schools, Warrington, on Monday evening. Upwards ef 150 persons partook of tea, the-following ladies presiding at the tables :—Mesdames Meese, Dagnall, Green, Balshaw, Chorley,and Edgar, Miss Shirtcliffe, and Miss Madelev. Tea was succeeded by the usual social gathering, at which there was a good atten- dance. The Rev. T.Rigb3N.the vicar, presided, and the Rev. F. C. Shirtcliffe, his curate, was present among the audience. The following , programme of vocal and instrumental music ,was ' gone through :—Plano solo, Irish melodies, Miss Longson; glee, " Maiden of the Fleur de Lys" violin solo, "Impromptu," Mrs, Colin Jackson ; glee, "Sands of the Dee " ;, recitation, "A day too late," Miss Longson; song, Mr, Ifitowlson ; glee, "The ferry maiden ;" violin solo, Mrs. Jackson; vocal duet. "The angel," Mrs. Jeckson and Miss Longson; glee, " 0 +who will o'er the downs." The glee party consisted of the Rev. T. Rigby -(bass), Mrs. Colin , Jackson (soprano), Miss Longson (conttalto), and Mr. Knowlson (tenor), At the close of this part of the entertainment, 'The CIAIBMAN addressed the meeting. He said that was the fourth tea party they had had in that room since he was appointed to the incumbency • of the parish, and he thought they could safely say that the two or three years that had just gone past were' by far the most important in the history of St. Peter's parish. Three years ago, he said, everything was in the future. They were then looking forward to better times in the future, and now they could look back•to the past and be thank- ful that they had been taken out, of that schoolroom for Sunday service. That was one great step. Last year at the tea party they were congratulating themselves on having got into the new church. This year they had to congratulate themselves that they had not only got into it but paid for it. The church and fittings had costs over £4,500 and this had been paid, and that was a great sum for a large parish like that, and they had every reason to be thankful for what they had done. They wanted now an organ and a boundary wall. At the last vestry meeting they doubled the organist's salary. (Applause.) His salary befOre was very myth like a midshipman's half-pay, three farthings a ye tr paid quarterly (laughter) but it was doubled. The mitiical part of the service had improved, and the last harvest thanksgiving festival was one that could not be excelled by any service in the town, and they had their own band and choir and wanted no helpers. The finances were on the whole satisfactory. Last year they had the largest grant as well as the" best report they had ever had, as the resqlts of the school examination. They got nearly £2OO grant ; three years since it was only £145. Three years ago at the end of January the Gov- ernment grant was spent, and they had to carry on on the school pence till the following November, before receiving any: more grant, but he was happy to say that at the end of January this year they were at least £lOO better off, allowing for there being no outstanding bills, than at the, corresponding, period three years ago. The rev : gentlernin,as a :matter of cengtatulatiOn for church- men, mentioned that the Criminous Clerks' Bill was being brought into • the • House of Lads, by the -Archbishop of JP Canterbury ,' to , facilitate the re- riabval. of clergymen who ,do not do their work Or set a good, example te the parish ; and he also re- ferred to the question of:inequallty of the endowriten;s of the church. In some respects people who complained of these, he said, were right, • but in other respects, wrong. For example in the case of new. parishes, sup- pose some one left St. Peter's an endowment of £5,000, and did net leave anything to a neighbouring new parish. Well, that new pariah . would ,net have any right to grumble. If corns one left hiitk kllclo,ooo, it would be • nobody's. place to grumble because it had not been lett to him. But in the ease of old parishes people were 4aite right in grumbling about the difference in the en- clowm nts of the'ohurch. When an' old parish was cut up into more; than one parish the eadowments,' he Con- tended, ought to he cut up too,but it would be generally found that this Was not the case. The old parish of War- rington eatepded formerly as far as Glazebrook,and, he believed,toolt In Sankey Bridges. Endovinients were left for the whole of the 'old parish, of which St. Peter's formed a part, and he maintained, that when that 'old • parish was diyided, the endewments ought to have been divided too.; He did not say that because he would gain' by it ; it;would be for the benefit of the parish. But the endowments 'of Warrington old parish church, instead ef, , being divided, were now confined to that one part of • the' old parish of Warrington which belonged to the 'parish church. But the endowments belonged to the whole of the old parish, and St. ,Peter's had as much moral tight tea part of the endowments as the parish church had. (Applause.) St. Peter's was the poorest parish in the town and was the worst endowed. The endowment of that large parish, the second' largest in the town, would not amount to £l6O or £l7O. The endowment was not only the least in the town but the worst paid. St. Peter's was the unfortunate owner of a Welsh tithe, and it was very badly paid. He was the first vicar of St. Peter's, who had had to sell people up, but there was one' man who would not pay him 40. year, and if he liked to break the commandments for the sake of 44d. he could do it. The Chairman con- cluded :fif ibanking the churchwardens, sidesrnen, : organist; and choir, and others, who had assisted him, ' • and those who had contributed their help that evening., (Applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded to the last-mentioned, On the proposition of the Rev. div.p: PUBLIC MEETINGS.

It Is seldom the case that foreigners who travel at reticle but a short time in Great Britain arrive at a itlat comprehension of the intricate, ill-defined, tc,_iiventional arrangements of society in this coun- t, and, in perusing the explanations which they r'ler in their published works on many of our !Institutions, we at once perceive and pity the errors wit° which, in nearly all cases, they can hardly pre- Vent themselves from falling. The following candid !Wtlele on public meetings, from the pen of a French Writer, may be presented as an exception to the rale A man of wit said, 'The language of despotism It *bad your own concerns; that of liberty is, At- tend to things that don't concern you.' 111 this pithy form he announced a grand truth. In a free °3lllltry nothing that affects any class of citizens ?ail be foreign to the rest of the community. There ‘s,cot an Englishman, however humble the rank in Which he was born, who is not justly entitled to think that his opinion is of some weight in the Pairs of his country; and, reciprocally, there is no Lndividual so exalted as, for his daily conduct, to be "erupt from the examination and judgment of the ...With us, on the Continent, publicity is considered `b an extreme resource, to which we have recourse OOly iu desperate cases, and after having exhausted other means of attaining our object. If persons Magage in an undertaking of public or private con- cern, they always found their hopes of success on • e disposition of men in power; business is con- ducted in the closet of the minister, or in the Wing. room of some man of weight. While there an chance of succeeding through favour, it Would appear rude or indiscreet to speak out, and lan on the public to judge of our griefs or projects. ingland, publicity is a matter of common right; :"..en address themselves to the opinion of the public Mice ; this is the first power, the support of which it'lley solicit' and even men desirous of treating with overnment would begin by seeking popularity, Well knowing it would be for the interest of their bit ion 4..18 an abuse to be reformed—an improvement to be rioroduced—a right to be claimed—a new institu- tionu to be founded—whether it concern religion, Morality, liberty, or the public wealth, the first indispensable step is to enlighten public opi _ion on :4e, point in question. The attempt to fix the , attention is begun by writing pamphlets or l',,aragraphs in the newspapers. Then a few people M note form a committee, and prepare a string of solutions, which are submitted to general dis- .,ellssion. When agreed so far, a meeting is called, either in the open air or in one of the large rooms Pted to the purpose, which are to be found in wroost every large town in England. A chairman, called on by the public vote, presides over the tceeting the resolutions are discussed, and put to the Vote' and, amid the most stormy debates, a ain familiarity with the forms of deliberation, uoiare on to all classes of people, maintains order wlcl protects the rights of the minority. Frequently, at these meetings, orators, before 1;11 known, appear in public for the first time, and display talents that perhaps pave the way for their roture admission to the senate. The next day their °Neches are printed in all the newspapers, and 14esound throughout all England. The first meeting Rives rise to others, men's minds are enlivened and Warmed, and the public opinion acquires a degree Of force, any resistance to which would be useless. It L. not without reason, therefore, that the Eng- . ill set so high a value on the right to assemble for the discussion of public affairs, and place it in the first rank of their constitutional prerogatives. The tight of petitionin..b, as they conceive it, is nothing ut tne right of meeting to deliberate on the Ilequests or complaints expressed in the petition; for the Houses of Parliament are not expected to decide, like judges, on every requisition addressed to it. Particular cognisance is taken of a petition, Ottly when it is made the subject of a motion by some one of the members. The right of introducing a subject is no given indiscriminately to the public at large, which would be a confusion of power leading to anarchy. But what is justly required is that the public opinion should enjoy the utmost latitude in forming and expressing itself. In a country where everything is treated publicly :•—Where everything is subjected to discussion, from the most important questions of legislation to the 'tightest of local affairs—the talent of speaking taus At tit naturally be an object of universal ambition. the 001, and even in their play, children exercise anJlves in this species of eloquence. At Eton ot Westminster they frequently form a little House °crop:lons, subjected to regulations similar to those 4 of the Parliament. When at the university, the Young men unite in debating societies, where questions of history, philosophy, legislation, and Political economy are discussed in form. At these are frequently developed the germs of the greatest talents. and an orator, whose eloquence will some 'a..7 be the pride of England, may have felt the first :Park of his genius elicited by the applause of his "ellow-students. The debating societies, however, are merely sup- plementary, and not essential pasts of the system; but all the institutions that constitute the basis of the social order—as juries, managing committees, Municipal councils, parochial and county meetings, d elections, presume habits of speaking, and a litowledge of the forms of deliberation. We scarcely !lad a man that has received any education who r,ces not know how to preside at a meeting, direct a debates, and put questions to the vote in due e`trer, There are indispensable notions in respect t"! i_tala, which are so familiar to the people of Eng- •ola..d that no one would think of making them an "lect of study; while with us, they who have c`t_cm'a old in our deliberative assemblies still remain 440iortuat of them. aioPublic dinners are one of the most common occa- ei.wa of the exercise of oratory. The object of these n. 4:--ers is to keep up the spirit of an association, or • enoourage the study of some science, by bringing "nether persons who otherwise would have no IPActtunity a freely communicating to each other their Ideas; or to keep alive political opinions, by celebrating a the anniversary of an important event, Le birth of a great man, or the election of a mem- of the House of Commons dear to his country. tothbit6.- is more original than these political dinners. ..._44aay times I have seen nearly three hundred per- Seated at the same table, and electrified by the ""▪ uwe sentiment, without the vivacity of their eMOtions pres eating them from observing with the tost methodical regularity all the usages estab- hod on such occasions. 14- chairman is seated at the head of the table. No ,—eeting takes place without this formality, which 1...,"'arc8 indispensable for securing order and regu- -`ntY in every kind of discussion. The English of all • causes have a remarkable tact in this respect; if a speaker deviate ever so little from the _tablished rules of decorum, a cry of Chair 1 resounds on all sides. This is a kind of vyPeal to the abstract idea of a president, informing Who executes the functions of one that he is ,31)eeted to maintain order, or restore the due state the question. At the other end of the table sits tthe deputy.chairman, whose business is to preside When the chairman himself is called upon to take in the debate; for there are two invariable 74orns—one, that the meeting must never be with a head; the other, that the person who is orciating as president cannot act as a pasty in the —bate at the same time.

div.head: ?letters' to the attar.
div.p: ?letters' to the attar.
THE INCREASE OF SALARIES.

Sir,—l have for the last few weeks scanned your pub- ication, with the expectation of seeing some protest against the extravanganee of our Town Counei, in recklessly voting £lOO per year extra, to the Borough Surveyor. This gentleman, having already £3 per week, must, forsooth, have other £2 per week added. Person- ally, I have no feeling against Mr. Longdin, but, I think, if the Town Councillors have plenty of money to dispose of, they may find a better way than giving it to a man who has already got plenty. If they will look around, they will find men who are working for the Corporation, who can scarcely keep the wolf of poverty from the door. But what astonishes me, Mr. Editor, is, how men like Mr. 11. Roberts Mr. Flood, Mr. Plumpton, Mr. Beaman, &c., men who claim to be representatives of working men, can vote such salaries to Corporation officials. I wonder if these men had to find the money out of their own pockets would be so free and lavish with it. I think the time is coming when extravagant salaries should be lessened instead of increased. Our gas is so good and cheap that we need no alteration, and, our rates are so low that the councilors could not poss- ibly thing them down a mite; our sanitary conditions are so perfect that anyone living in Warrington, lives in a heaven of purity. And of course, as a result, there is no work for our councillors but to raise salaries.—l am, yours respectfully, DOT.

div.head: "KING DICK!"
div.p: "KING DICK!"
"KING DEATH !"
King Dick, he's a rare rum fellow, lie lives wheer good ale flows free; An' he goes to bed fine an' mellow,

Two iieets eawt o' ey'ry three! In promisin' t' do an' not doin', Ile byets aw i'th' present or past ; But my face aw'm not beaun to be pooin— He's sent me my hare--at last! His greyt skill i' makin' excuses, Knocks to tits any tailor or Jew ; An' to show yo' tiler different uses, Avv'll gie yo' a sample or two. But don't think these yarns are my hatchin', Fer aw cudn't, if even aw dass'd; An' aw caun't see why I shud be ratchin'— He's sent me my bare--at last! Well, it's seven lung yer sin', aw'm thinkin', He promis'd to send me a Pup; But to-day, wi' his e'en slyly winkin', He sex as its not quite grown up ! Aw thowt that this" rowzer " wud shame him, Or reet in his wizzen stick fast ; But aw don't see ez I owt to blame him— He's sent me my hare—at last ! He vowed he wild send me Sum Unyuns,

Ez big ez a helephunt's yed ; But he sez neaw he's trubbl't wi bunyuns, An' csun't get his feet eavvt o' bed ! Many a one wud ha' savagely blest him, Wi' words that hed " e'en.." in, and " blast ;" But aw connot forget that—Lord rest him ! He's sent me my hare--at last ! He towd me he'd send me a Dozen 0' Number One Ale—best thay'd got ; But he rites me, an' sez, "Dear Cuzzen, Owd John an me's polish% aw th' lot !" Here mi rhyme its full time aw wur endin,'— Why, midneet hez lung sin gone past ; An' aw'm thankful to say, Dick, theaur't mendin,' Per theau's sent me my hare at last ! TEM 0' PEGS. Bands o' m—now, nod moosick ; we'll say bands o' discord wi' processions, an' banners tellin' fooak as "of such is the Kingdom of Heaven.' Well, aw'm nod beawn to believe tkad.
I' parenthesis here's a 'affable paragraph for Booth an' Company to read on their triumphal procession; aw copy id fro' last Wensda's "Manches- ter Guardian."

"Curate (24 years standing), with six children to educe' e, urgently appeals for help. No money in hand for coals or food. Any assistance thankfully acknowledged," &c. In the Church of England such things should be impossible. What of the curate's rector ? What of his Bishop ?" I' repoort published, Booth says, iv th' public fled stumpt up th' million peawnd he axt for, they (th' Army) wodn'd ha' bin foorced to be so keerful i' their eawtlay as they'd hod to be ! Good owd keerfulness ! Good owd eawtlay ! ! "With regard to the Over-The-Sea colony he had not yet decided where it was to be. He was in the position of a man with too many sweethearts." An' this Morland blackmailin' case—aw hooap he'll ged ten year; an' Mrs. Osborne's to be tried on th' twelfth o' next month.
