div.head: CATASTROPHE NEAR BRADFORD,
div.p: CATASTROPHE NEAR BRADFORD,
FALL OF A FACTORY CHIMNEY. 14 PERSONS KILLED: MANY INJURED.

A terrible disaster occurred at Cleckheaton, near Bradford, on Wednesday, by which there is little doubt fourteen persons have been killed and a large number have been injured, several of them fatally. At ten minutes to five o'clock a chimney sixty yards high fell upon a spinning and weaving shed occupied by Mr. Wesley Barraclough. Nearly sixty persons at the time were at work in the building. The chimney crashed down upon the structure and demolished more than half of it, nearly thirty persons, chiefly girls, being either buried beneath the many tons of de4ris or, as was actually the case with some half-a-dozen fortunate ones, escaping in a most marvellous manner from what in their position and circumstances might be regardvd as almost certain death. Those who were uninjured hastily fled from the mill. Attracted by the tremendous noise I caused by the falling chimney, a great crowd soon assem- bled. The Cleckheaton Fire Brigade and the fire brigade from a neighbouring mill were soon on the spot with a large corps of volunteer workers, and under the super- intendence of the police the work of rescuing the living and removing the dead was soon begun. It proved, however, to be a work of immense difficulty. ' The first two bodies were extricated in a few minutes, but after that they were only discavered slowly and released with difficulty. At nine o'clock eight dead bodies had been recovered and ten injured persons had been removed, either to their homes or to an office in the vicinity. The doctors pronounced that several of these were badly injured, and, it is feared, that some of them may suc- cumb. The mill upon which the chimney fell, is, as has been stated, occupied.by Mr. Wesley Barraclough, who rents it with the power attached from Messrs. Thornton Bros., machine makers, whose premises adjoin and Whe are the owners of the chimney. The chimney was built some fifty years ago by Mr. Thornton's father and his uncle, and was sixty yards high. It was of brick. At the time of the accident two men were engaged upon it making repairs near the base. The men were in the employment of Messrs. Moulson and S ms, of Bradford, who had been engaged by Mr. Thornton to do whatever was necessary to the chimney. Mr. Barraclough had been somewhat anxious with regard to its condition,and Mr. Thornton:had taken steps to get whatever was wrong remedied. The building which the chimney partially destroyed was a four-storeyed one. The top storey was occupied by nine spinners; the third was devoted to flannel making, and in it were looms tended by twenty-six 1 weavers; the second storey was also occupied by flannel looms, at which twenty-four weavers were at work ; while on the bottom floor were other spinning machines, under the care of five men and two boys. Thus there were over sixty persons engaged in the place, and about , half of these either lost their lives,meeting a most shock- ' ing death, or have been seriously injured. As the dead were recovered they were taken into a large machine shed which forms part of the works of Messrs. Thornton Bros., close by, and were one by one identified by the sorrowing relatives as they congregated round. Admirable assistance was rendered by about ten members of the Liversedge section of the Ambulance Society and by a rather larger number of members of the Cleckheaton section. As the night wore on tbe scene inside the the mill lost none of its interest. By the light 3f strong naptha lan- terns some hundred men were busily at work removing as fast as they could the tons of debris which still ap- parently covered some five human beings. Strong ropes were made fast to huge iron girders and large numbers of men slowly removed these impediments to the work of rescue, but the interyals between the discovery of the dead bodies became longer and longer as midnight ap- proached, and it is probable, as in the case of the New- lands Mill disaster at Bradford, many hours wia elapse before all the missing have been traced. The disaster at the Marsh Mills, Cleckheaton' has resulted so far in fourteen persons being killed, and it is probable that the list of fatal cases will be enlarged, the conditioa of two or three of the injured leaving but the very barest chance of recovery. The statement made in the first account of the accident that the chimney had been copsidered by the workpeople and others to be unsafe was to some extent confirmed on Thursday in evidence given before the Coroner, and in some remarks made by Alderman Mnulson, of Bradford, whose Arm had undertaken the repairs which were being carried out when the disaster happened. A witness at the inquest stated that her sister, one of the persons kill-d, said on Tuesday last that the chimney was giving way.

div.head: lAA M iiNiut, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 27, 1892.
div.p: THE lAA M iiNiut, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 27, 1892.
THE STREKE OF GAS STOVE MAKERS AT WARRINGTON.

The strike still continues up to the period of our going to press; and the strikers appear to be deter- mined to stand out to to the last. They are in receipt of the following allowance per week:— Married men, 125., unmarried men, 84., and boys 45., and these sums are augmented by subscriptions. Pickets have been regularly stationed near the works, and the police have been constantly patrolled in force to preserve the peace. In consequence of the illness of Chief Constable Hunt the deputation appointed to meet him as to charges made by the pickets against the police were unable to wait upon him on Wednesday morning as decided ; but proceeded to the office of the Town Clerk who promised to communicate with Mr. Hunt on the matter. The deputation, we are informed by the President of the Trades Council stated to the Town Clerk that the pickets had a perfect right to accost and use influence with non-union men so long as they used no threats or violence. The Town Clerk, we learn on the same authority, informei them that this was quite correct, adding that there must be no congregating in the streets, so as to cause obstruction. The members of the deputation say that the alleged interference of the police with the pickets on account of their merely peacefully accosting:the non-unionists has now ceased. Over 50 of the non-unionists who had been set ou by Messrs. Rich- mond in place of the strikers have been induced to return horns to the various places from whence they came,their fare& back having been paid out of tbe union funds. On Thursday afternoon the deputation appointed to meet the directors of Messrs. Richmond and Co.'s works had their meeting with them.. The Directors proposed that the men now employed be retained and that the men on strike be. allowed to come back as unionists so far as the vacancies would allow, but the deputation declined to accept these terms, stating that they were authorised to say that all the men on strike, must be taken back into the firm's employment, or none. Is meeting of the strikers was held at the Cross Keys on Thursday night, at which the result of the interview was, reported.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
COLLISION ON THE SHIP CANAL.

On Wednesday night, as the steamship Cecil, belong- ing to Messrs. Brundrit, of Runcorn, was steaming, up the Ship Canal to Weston Point, it collided with a barge anchored at Ellesmere Point. The barge, which was filled up with mud, at once sank, and it is expected to be an expensive operation to raise her. The Cecil was anchored, and again proceeded to son on Thursday.

div.head: STRIKE AT WESTON POINT.
div.p: STRIKE AT WESTON POINT.

The men known as ropers in connection with the Ship Canal works at Weston Point, struck work on Saturday, because of a reduction in their wages of one penny per hour. During the period when operations were being pressed forward to get water at Ince, the men engaged as couplers, or ropers, had ' their wages raised from sd. to 6d., but now that this work is com- pleted the employers have reduced the remuneration to the old scale, which is in vogue at Manchester and Eastham. The men seemed determined to resist the reduction contending that they deserved more than others considering the conditions under which they had to work on the Marshes, but, they have now re-com- menced work on their masters' terms. ANOTHER FATAL ACCIDENT. On Saturday morning, about half-past eleven, George Holden, of Ashridge-st., Runcorn, met with an accident, attended with fatal results. He had been engaged as a roperunner on one of the engines on the Manchester Ship Canal Works. On the day named, however, he was as- sisting in getting in working order a portable engine. He was sent to fetch a chisel off the wall on the other side of the canal. In order to take a short cut, he went past where an engine was pumping water out of the canal into the river, situated on No Man's Land. He seems to have been creeping under the machinery, when the crank caught him on the chest, and pinned him against one of the uprights. On being released he fell down, and scrambled a yard or two away. P.S. Gos- ling, who was in the vicinity, saw the accident, and sent P.C. Rutter to his assistance, whilst he went for the ambulance. The place was difficult of access, and in the meantime, a. young man named Rutter was by the side of the injured man. He got the help of an engine- driver, and the two then placed Holden on the engine, and immediately took him to Latchford hospital. Soon after arriving at that institution the poor man expired.—The inquest was held at the Ship Canal Hospital, at Latchford, on Tuesday afternoon, before Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner. The jury having inspected similar machinery in operation on the Latch- ford section, Constable Millington explained how the accident occurred. On returning to the hospital the evidence was taken and it was in accordance with the facts given above.—Sergeaut Gosling said the machinery was in motion at the time, and the deceased must have seen that that was the case. It was evident that the deceased thought he would have time to avoid the crank. As soon as the accident was found out, the deceased was picked up, placed on a stretcher, and con- veyed by rail to the hospital. The deceased ought not to have gone the way he did.--A witness named Frith said be had never previously heard of anyone going the way the deceased did.—Evidence of the death having been given by the Matron of the Hospital (Miss Teraro), the jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

div.head: IN IMPORTANT REPORT.
div.p: IN IMPORTANT REPORT.

An important report has been issued relative to the position of the Manchester Corporation towards the Ship Canal. The document gives the opinion of Mr. Moulton, Q.C., that it is not advisable to present a petition against the Ship Canal Bill in Parliament for the purpose of ob- taining clauses giving to the Corporation a majority of the directors on the Board of the Company. It would be, Mr. Moulton says, wholly at variance with the cus- tom of Parliament to grant such powers on a hostile petition; and, even if Parliament were prepared to do so, the company could itself abandon the Bill, and thus prevent the clause from taking effect. He advises that steps should be taken to measure up and estimate the cost of such portions of the work as it is not intended to put to contract by tender as a course which would be of great We in guiding the future action of the Cor- poration. Thu Joint Committee in view of Mr. Moulton'd opinion, and of the undertaking of the Ship Canal direc- tors as to the perm anence of the Executive Committee with a majority thereon of Corporation directors,recom- mend that the Corporation shall not petition against the Bill, and also that the directors be requested to furnish the Corporation with a plan of the canal and its equip- ment as intended to be completed, and to supply each month progress sections of the entire works.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL IMPOI3,TANT ARRANGEMENTS.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL IMPOI3,TANT ARRANGEMENTS.

We understand that the Manchester. Ship Canal Company have been approached on behalf of the Corporation of Warrington, on the subject of the construction of the dock at Warrington, and that they have agreed to insert clauses in their Bill un- dertaking that the dock shall be completed within the three years proposed by the Bill. The company further undertake that the dam and the lock,which will enable vessels to get out of the Mersey into the canal, shall be completed by the time that that por- tion of the canal between Eastham and Latchford is opened for traffic. It would appear from this that the company are prepared to meet the wishes of the Corporation; but we believe that, as a matter of precaution, a petition will still be presented against the Bill by the Corporation. At a special meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, held yesterday, a deputation, consist- ing of Messrs:. J. Fairclough, W. Pierpoint, and J. IL Pleasing, was tip Pointed to wait; in conjunction with a deputation representing the Corporation, upon the Ship Canal Comkrany, in reference to their Bill.

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER AT BOLTON.
div.p: THE ATTEMPTED MURDER AT BOLTON.

The man Whiteley was brought before the Bolton magistrates, on Thursday, on remand, charged with attempting to murder, in a lonely by-street, a married woman named Mather, under circumstances already reported. The woman still lies in aprecarious condition at the infirmary, and the surgeons will not allow her to be moved. Mr. Hall, public prosecutor, in opening the case, said he had now sufficient evidence to connect Whiteley with the crime. •

div.head: LOCAL GOVERNMENT (IRELAND)
div.p: THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT (IRELAND)
BILL.

The new bill prepared and brought in by Mr. Balfour, Mr. Jackson, Mr. Ritchie, and the Attorney-General for Ireland under the title" a bill for amending the law re- lating to local government in Ireland and for other pur- poses connected therewith " has been issued with the Parliamentary papers. It consists of 78 clauses, and oc- cupies without certain schedules annexed 52 pages of letterpress. The main features of the measure have of course already been made known. Clause 5, dealing with the "removal of elected and substitution of ap- pointed councillors," which has excited the greatest amount of hostile criticism, reads as follows :

1. Any twenty cess payers of a county may apply to a judge of assize for leave to petition the high court for the removal of the councillors of a county or baronial council on the ground of cerruption, malversation, or oppression, or of persistent disobedience to the law, and the judge of assize, if of opinion after hearing evidence that there is a prima facie case, may give such leave. 2. The petition shall be presented by the said cess payers within twenty-one days after leave is given, and shall be tried by the judges on the rota for the trial of election petitions, and shall be presented and tried and notice thereof served and security for costs given iu like manner as nearly as may be as if the petition were an election petition.

3. At the conclusion of the trial the judges shall de- termine whether the charges inl the petition are or are not proved : and • (a) If they find proved a charge that a eounciller knowingly and wilfully has committed an act !Df cor- ruption, malversation, or oppression, or persistently disobeyed the law, they may disqualify him for seven years from holding office as a county or baronial coun- cillor ; and (b) If they find proved a charge of any act or default of the council which can be remedied they may order the council to remedy that actor default within the time limited by the order; and (c) If they find proved a charge that the council have knowingly pursued a course of corruption, malversa- tion, oppression, or persistent disobedience to the law, they may order all the councillors to be removed, and if any such order to remedy an act or default is not complied with by the council, the judges for the time being on the rota for the trial of election petitions may order all the councillors to be removed. 4. The judges shall in any case order by whom and in what proportions the costs are to be borne whether by the council, by the councillors or. any of them, or by the petitioners. 5. Upon an order of removal being made, the chair- man and councillors of the council shall cease to hold office, and for such terin,not exceeding three years, as is fixed by the order, such persons, not less than five, qualified to be councillors of the council as the Lord- Lieutenant appoints (of whom one, namedtby the Lord- Lieutenant, should be chairman), shall during his plea- sure form the said council, and have the same authority, and be in the same position as if elected chairman and councillors.

- 6. Within one month before the end of the said term new councillors and a new chairman shall, on days fixed by the Lord-Lieutenant, be elected, and if those days are not the ordinary days of election, they shall be elected as if they were the ordinary days of election ; but the persons elected shall hold office for the same time only as if they had been elected at the next preceding ordin- ary day of election. Until the day so fixed no councillor of such council shall be elected.

div.head: MEETING OF THE TRADES COUNCIL
div.p: MEETING OF THE TRADES COUNCIL

CM Tuesday evening, a meeting a the Warring- ton Trades Council was held in the Cocoa Rooms, llorsemarket-st., the principal business being to receive as a deputation from the head office of the National Union of Stove Grate Workers(Rotherb am), Mr. li. Sanders, general seeretary, in reference to the present strike at Messrs. Richmond and Co.'s. Academy-st., Warrington. Mr. John Price, presi- dent of the Trades Council, occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance. Mr. SANDEna, having been introduced, said he thanked the Trades Council for the very prompt merrier in whiph they had stepped into the breach between the employers and workmen in the matter of the strike at Messrs. Richmond and Co.'s. It was one more proof of the necessity of Trades Councils. He was sure that a dispassionate and disinterested view of the situation would be taken by those gathered there that night, and an impartial judgment given. Messrs. Rich- mond and Co. were a very new firm, and some nine months ago their workmen applied to the Union he represented to be attached to it ,• and before he entered Warrington some 0 names had been sent in for member- ship. That was the introduction of Unionism in con- nection with Messrs. Richmond and Co. All went well until a few weeks ago, when the firm commenced to introduce a system of piece work in place of that of day work, which had been in vogue, in connection with the fitting department. When he mentioned that the prices in the day work department had been excessively low, ranging from 18s. a week to the highest sum, paid to skilled workmen, 2.55. a week, it would be recognised how necessary it was that something should be done. They were anxious to avoid a dispute with Messrs. Richmond, and the men were called to- gether, and the matter of piece work prices was gone into. Some of these were satisfactory, some not. It became necessary for him to meet the firm, so as to do away with some little friction that existed. They came to an understanding, and, as he thought, a final settlement, but after he had left they upset the agree- ment, and the men became dissatisfied. The neat time he came to Warrington he saw two of the directors. The men had been asked to send in a statement of union men and non-union men. Some of the men objected to the union, and it was thought advisable to settle as speedily as possible whether Richmond and Co.'s should be a union or a non-union shop. The firm issued a ballot paper to their workmen, the terms of which were very ambiguous indeed :—" Are you in favour of forcing every workman of this firm to belong to the union ?" Trades Unionists did not desire to force men ; some men they thought were better out of the union. The restet ' of the ballot was that a considexable number of men felt unable to go so far as to vote in favour of compelling other men to join, because he distinctly stated they did not want every man in the place to do so. A considerable number voted against the proposition be had referred to, and to settle the matter he went before the directors and argued the question out, and the arrangement come to was that as a union they simply desired the right to give notice to those who had joined the union that they must pay their dues and rank themselves as union men, or not expect CO have the benefits of union men. He also said he would very much like that all the men put on in future, should be union men, but said that as regarded eight men who did not wish to join the Union the union was quite content that they should work on with the other 70 men. The next thing he heard was that a cer- tain matter in connection with prices so incensed Messrs. Richmond against unionism that they said to the men "The price you will have to pay for the satisfaction we give you is that you must give up your unionism." The men preferred to stick to the principles of unionism rather than sell themselves for the time being to the firm. Twenty-two fitters remained outside rather than accept such terms, and then commenced the war. Messrs. Richmond and Co. had advertised in many newpapers for non-society men as moulders, fitters, grinders, glazers, pattern makersatc.,to fill up the places of the union men, and had thus thrown down the gauntlet and declared war. It was not now a matter of prices, but of fighting the principles of unionism. Messrs. Richmond had de- eideci to make their place into a non-union shop. The Union were not so dissatisfied with the prices in dispute as they were with regard to the attempt to put down the principles of unionism. It was one of the main charges against unionists that they csierced non-union men, but Messrs. Richmond and Co., by their action against their union men,had come out as full-blown coercionists. The speaker concluded by an appeal to the Trades Council to support the strikers. Councillor FLoon said he had known of such a case as that of coercing unionists to become non- unionists before, but not in Warrington. Nofirm of any ' creditor reputation ought to allow it to go forth, that they declined theskill and ability of competent workmen simply because they chose to protect themselves by trades unionism. The Trades Council were bound in honour as the medium of arbitration to demand from Messrs. Richmond and Co., what they prop3sed as a basis of settlement. If the Trades Council failed let them appeal to the Chamber of Commerce to use their endeavours to bring about an understanding with the firm. Mr. J. Rudge, Mr. S. Wright, and the Chairman ad- dressed the meeting. Mr. W. H. Beeeoce proposed, and Mr. CHRIMES seconded, that a deputation be appointed to wait upon Messrs. Richmond ;and that if they failed to bring about an ansicable settlement the Trades Council continue to give their utmost support to the strikers. The resolution was carried unanimously. A deputation was also appointed to wait upon the Chief Constable as to charges made against the police by the strike pickets. CHARGES OF ASSAULT AND INTIMIDATION. At the Berough Police Court, Yesterday, before Alder- men Harrison (chairman), and Wright, and Dr. Gornall, Wm. Hodgson, of 29, Dickenson-st., a pattern filer, one of the strikers, was charged with assaulting on the 23rd Inst. . Frederick Joseph Percival, an errand boy, living in Academy-st., and employed by Messrs. Richmond and Co., gas stove manufacturers, Academy-st., War- rington. Mr. Browne appeared foy the prosecution and Mr. Longton for the defence. Several members of the Trades Council and some of the strikers were present. Mr. Browne said he was instructed to press the case,and caaracterised the assault as a brutal one. He could have brought other charges against the defendant under the Trades-Protection Act, 1875, but contented himself with the present one. On behalf of the Company he asked the Bench to protect Messrs.Riehmond's employes from these serious annoyances that were being carried on by the men on strike against those employed by the firm. The complainant said he was empleyed by Messrs. Richmond and Co. It was his duty to give out checks to the men as they went into their work. He had given the defendant cheeks every day. He was sent with a telegram to the Mersey-street Post Office, and in Mersey-street, the defendant, without speaking to him, kicked him, and hurt him so that he cried. The defendant did not give any reason why he kicked him. —Mr. Browne : If he had we should have taken other proceedings.—The complainant in answer to Mr. Long- ton, said he was not listening to the defendant's conver- sation, and the defendant did not threaten to kick him if he did not go. Witness used no foul expression to him, and gave him no provocation.—Mr. Ward, manager for Richmond and Co., said he received complaint about Percival being kicked. He applied for a warrant on Wed- tiesday, as instructed by the firm, but the magistrates refused to grant a warrant. The firm had had to have the police patrolling in front of the works for some time.— Mr. Longton said the lad was listening to the defendant's conversation with a friend, which might have been in- teresting to Messrs. Richmond and Co., and hence the defendant lifted his foot to him, not to kick him but to drive him away.—Alfred Barnes, 138, Church-st., stove grate fitter, slid he was with the defendant on the occasion picketing.—Mr. Browne: Are you aware that you are liable to three months' imprisonment for that ? , Witness : I am not.—Witnem corroborated Mr.Longton's

statement as to the boy, and on being pressed by Mr. Browne, suggested that he might have been prompted by the firm .—George William Harbron, employed by Messrs. Richmond and Co., deposed to the lad complaining to him of being assaulted.—The defendant was fined 55., Including costs. Frederick Arnold, of Buttermarket-at., one of the strikers, was then charged before the same magistrates, except Alderman Wright, who had left, with intimidat- ing, also with assaulting Joseph Shipley, one of the new hands employed by Messrs. Richmond and Co.—Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution and Mr. Longton for the defence. Mr. Browne said that subsequent to the offences complained of Shipley received a note, in consequence of which he and other men employed by Messrs. Richmond had to be sent home in a cab. Mr. Browne also remarked that the firm paid as high a rate of wages as any firm in Warrington. In one instance a man got £3 45., and in another a man got £3' Is. Bd., for 44 hours work each. The firm did not care whether men were unionists or not so long as they did their work ; but they did object tip the union men trying to prevent the non-union men from working.—The complainant said he came from Derby on Monday morning to work for the firm in the place of the defendant. He had been out of work 11 months. On Tuesday night he was be- ing seen home to his lodgings, and the defendant ran after him, touched him on the shoulder, pulled him round, shoved him against a window, and getting in front of him prevented him going on. Hetried to per- suade him to join the union, swore at him, and lifted his hand and said "I could "—then stopped. Witness corroborated Mr. Browne as to the receipt of the note. —Mr. Longton :I may say at once that we have not seen that letter as far as we know.—Mr. Btowne said the defendant's name was attached to it, but the handwrit- ing was unknown.—Witness said in consequence of what had happened he would like someone to go home with him.—By Mr. Longton : He had formerly been in the union. He knew the defendant, having worked,and been in a strike with him, at Rotherham. The defend-- ant did not hurt him when he assaulted him. The defendant called him with an oath a monkey, and said "Do you reckon yourself a man ? Why don't you come with me to the union " Witness did not want to press the case.---Some conversation took place between Messrs. Browne and Longton in which the former admitted that Messrs. Richmond and Co. had taken out the summons for intimidation.— Witness said he told the magistrates on Wednesday that he was not hurt or frightened. He would not be afraid of being physically hurt.—John Brimelow, who was in company with the complainant on Tuesday night, con- firmed his state:nent as to the assault.—Mr. Longtou said he did not think, there being no violence used, that the magistrates should be asked to interfere in this dis- pute to assist the masters.—The Chairman : No, we are not asked to do so. On Mr. Longton's ap- peal, Mr. Browne, with the concurrence of the Bench, withdrew the charge of assault.—The Chair- man said the Bench believed there had been assault as well as intimidation. Men had a right to combine for protection, but a man had a right to sell his labour for ss. a week if he liked; and to interfere with him was to interfere with the liberty of the subject.—Mr. Browne: They don't seem to know it is an offence.— Mr. Longton : They know now, I have told them, and it won't be repeated. The Chairman said it was no use imposing a light penalty, as it would be subscribed by others ; and fined the defendant £5 and costs, which was paid by the Union.

div.head: CAUSES OF THE DISPUTE.
div.p: THE CAUSES OF THE DISPUTE.

We have been provided with statements of the dis- pute by Messrs. Richmond and Co., and "By one of the strikers," which are too lengthy to be given in full owing to the pressure upon our columns, " One of the strikers " after enumerating some matters that were in dispute as to the payment for certain classes of work, says that when the men waited upon the manager (Mr. Ward) in a body they were told " If you do not like it, leave it," the fitters then leaving the works in a body. On the Friday following several moulders were told that they must either sever their connection with the Union cr leave the works, and con- sequently they left the works. On the Saturday the remainder of the men connected with the Union were discharged, but were informed that they could all go back as non-Union men. In their statement Messrs. Richmond and Company say that, up to the date of the withdrawal of the men, the directors had neither shewn nor expressed any bias either for or against Unionists or non-Unionists. At the interview with representatives of the men the direc- tor,, in answer to a question of one of the men said that the men might still con- tinue as Unionists making a reservation only against the Stove Grate Workers Union—but upon the condition that all feeling of strife as between them and non-Unionists must be suppressed. This added that the directors feel themselves under an obligation to the new men who wish to remain to keep them in their places.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
A COLLISION AT EARLESTOWN.

At the above Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Wynne Foulkes, a case was heard in which Charles Haseldine, baker of Earlestown, sued John Griffiths, of Ashton-le- Willows, for recovery of £5 16s. 2d. for damage caused to a van through the defendant driving into it with a waggonette at Earlestown, on the 21st of August last. Mr. Longton appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Bolton, of Wigan, for the defendant. Evidence was given by the plaintiff, Annie Haseldine, his little daughter, and Mrs. Hiainbotham, who had been in the habit re- gularly of being driven as a passenger by the defen- dant, and from their account it appeared that the van and the waggonette when the latter was returning from Haydock came in collision at the corner of Market- st., Earlestown, as the waggonette was turning the ! corner. The driver turned somewhat wider than usual, ! so as not to allow room for the van, which was close to the curbstone, and on its proper side. The defendant was going at a trotting rate at the time. The plaintiff plucked at the reins to avoid tbe accident, bet the defendant did not pull up, and no one on the wag- ! gonette shouted • before the collision.—Mr. Rourke, wheelwright, who had repaired the van ''euve evidence as to the damages.—The defendant said the van was three quarters of a yard from the curb, though Robert ilaseldine, a collier, one of the waggonette pas- sengers and a witness for the defendant, said one and a half yards. The defendant asserted that he shouted before the collision, and did not turn more widely than usual. He was not trotting when the collision occur- , red,but had brought the waggonette to a standstill. The ' pole of the waggonette was in the middle of the road. The street was from six to seven yards wide. Robert Haseldine in Ms evidence said the defendant turned very slowly, and was close to the curbstone on the opposite side to the van.—Wm. Haseldine, a boy, said the waggonette ran into the van, and afterwards said the former was at a standstill when the collision occurred. Ultimately he said both conveyances were going slowly at the time.—Wm. Griffiths,the defendant's son, also gave evidence, and Mr. Kenyon a wheelwright, gave it as his opinion that some of the items of damages were excessive, though his evidence was somewhat shaken on this point by Mr. Longton. His Honour gave a verdict for plaintiff for £s6a.

div.head: MR. MORLEY AT READING.
div.p: MR. MORLEY AT READING.

Mr. John Morley was the principal speaker on Wed- nesday evening at a great demonstration held in the Town Hall, Reacling, in connection with the annual meeting of the Home Counties Division of the National Liberal Federation. He devoted his speech mainly to the consideration of the Irish policy of the Government. Referring to the Land Act of last year, which had been vaunted as a great monument of constructive legislation, he compared it to a tombstone, which also was some- times a great monument. He should not be I surprised if a Bill were brought in this Ses- sion to tinker this immortal monument. He dwelt at considerable length on the objections to the Irish Local Government Bill, and quoted largely from Tory news- papers, of which an epitome had been sent to him, to show that the chorus of reprobation was unpreced- entedly unanimous. Mr. Morley went on to say that the general election might perhaps take place in a few weeks, and the Liberals would then have an opportunity of showing their opinion of the Government and all its works. There was an enthusiastic demonstration at the railway station when Mr. Morley left, repeated on a smaller scale at Maidenhead.
THE WIDOW AND THE FICKLE LODGER.

At the Manchester City Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. J. Ileaci lam, stipendiary magistrate, a young man named Richard Crean, vi ho described himself as a striker, of Legli-street, Earlestown, was charged with stealing a watch and chain value £3, the property of Edith Stockton, a widow, living in Rutland-street, Ilulme. In the early part of the present month the prisoner went to lodge with Mrs. Stockton, and before he had been in the house very long began to pay his addresses to the lady. He presented her with an engagement ring, and she accepted him as her second husband. At the end of the first week, however, the prisoner seems te have reconsidered his determination to take the prosecutrix for better or for worse, and de- camped, taking with him the watch and chain, and also forgetting to pay for his lodgings. Mrs. Stock- ton gave information to the police, and Detective Sergeant NI alker traced the prisoner to Earlestown. The police there were communicated with, but the prisoner gave himself up to the Warrington police on Sunday. Replying to the Stipendiary, the pris- oner said the prosecutrix gave him the watch and chain to wear, but this the lady denied. It was further stated that since the 16th the prisoner had married a young woman at Earlestown, with whom he said he had been keeping company for the past eighteen months. Crean produced documents show- ing that he was endeavouring to be.come a member of the Royal Irish Constabulary. The case was adjourned to enable inquiries to be made relative to the antecedents of the prisoner,

Cnorr POST OPFICZ.—In consequence of the continued indisposition of his wife, Mr. Richard Turner, postmas- ter, has resigned his office, and a notice is published, stating that the transaction of money order business at the above office is suspended for the present. Any money order drawn upon the office will be paid on application at the Post-office at Warrington, or the money will be sent if a written application to that effect be madb to the postmaster, enclosing the money order, duly' signed, and giving the postmaster's name and address.

div.head: CADISHEAD,
div.p: CADISHEAD,

ENTererantan.—A public entertainment was-held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Saturday evening. There was a large attendance. Solos were sung by Miss M. Johnson and Mr. P. Marshall. Mrs. Patterson gave a recitation. The Rev. B. Yates addressed the meeting, the subject being "England's drink bill." Mr. A. Gatenby presided over the gathering. A collection was made at the close to meet expenses. ST. Msay's,Catraca.MlSSlON.—ln connection with this place a concert was hela in the schoolroom, on Monday evening. A good programme had been arranged, but it suffered from alteration, one of the artistes being unable to attend. Mrs. Wilmot, Miss Leather, Mr. Wilmot, and Mr. Harding sang" Softly fall the shades of ni,ght "and "Hush thee, my baby." Mr. Alfred Smith played pianoforte solos with taste and expression. Mr. Gregory Harding was effective in " The Wolf." " The. Sexton, and " The Diver." Miss Leather contributed "Strangers yet" and "This work-a-aav world." Mr. S. Green recited "The Lifeboat " and "The Bella of Lee" with force and expression. Miss Florence C. Taylor rendered "Tit for Tat "' and " When the heart is young,:' being recalled for each. Mr. Samuel Stott was very successful in his selections on the violin, each piece being encored. Mr. Green contributed "English, you know," and as an encore, " You can't think of everything." The.concert was fairly attended, considering the- stare of the weather.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

THE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION.—The election of a County Councillor to represent the Lymm electoral division will take place on Saturday, the sth March. Nominations must be delivered at the Local Board offices, before five o'clock in the afternoon, on Friday, the 26th February. Mr. F. A. Janion, deputy returning officer for the division, will-attend at the. Board offiees to-day (Saturday), between two and four o'clock, to hear and decide objections to nomination papers.

div.head: ITMA2 LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: ITMA2 LIBERAL CLUB.

The annual soirde in connection with this club, was held in the Congregational schoolroom, Lymm, on Tues- day evening. After an excellent tea had been partaken of by about 260 persons, a capital programme, consisting of solos, duets, and recitations, was gone through. Mr. Dutton presided, and he was supported on the platform by Mr. T. B. Leadam- (the Liberal conciliate for the division), Messrs. Stvanivick, G. L. Welford„ G.. IL Watson, F. S. Graff, A. Shelmerdine, W..Daviess and the Revs. C. Clay and G.. H. Southall.—The Chairman in introducing the candidate, said thlt the result of the by-electionsshOuldencourage the Liberals of the division A striking example was the Rossendale election. (Ap- plause.) Another good reason 'for rejoicing was the fact of the diminishing majority of the Conservatives in the House of Commons. He thought that they might fairly assume that their opponents were getting to the end of their tether. (Cheers.)—Mr. Leadam, who met with a cordial reception, said he had no doubt that they. had all read, in books of travel,_ how travellers driving across the icy steppes or the plains of Russia are at times pur- sued by wolves, and how, when the hungry pack ap- proached nearer and nearer„the travellers threw out to the wolves, one by one, such burdens as might servo to lighten their vehicles, and., how too often it happened that their efforts to escape were unavailing when the wolves overtook them. That allegory might apply to the present Government.. The previous night they saw the last sacrifice made by the. Tory party of their fine old- fashioned principles„with the hope of averting the venge- ance of the Liberal wolves which had been, so long in pursuit. Mr. Chaplin abandoned his. hostility to small holdings. The abandonment of the Tory opposition to the small holdings was the last of the Tory principles which had been thrown over during the, last five years. Mr. Balfour had introduced, into the House of Commons a fine old Tory measure, which he called his Irish Local Self-Government BBL No one spoke or thought about that Bill now without a smile. This Irish County Council Bill, ha thought,, might be more fitly named the Irish County Council Coercion Bill. There was quite a difference between English local self- government and the proposed Irish local government. In the proposed tneasure there was a device by which the councils could be packed like the juries, or sup- pressed when there was a Liberal majority. The speaker then said that the Liberal cause in the Altrincham divi- sion was going ahead like a house on fire. Every day the Liberal party waxed stronger, and the Conservative party got weaker. 'Rite. Conservative candidate was .very much where he was. Be continued to dance, al- though they declared that the empire was in danger. More than one lady had,however„told him (Mr. Lead/1m) that Mr. Disraeli does not dance well. (Laughter.) Mr. Leadam also informed those present that he would never solicit a vote. He believed that to do so was, to some extent, a Violation of the law. The dissoltitiob, he thought, would take place some time in March. The Tories could not carry on the trick of not paying their debts any longer. When the dissolution came it meant the "crack of doom" for the Conservative party in the Altrincham division. (Cheers.) The following are the names of those who contributed towards the evening's enjoyment :—Mr. Payton' Mrs. Haydock, Mr. Faye, Mr. bunkerley, Miss Brown, Miss Bardley, Mr. Wallington, Mr. Everton, jun., Mr. Roberts, and Mr. Ford.

div.head: SVPPOSED SUICIDE OF A WARRINGTON
div.p: SVPPOSED SUICIDE OF A WARRINGTON

MAN. Yesterday, the body of Thomas Woreley, puddler, living at 69, Haydock-st., Warrington, was found in a shed on Mr. •Bennett's farm, off Manchester- road, at Padgate, with the throat cut. The deceased it is supposed had committed suicide. He was bound over at the police court some months ago for attempting to cut his throat. He had been missed from home for a few days, and was last seen going in the direction of Dobby's Locks, where the water was dragged, under the supposition that he might have drowned himself.

FRODSHAM DIVISION. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Having been requested by a number of electors of the above division to accept the position of candidate for the County Council, I beg to leave to place 'my services at your disposal. If you do me the honour to elect me, I shall feel it to be my duty to assist at all times in a good and economical management of county business. Being a large ratepayer myself. I feel very keenly the way in which county rates have increased during the last three years, being now nearly double what they were. I therefore hope I may soon have an opportunity of helping ta arrest this increase, and doing all I can for the benefit of ratepayers, great and small, in the county. As I believe lam pretty well known in the division, and held meetings mall parts of it three years ago excepting Frodsham, I don't purpose at present repeating them ; neither do I wish to embarrass any electors by asking for votes which they prefer to give to another ; but I hope,on the day of election, that all my friends will give me their support, and what assistance they can in bringing others to the poll. I have the honour to remain, Your obedient servant, THOMAS BAXTER. Dutton Hall, Feb. 10th. 1892.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS. RUNCORN NORTH ELECTORAL DIVISION. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Yout District Liberal Association having unanimously asked me to offer myself as Candidate at the forthcoming Election, I have great pleasure in:doing so, and trust that by your good will and active assistance I may have the honour of representing my native town in our County Parliament. If I am returned as your Member I shall endeavour on all occas- ions to watch over and promote the Interests of this division, and as a man of business keep a watchful eye on the expendi- ture of the County Rates. I shall also give my earnest attention to the administration of the varied business under the control of the Council, and trust that if elected my attendance and action may show that your confidence in me as your representative has not been misplaced. It is difficult, within the limits of an ordinary advertise- ment.to refer to all the questions coming or likely to come under the notice of the Council, but I hope before the day of Blection to have several opportunities of a more extended reference to them and also the pleasure of making your personal acquaintance. Faithfully yours, WILLIAM OCKLBSTON. Halton-road. Runcorn. February 18th. 1892.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE RUNCORN NORTH ELECTORAL DIVISION. LADIES AND GENTLEDIEN,— Three years ago you honoured me by electing me your Representative on the County Council, and I venture again to appeal to you for your votes and interest at the ap- proaching Election. I solicit yeur support on the same lines as I did previously —as an Independent Candidate—believing that the business of the Council is best conducted without the introduction of politics and my constant aim has been to serve the Division without respect to Party. If elected I hope to pursue in the future the same policy. I am strongly in favour of the proposed roadway across the Hersey, believing it will considerably bfnefit both Counties. Any measure having in view the adoption and maintenance of all main roads as county roads shall have my careful con- sideration and support, Technical Education shall have my best attention, but I feel that the dispotial of the grants will want careful attention. Should it be your pleasure to again elect me I will do my utmost to protect your interests and advance the prosperity of this important Division. I am, L Idles and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, C. W. HAZLEHURST, Runcorn, Februar y 18th,1892.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE SOUTH DIVISION OF RUNCORN. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Three years ago you did me the honour of return lag me as your first representative in the Cheshire County Council. Having endeavoured to serve you diligently and faithfully during that period, I venture again to ask for your renewed confidence and support. It is impossible, within the limits of a brief address, to deal with the various matters which have engaged the atten- tion of the Council, but I may be permitted to refer to one or two which more immediately concern the town and neigh- bourhood of Runcorn. By the Customs and Excise ActlB9o, a large sum of money was placed at the disposal of the Council 'for the purposes of Technical and Annual Instruction. As a member of the committee charged with the distribution of that fund, I have endeavoured to utilize it to the beet advantage, in providing effics..nt commercialand technical Instruction for all classes I of the community. An annual grant of £220 has already been made to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners by the County Council, and I would use my best endeavours to obtain from the same source a substantial grant towards the erection of a Technical Institute in Runcorn, so that the town may possess a w wthy building in which to carry on its educational operations. The question of the County roads has also received my attention, and it is gratifying to know that there is every probabilltyof the main road leadiag from Halton boundary to Runeorn Railway Station being at an early date either taken over by the County Council or made the subject of an annual grantby the Council, either of which would mean a saving to the ratepayers of Runcorn of about £2OO per annum. At the last meeting of the Council a resolution. which I had the honour to move, was carried appointing a committee to report upon the question—of vital importance to Runcorn— of a vehicular bridge across the Mersey, connecting the towns of Runcorn and Widnes, thus affording a valuable- means of inter-communication between the Counties of Lan- cashire and Cheshire. This scheme has my heartiest sup- port, and no effort on my past would be wanting to make the desired means of communication an accomplished fact. 1 In thus appealing for your suffrages, I do so on purely independent lines. I seek to enter the Council untram- melled by ties of party or sect, and if returned I shall con- sider all questions, from whence and by whom introduced, from the single standpoint of an Independent ratepayer, anxious only to secure the happiness and well-being of his fellow-citizens, and the industrial and commercial pros- perity Of the County In which their lot is cast. I have the honour to remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, PHILIP SPEAKMAN. The Mount, Higher Runcorn, February 17th, 1892.

LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON-IN- MAKERFIRLD DIVISION. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Having received a numerously signed requisition from rate- payers of all political opinions in the Division inviting me. to become your representative on the County Council, I have considered it my duty to accede to the request, and I have pleasure in placing my services at your disposal. My long residence among you and personal knowledge of the requirements of the Division will enable me to protect and promote your interests on all occasions. If I am honoured by your confidence and support my earnest endeavour will always be to advance your prosperity and well-being. am, Ladles and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, CHARLES B. F. EORRON. Wargrave, February 25th, 1892.
